So the first pass measures an over-estimate and over-removes: with the default 20 MiB bound and ~1 MiB request images, a conversation with 15 request images (≈20 MiB base64) but 2 MiB masters budgets 40 MiB and trims the oldest ones anyway. Only after the trimmed set is materialized does the exact second pass (line 236-241) run — on messages that have already had images irreversibly replaced with placeholders.

The DeepSeek adapter got this right: it passes `representation: 'raw'` for the estimate and a `byteLength` against the exact request version (`llm-deepseek/src/adapter.ts:537-544`). pi-ai inlines every image into every request body, so the over-trim shows up as lost conversation images for long image-heavy sessions.

findings.title: Stale-file retry fires on any HTTP status whose body merely mentions a file id — a non-retriable INVALID_REQUEST becomes a duplicate upload plus an immediate re-send
findings.detail:
`staleFile` is computed as `usedFiles.length > 0 && providerRejectedFileId(detail)` with no status gate. `providerRejectedFileId` only pattern-matches the joined `code`/`type`/`message` text (`/\bfile.../` + `/expired|not found|deleted|.../`) — so a 429 or 500 whose message happens to contain "file" and "not found" (a proxy/gateway error mentioning files, a rate-limit detail quoting the request path, etc.) is classified as a stale file id.

The recovery then (a) invalidates the *correct* cached mapping and (b) `continue`s the request loop with `body` unchanged. Nothing between the offload at line 537 and `JSON.stringify(body)` at line 601 re-runs when `representation` is still `'file'`, and the cached id has just been deleted from the local index — so `ensureUploaded` re-uploads the identical image. The POST is then re-issued with the same payload. If it fails again, `fileAttempt === 1` drops out of the branch and throws.

Net effect on one misclassified transient error: one wasted full image upload plus one duplicated POST — a double cost for a failure that was never retryable. `providerRejectedNormalizedImage` (line 646) correctly gates on `response.status === 400`; the stale-file path should carry an equivalent status gate.

findings.title: SDK `session/prompt` commits caller-supplied `contentBlocks` verbatim as a durable user message with no content validation
findings.detail:
`handleRequest` dispatches `params as unknown as SessionPromptParams` and `prompt()` then does `createUserMessage({ content: params.contentBlocks, source: { kind: 'user' } })`. `createUserMessage`/`createMessage` (`llm/src/message.ts:192-200`) only brand an id and deep-freeze — they do not validate the block vocabulary, roles, or nesting. The blocks go straight into the durable session log and later into every model request.

A `contentBlocks` payload containing a `{ type: 'tool-result', toolCallId: <any id>, content: [...], isError: false }` block is therefore admitted as a *user* message and reaches the model as an authoritative tool result for a call the model never made — the prompt-injection surface this cluster hunts for. `initialize`'s fields are equally unchecked (`this.model = params.model`, `this.cwd = resolve(params.cwd)` — a non-string cwd reaches `path.resolve` and throws a raw TypeError instead of a JSON-RPC invalid-params).

This is a real asymmetry: the ACP bridge validates the same boundary (`acp/src/content.ts:132-148` rejects unsupported block types before building the message) and the SDK protocol types claim `{ sessionId: string; contentBlocks: ContentBlock[] }`, but nothing on the wire enforces it. Some validation mirroring `admitAcpPrompt`'s closed-union switch belongs here.

findings.title: Loopback classifier accepts non-canonical IPv6 spellings and IPv4-mapped IPv6, widening the Host fence in a loopback-only deployment
findings.detail:
`isLoopbackHostname` special-cases exactly the strings `'localhost'` and `'[::1]'`. WHATWG URL also emits bracketed `'[::ffff:127.0.0.1]'` for a request to `http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/...`, and the IPv4 branch only checks `parts.length === 4 && parts[0] === '127'` with a regex of 1-3 digits per octet — so `'127.000.000.001'`, `'127.0.0.001'`, `'127.0.00.1'` and `'127.00.0.1'` all return true. All of those are legal, distinct `Host` header spellings; every one of them passes the fence.

This matters most where `isTrustedApiRequest` is called with an empty trust list, which is the loopback pinning of the whole privileged plane (`PRIVILEGED_METHODS` in `client/connection/src/index.ts:145-148`, and the `'loopback'` authority in `rpc-host.ts:82`). For a rebound page served over plain HTTP there is no Origin and no Fetch-Metadata on navigations and image reads, so the Host check is the entire defence and it is what a rebinding attacker writes. The IPv6-mapped case is the sharper one: on an IPv6-capable stack `::ffff:127.0.0.1` is a routable form of loopback that a resolver can name.

Compare `assertTrustedAuthority` (`api-request-trust.ts:54-58`), which deliberately refuses anything WHATWG would rewrite precisely because a non-canonical spelling must "fail the load loudly instead of being ignored until requests 403 or quietly changing the grant". The loopback predicate has no such normalization.

findings.title: bridge() does not contain a rejection from apiHandler.fetch — the shared /api carrier surfaces carrier faults as HTTP 400
findings.detail:
`bridge` awaits `apiHandler.fetch(request)` with no try/catch, so a rejection escapes to the webserver's per-request catch, which logs and answers `res.writeHead(400)` when headers are not yet sent (and `res.destroy()` when they are). `apiHandler` is the shared fetch handler composed by `createSharedFetchHandler`, whose non-intercepted path is the whole apiProxy (`rpc-host.ts:79` -> `toFetchHandler(apiProxy)`). Any carrier-level throw — a session that no longer resolves, a bad payload shape the two-level parse rejects by throwing, an abort — is therefore reported to the browser as **400 Bad Request**, i.e. the client's own fault, instead of a 500 or a protocol error envelope.

The downstream symptom is already visible on the browser side: `createWebConnectionRpc.call` throws `transport failure for ${channel}/${endpoint}: HTTP 400` (`client/rpc.ts:44-46`), losing the rpcId-correlated envelope entirely. Mid-stream (SSE downlinks share this bridge) the webserver instead destroys the socket with no error frame.

The bridge already owns an `AbortController` and is the module that documents "carrier vs business" separation; a try/catch around the fetch that emits a 500/envelope before the SSE body starts would keep host faults off the client's tab.
findings.evidence:
const response = await apiHandler.fetch(request)
  res.writeHead(response.status, Object.fromEntries(response.headers.entries()))

findings.title: closeBlock synthesizes `CallId('')` instead of a per-block identity when a tool call arrives with no id
findings.detail:
A tool-call block opened because the wire carried `tool_calls` deltas but never a `call.id` assembles to `{ id: CallId(''), name: block.name ?? '', ... }`. `CallId('')` is an empty string that survives `createMessage`/`deepFreeze` into the durable log and into the agent loop, where tool results are correlated by call id — two such blocks collide, and every subsequent tool-result message for the second call lands on the first.

`BlockAssembler.assemble` handles exactly this case by synthesizing a stable per-index id (`llm/src/assembler.ts:126`: `id: partial.toolCallId ?? CallId(`call-${index}`)`), and the same file's sibling `name: block.name ?? ''` silently permits an unnamed tool call with no diagnostic. The OpenAI-compatible wire does send `call.id` on the first delta, so this needs a non-conforming gateway/proxy — but the module is explicitly written at a network trust boundary ("Defensive: fields that the MCP spec declares required ... are guarded with fallbacks because this is a network trust boundary" appears across this cluster), and the analogous empty-credential case in the same package is hard-failed via `assertUsableApiKey` rather than passed through.

findings.title: Handler throw on a shared RPC channel answers a bare-text HTTP 500 instead of a server-response envelope
findings.detail:
`rpcFetchHandler` catches a rejection from `handler(...)` and returns `new Response(`handler failure: ${String(error)}`, { status: 500 })` — plain text, not `{ type: 'server-response', rpcId, result }`.

Two concrete consequences: (1) `client/rpc.ts` only builds the `RpcResult` from a parseable envelope, so the caller sees `transport failure for ...: HTTP 500` and loses the rpcId correlation the protocol exists to provide; (2) `String(error)` renders a non-Error throw as `[object Object]`, discarding the message. The typert gateway itself is well-behaved (`rpcFailure` in `api/gateway/src/index.ts:639-657` converts every throw into `{ ok: false, error }`), so this only bites handlers registered by other plugins on `ctx.connection.rpc.handle` — but that is a public registration seam with no contract enforcement, and the module already has `errorResponse(rpcId, error)` two functions below that could carry a synthetic rpcId.

`rpcFetchHandler` also has no request-signal propagation guard: the `request.signal` passed to `handler` is the bridge's abort controller, which is fine, but the 500 path does not distinguish an abort from a real failure.

findings.title: One unadmittable image in an MCP result collapses every image block to the same generic diagnostic
findings.detail:
`prepareImageProjection`'s final `catch` (the `attachments.saveImages(decoded)` path) projects *every* image block through `block => ({ type: 'text', text: imageDiagnostic(block, reason) })`, dropping the `index` argument. When the batch fails, every image in the result therefore gets the identical reason string, so the model has no way to tell which of N images was rejected by admission.

The function already threads `index` correctly in the two earlier branches (`validationErrors.get(index)`, and `byIndex.get(index)`), and `imageDiagnostic(block, reason)` renders `block.mimeType` — so with one bad image among several, all N lines read the same mime type and the same reason, actively misinforming about which bytes were refused. Passing `(block, index)` and reporting the per-index reason where `saveImages` provides one (or explicitly naming that the batch is all-or-nothing) would keep the diagnostic honest.

find:cf-llm.summary:
Overall the cluster is unusually well-hardened: the LLM seam, DeepSeek adapter, pi-ai adapter, LSP framing/translation, gateway reflection boundary, and the client Host trust fence all show deliberate threat modelling (closed-union switches, structural guards on every wire payload, credential snapshots bound to endpoints, exact rpcId echo discipline, JSON-safety asserts on every typert argument and result). I found no exploitable secret leak, no sandbox escape, and no data-loss path.

The gaps that survived verification cluster around one theme: defensive code that is *structurally* thorough but *numerically* or *terminologically* under-constrained at the boundary with an untrusted peer. The highest-impact one is MCP `tools/list` pagination, where trusting an external server's cursor unbounds a loop that plugin activation and host unload both await — a third-party process can wedge the harness indefinitely. The LSP connection drops string-id JSON-RPC responses (JSON-RPC-legal) and, because the resulting hang is an abort rather than a transport failure, the poisoned instance is never evicted from the workspace pool. Two adapter issues are cost bugs rather than correctness bugs: pi-ai's first offload pass budgets against master attachment bytes instead of request bytes, over-trimming images by roughly 4x, and DeepSeek's stale-file recovery fires on any status whose body merely mentions a file, duplicating an upload and a POST for a failure that was never retriable.

On the trust boundary, the SDK JSON-RPC server is the weakest link: it casts wire params with `as unknown as` and commits caller-supplied `contentBlocks` straight into the durable session log, so a caller can inject a forged `tool-result` block — the exact prompt-injection surface the brief targets — while the sibling ACP bridge validates the same shape properly. The stdio transport it sits on writes frames fire-and-forget with no 'error' listener, so a broken parent pipe becomes an uncaught EPIPE crash rather than a clean exit. Finally, `isLoopbackHostname` accepts non-canonical IPv6 and zero-padded IPv4 spellings of 127.0.0.1, which is the sole Host fence for the loopback-pinned privileged method set on plain HTTP; the adjacent `assertTrustedAuthority` already refuses exactly this class of spelling elsewhere in the same package.

The remaining findings (http-bridge's uncontained handler rejection, the bare-text 500 on shared RPC channels, the empty synthesized tool-call id, and the collapsed per-image MCP diagnostic) are narrower but share the same shape: a failure path that reaches the wrong layer or loses the one piece of information the next consumer needed. None of them block shipping; the MCP pagination bound, the LSP string-id case, and the SDK content validation are the three worth fixing first.

findings.title: QUANT_AVX2 is never defined for any TU — the entire AVX2 kernel set is dead code in every build
findings.detail: cmake/arch.cmake sets QUANT_AVX2 as a CMake *variable* and configure_file() writes it into build/quant_config.h via `#cmakedefine`, but **no source file anywhere includes that header** (grep for `config.h` includes across include/src/tools/bench/tests returns nothing), and compiler.cmake only adds `-mavx2`/`/arch:AVX2` flags — it never passes `-DQUANT_AVX2`. Every `#if defined(QUANT_AVX2)` in src/math is therefore false, so math_avx2.cpp, math_avx2_vec.cpp and math_avx2_tiled.cpp compile to empty translation units and the scalar math.cpp is the live implementation on every platform, including MSVC x64 where arch.cmake explicitly forces AVX2 "ON". build/quant_config.h confirms it: `/* #undef QUANT_AVX2 */`. Consequences: (a) all AVX2-named benchmarks (bench_kernels.cpp:66/72/192) silently time the scalar path; (b) the project ships no AVX2 math despite 3 source files and a dedicated cmake arch-detection function; (c) every latent bug in those files is invisible until someone "fixes" the config and suddenly enables hundreds of lines of never-executed code. Related inconsistency: math_avx512.cpp guards on `__AVX512F__` (compiler-defined, so it IS live when QUANT_AVX512 is on) while its AVX2 siblings guard on a macro nothing defines.
findings.evidence:
cmake/compiler.cmake:23:  if(QUANT_AVX2)
    add_compile_options(-mavx2 -mavx -mbmi2 -mfma)
  endif()   # <-- no -DQUANT_AVX2

build/quant_config.h:7: /* #undef QUANT_AVX2 */

src/math/math_avx2_tiled.cpp:9:  #if defined(QUANT_AVX2)   // always false
src/math/math_avx2_tiled.cpp:568: #else // !QUANT_AVX2 — scalar fallbacks  // always taken

findings.title: AdamW (and ZeRO's copy) bias correction is wrong — updates are sqrt(bias_corr2)x too small during warmup
findings.detail: The update is written as `lr_adj = lr * sqrt(bc2) / bc1` applied to `m / (sqrt(v/bc2) + eps)`. Expanding: this equals lr*(m/bc1) * bc2 / (sqrt(v) + eps*sqrt(bc2)), whereas the correct AdamW step lr*(m/bc1)/(sqrt(v/bc2)+eps) equals lr*(m/bc1)*sqrt(bc2)/(sqrt(v)+eps*sqrt(bc2)). The ratio of implemented to correct is sqrt(bc2). With the default beta2=0.999 at t=1, bc2=0.001 so every parameter update is ~31.6x too small, converging toward correct only as t grows. AdamW is the default optimizer for Trainer::compile (trainer_core.cpp:201,1261), finetune.cpp:18, agi_extended.cpp:254 and tools/train.cpp — so the entire warmup phase of every training run is numerically wrong in a way that looks like "training is just slow to converge" rather than a crash. The identical formula is duplicated in ZeroOptimizer::step (zero_optimizer_core.cpp:222,244), so the ZeRO path has the same defect.

findings.title: DistributedContext keeps reduce_buffer_ and the barrier per-instance, so multi-rank TP/FSDP/DDP never actually reduce
findings.detail: reduce_buffer_, reduce_mutex_, barrier_mutex_, barrier_count_ and barrier_gen_ are all non-static members of DistributedContext (distributed.h:40-52). The only configuration in which the primitive works is the one tests/test_all.cpp:77-95 exercises: a *single* shared context object driven by N threads, which is why that test passes. Every production wrapper instead constructs its own — TensorParallelManager::ctx_, DistributedDataParallel::ctx_, FullyShardedDataParallel::ctx_ — and, worse, five call sites build a **fresh context per invocation**: tensor_parallelism.cpp:374 (ColumnParallelLinear::forward), :430 (RowParallelLinear::forward), :505 (HeadPartitioner::sync_output), :536/:544 (SequenceParallel::gather/allreduce), and fsdp.cpp:679 (FSDPBlock::sync_gradients). A fresh object's barrier_count_ starts at 0 and its reduce_buffer_ is private, so with world_size>1 the first thread waits forever for world_size-1 arrivals that no one else can ever produce — a hang, not a wrong answer. Even if callers instead gave each rank its own long-lived context, the private reduce_buffer_ means each rank sums its own data into its own buffer and reads it back: a silent no-op. fsdp.cpp:601-606 already documents this exact hazard for gather_and_install and "fixed" it by special-casing world_size<=1, but the identical pattern is left live in sync_gradients and all five tensor_parallelism sites. Net effect: no configuration of this codebase performs a real cross-rank reduction; DDP/TP/FSDP training is either a hang or an unsharded single-process run.

findings.title: gemm_tiled's AVX2 micro-kernel computes only 16 of the tile's N columns — 75% of every output tile is wrong
findings.detail: TILE_N is 64 (include/quant/math_tiled.h:17) and gemm_tiled tiles N in strides of TILE_N, so n_tile is typically 64. It then dispatches to the 6x16 micro-kernel whenever n_tile >= 16 (line 348). But micro_6x16_ab (and its _atb/_abt/_atbt variants at :132/:160/:190) has no inner column loop at all — per k it loads exactly b0 = B[k*ldb+0..7] and b1 = B[k*ldb+8..15] and stores exactly 16 floats back to C. Columns 16..n_tile-1 are never read from B and never written to C, so they keep whatever beta*C left there. I compiled a verbatim copy of micro_6x16_ab with clang++ -mavx2 -mfma and ran it at M=6,K=64,N=64 (the shape bench_gemm_tiled.cpp checks): 288 of 384 output entries are wrong, max_abs_err=7.98 versus a 1e-4 tolerance. bench_gemm_tiled.cpp:26-38 has a parity gate that would catch this, but per finding #1 the AVX2 file is not compiled today, so the gate only ever exercises the correct scalar path and the bench reports PARITY_OK. The moment QUANT_AVX2 is correctly defined this becomes a silent 75%-wrong GEMM in the inference hot path.

findings.title: vec_fp16_to_fp32 decodes subnormals 4x too small, and the AVX2 copy has the same bug in its scalar tail
findings.detail: For an FP16 subnormal (exp==0, mant!=0) the value is mant * 2^-24. The code computes `m = mant/1024.0f` (mant * 2^-10) then multiplies by 1.5258789e-5f (2^-16), giving mant * 2^-26 — a factor of 4 too small. The encoder in the same file is correct: vec_fp32_to_fp16 (line 525-527) shifts by (1-exp) and >>13, which round-trips 2^-24 to code 1, so encode and decode are asymmetric and any weight below ~6.1e-5 is silently shrunk. This is on a live path: src/codec/quant_engines_fp.cpp:415,421,441 call these for the FP16 weight engine, so small-magnitude quantized weights decode at a quarter of their true value. math_avx2_vec.cpp:531 repeats the same formula for the n%8 scalar tail after an F16C main loop, so in an AVX2 build the conversion is correct for the first n-(n%8) elements and 4x wrong for the last up-to-7, i.e. the result depends on n mod 8. Note math_avx2_vec.cpp is currently dead (finding #1), so today the fully-broken scalar version in math.cpp is what runs.

findings.title: DDPMode::ASYNC self-deadlocks: sync_gradients and its own worker thread both lock the same non-recursive mutex
findings.detail: sync_gradients() takes async_mutex_ whenever mode_ == ASYNC (line 104-106), and async_sync_loop() takes async_mutex_ (line 353) immediately before calling sync_gradients() (line 354). std::mutex is not recursive, so the worker thread locks it, re-enters sync_gradients, and blocks forever on its own lock. This fires on the first loop iteration — 10ms after construction — and only when world_size > 1, because the `world_size_ <= 1` early-return at line 102 masks it otherwise. So ASYNC mode appears to work in every single-process smoke test and hangs immediately in any real multi-rank run. The constructor at line 18-21 starts the thread unconditionally, and ~DistributedDataParallel (line 25-28) then join()s it, so even a teardown path hangs. The mutex also does nothing useful for correctness: sync_gradients only holds it while calling sync_gradients's own body, providing no exclusion against a concurrent user-called sync_gradients.

findings.title: ZeroOptimizer::reduce_scatter_grads never clears comm_buffer_ between parameters, so every gradient accumulates all previous ones
findings.detail: The loop over parameters accumulates each rank's gradient into the shared static comm_buffer_ at indices [0,n) and reads the sum back, but never zeroes the buffer before the next parameter. comm_buffer_ is a static member that persists across calls, and `resize(n, 0.0f)` only zero-fills *newly grown* elements, so the values from parameter i remain in place when parameter i+1 is processed. Parameter 0 gets a correct all-reduce; parameter 1 gets (its own reduce) + (parameter 0's reduce); parameter k gets the sum of the reduces of parameters 0..k. The pollution also never resets between steps, so the error grows monotonically for the life of the process. The final `p->grad().zero_()` for non-owners (line 209-210) masks nothing — the owning rank applies a gradient that is a mixture of many unrelated parameters. Contrast internal_reduce_scatter (line 294), which does `std::fill(...)` after use, confirming the omission here is an oversight rather than a design choice. Note the comment at :184 says "reduce-scatter" but this is an all-reduce followed by zeroing, not a scatter.

findings.title: internal_all_gather writes world_size x local_bytes into a buffer sized for local_bytes — heap overflow on any multi-rank use
findings.detail: internal_all_gather is documented (zero_optimizer.h:152) as taking a `float* local_data` sized local_bytes, and its only caller, all_gather_params (line 298-317), passes exactly that: `float* local_data = param->data<float>(); int64_t byte_count = n * sizeof(float);` where n is the parameter's own numel. The gather phase then loops r over all world_size ranks and does `memcpy(local_data + r*local_floats, &comm_buffer_[r*local_floats], local_bytes)` — writing local_bytes at offsets 0, local_bytes, 2*local_bytes ... (world_size-1)*local_bytes. Only the r==0 write lands in bounds; the remaining world_size-1 writes run off the end of the Tensor's allocation, corrupting whatever the refcounted Buffer's heap neighbours are. For any parameter and any world_size>1 this is an out-of-bounds write of (world_size-1) * param_bytes. The correct contract needs a destination buffer of local_bytes*world_size, or the gather should copy into a caller-supplied global tensor (as DistributedContext::all_gather at distributed.cpp:103-123 does).

findings.title: AVX2 gelu/geglu approximate erf with an order-9 Taylor series that diverges for |x| > ~3
findings.detail: gelu (line 283-299), geglu (line 645-660) and the tiled apply_gelu (math_avx2_tiled.cpp:425-441) compute erf via the truncated Maclaurin series x - x^3/3 + x^5/10 - x^7/42 + x^9/216. This alternating series is only accurate for small argument; the first neglected term is ~x^11/(11!!) which already contributes ~0.02 of error at x=2 and swamps the sum by x=3.5. At v=4.95 (x = v/sqrt(2) = 3.5) the partial sum evaluates to 1+erf ~ 167 instead of ~2, so gelu returns ~413 instead of ~4.95 — a ~83x error on the activation output, not a precision loss but a completely wrong value. GELU pre-activations routinely reach |x| in this range, so any model using GELU would produce garbage in exactly the regime where the activation's tail behaviour matters most. The scalar math.cpp:113 and the non-AVX2 tiled path correctly call std::erf, so this is a divergence between the two implementations that a parity test would catch if the AVX2 file were compiled (see finding #1). No argument reduction (e.g. |x|>2.5 -> clamp to 1.0) is present.

findings.title: Non-AVX2 gemm_tiled_act / gemm_tiled_bias_act silently drop GELU and SiLU, and both paths overrun C by ldc-M rows
findings.detail: The scalar fallback branch (the `#else` at line 568, which is the branch that actually compiles today per finding #1) handles only Activation::ReLU. GELU and SiLU fall through with no action and no warning, so a caller requesting SiLU gets a plain linear GEMM result — a silent wrong answer rather than an error. The same two functions in the AVX2 branch are correct on activation choice but share a second bug: apply_activation(C, M * ldc, act) at line 483 and :500 applies the activation across M*ldc contiguous floats. When ldc > N (padded/strided C) that walks into the row padding, and when the caller passes an ldc larger than the allocated row stride it reads and writes past the end of C. The scalar path has the identical `for (int64_t i = 0; i < M * ldc; i++)` at :657/:661. The loop should be per-row over N columns, not a flat M*ldc sweep. The tensor-level wrappers at :554/:562 pass C.numel() (correct) but the raw-pointer API — the one bench_kernels.cpp:385 uses — hits the broken form.

findings.title: Bucket::numel is never assigned by build_buckets, silently disabling TOP_K compression and corrupting the FP8 path
findings.detail: build_buckets() sets `current.size` (size_t) and `current.buffer` for each bucket but never touches `Bucket::numel` (include/quant/ddp.h:21), which therefore stays at its default 0 for every bucket in every DDP instance. allreduce_bucket keys both compression branches on it: the TOP_K_SPARSE guard `bucket.numel > 0` (line 132) is permanently false, so sparse compression silently degrades to a plain all-reduce with no indication that the requested compression is not in effect; and the FP8_QUANT branch allocates `std::vector<uint8_t> compressed(bucket.numel)` (line 140) — a zero-length vector — then loops `for (i = 0; i < bucket.numel; i++) buf[i] += (float)((int8_t)compressed[i]) * scale;` which does nothing, and finally divides every gradient by world_size (line 150-151) without ever having summed them. The result under FP8_QUANT is each rank's local gradient scaled by 1/world_size and never combined across ranks — a silently wrong training run. The standard all-reduce at :154 also passes `bucket.numel` (=0) as the element count, so even the non-compressed path is a no-op. The fix is to set `current.numel = current_numel` alongside `current.size` at lines 68 and 79, or to use `bucket.size` consistently.

findings.title: math::max() unconditionally loads 8 floats, reading up to 7 floats past the end for any tensor with fewer than 8 elements
findings.detail: max() guards only against an empty tensor (QUANT_CHECK(n > 0)), then does `__m256 mxv = _mm256_loadu_ps(p);` — an unconditional 8-float load at index 0 — and starts the loop counter at i=8. For any tensor with n in [1,7] this reads 8-n floats beyond the end of the Buffer. Small tensors are ubiquitous (scalars, per-head norms, 1-D gates, rank-1 slices), so this is an out-of-bounds read on a very common path, and because AlignedAllocator over-allocates it usually appears as a silent wrong max rather than a crash: the horizontal reduce at :607-611 folds in whatever bytes follow the allocation, so max() can return a value that is not present in the tensor. The scalar math.cpp:324-331 version is correct (starts from p[0] and iterates i=1..n). The correct AVX2 form needs a masked load or a scalar prologue for n<8, mirroring how gemv/dot handle their tails. Currently latent because the file is not compiled (finding #1).

findings.title: ImageNetClassifier's feature-dim fallback branch is dead-on-arrival: it always throws
findings.detail: feat_dim is computed as `feat.numel() / B` on the line above, so by construction `feat_dim != 768` is logically equivalent to `feat.numel() != B*768`. The branch then calls `feat.reshape({B, 768})`, and Tensor::reshape (src/core/tensor.cpp:176-179) is `QUANT_CHECK(new_shape.numel() == shape_.numel(), "reshape: size mismatch"); return view(new_shape);`. So whenever the condition is true, the numel check fails and the call aborts. The only way to reach the reshape without throwing is the case where it is provably unnecessary. Any ViT whose patch projection emits a feature width other than the hard-coded 768 — the exact scenario the `(feat_dim != 768)` guard was written to handle — aborts the process instead of degrading. The loop below (:192-198) also hard-codes `768` for the reduction, so even a successful reshape would be wrong for a genuinely different width; the real fix is to reject or adapt to the actual feat_dim rather than to reshape into a fixed constant.

find:tf-misc.summary:
Reviewed the math, trainer, multimodal, AGI, tools and bench clusters, deep-reading ~25 files. The cluster's own defensive work is visible and largely good (many "BUGFIX (bug census)" notes had already fixed real defects — Adafactor's i/d1 SIGFPE, Adabound's signed-step clipping, ParameterServer's ABBA and self-deadlocks, the DDP barrier generation bug), but the review found 12 defects that survived, several of them severe.

The most serious is architectural: QUANT_AVX2 is a CMake variable that is written into a generated header nothing includes and never passed as -D, so all three AVX2 math translation units compile to empty objects on every platform. The project therefore ships no AVX2 math, every AVX2-named benchmark silently times the scalar path, and a large body of never-executed SIMD code sits behind the flag carrying real bugs — including a 6x16 GEMM micro-kernel that computes only 16 of each tile's 64 columns (confirmed empirically: 288 of 384 outputs wrong at 64x64x64). The second architectural issue is that DistributedContext keeps its reduction buffer and barrier as per-instance members, so no wrapper class — TensorParallelManager, DistributedDataParallel, FullyShardedDataParallel — can perform a real cross-rank reduction; five call sites additionally build a fresh context per invocation, which deadlocks for world_size>1. The only working configuration is the one the test harness happens to use.

Below that, the live-code defects cluster on the training path: the default AdamW optimizer (and its ZeRO twin) applies bias correction with a sqrt(bias_corr2) error that shrinks every warmup update by up to 31x; ZeroOptimizer's reduce-scatter never clears its shared buffer between parameters so each gradient accumulates all preceding ones; its all-gather writes world_size times more bytes than the destination holds; DDP async mode self-deadlocks on a non-recursive mutex; and DDP's Bucket::numel is never assigned, so the FP8 compression path divides gradients by world_size without ever summing them. In numerics, the FP16 subnormal decoder is 4x low on the live codec path, and the AVX2 GELU uses an erf Taylor series that diverges past |x|~3.

None of these produce crashes in the current test suite — which is the common thread. The AVX2 set is excluded from compilation, the multi-rank paths are exercised only in the one shape that works, and the compression branches are keyed off a field that is always zero, so each defect is invisible to the checks that exist. The highest-leverage fix is to make QUANT_AVX2 a real compile definition and run the existing gemm_tiled parity gate against the AVX2 path, which would surface several of the above at once.

findings.title: QUANT_AVX2 is never defined as a preprocessor macro, so the whole AVX2 math library compiles to empty TUs
findings.detail: quant_config.h.in:7 uses `#cmakedefine QUANT_AVX2`, and quant_config.h is generated into CMAKE_BINARY_DIR and made visible through the `quant_config` INTERFACE target — but no source file anywhere includes quant_config.h (grep over src/, include/, tools/, engines/, bench/, tests/, inferno/ returns zero includes), and no CMake command ever adds a QUANT_AVX2 compile definition (grep for -DQUANT_AVX2 in the generated build/build.ninja returns 0 hits, while -DQUANT_USE_CUDA/-DQUANT_USE_DIRECTX/-DQUANT_USE_VULKAN do appear). Result: `#if defined(QUANT_AVX2)` is ALWAYS false. src/math/math_avx2.cpp:10 (`#if defined(QUANT_AVX2)`) and math_avx2_vec.cpp:8 compile to empty translation units, math_avx2_tiled.cpp:9 never takes its AVX2 branch and always compiles the `#else // !QUANT_AVX2` scalar fallbacks at line 568, and src/math/math.cpp:8 `#if !defined(QUANT_AVX2)` is always true, so the scalar implementations are what ship — while cmake/compiler.cmake:23 still prints 'ARCH: AVX2 detected' and adds -mavx2 -mavx -mbmi2 -mfma, and CMakeLists:67 still pulls in math_avx512.cpp. Proof of intent: .clangd line 7 and .vscode/c_cpp_properties.json line 32 both pass `-DQUANT_AVX2` to the IDE. The build system silently disables a whole SIMD library on every platform and configuration.

findings.title: coverage.sh zeroes gcda counters AFTER running the tests, then captures — report is always ~0%
findings.detail: Step 3 (line 33) runs the whole ctest suite and the .gcda counters are written. Step 4 then calls `lcov --zerocounters` (line 51) which resets every counter in the build tree, and only afterwards `lcov --capture` (line 54) + genhtml. Everything measured by the test run is wiped before capture, so the generated HTML/summary reports 0% for every file (or genhtml gets an empty .info). The correct order — zero → run → capture — is exactly what the in-tree CMake `coverage` target does (CMakeLists.txt:454-457), which proves the script's order is the mistake. The `2>/dev/null || true` on the zerocounter call also hides the only signal that lcov is misbehaving. Any coverage number produced by this script has been silently wrong since it was written.
findings.evidence:
# ── 3. Run all tests ───────────────────────────────────────────────
ctest --output-on-failure -j "$(nproc 2>/dev/null || echo 4)"

# ── 4. Generate coverage report ────────────────────────────────────
# Zero previous counters
${LCOV} --directory "${BUILD_DIR}" --zerocounters 2>/dev/null || true

# Capture fresh counters
${LCOV} --directory "${BUILD_DIR}" \
  --capture \
  --output-file "${REPORT_DIR}/coverage_raw.info"

findings.title: cross_platform_check.sh always dies with '$2: unbound variable' — the determinism gate never runs
findings.detail: The script sets `set -euo pipefail` (line 11), then defines `find_artifacts()` with `local out="$2"` (line 68) but both call sites pass only ONE argument (`find_artifacts "$WIN_DIR" > "$TMPDIR_WIN/artifacts.txt"`, lines 95 and 98; `$out` is never used in the body anyway — the function writes to stdout). Under `set -u` the unbound `$2` is a shell-level error that terminates bash immediately, so the `2>/dev/null || true` cannot catch it. Reproduced with bash 5: the script prints 'Scanning Windows artifacts...' and exits 1 without ever reaching checksum comparison. Net effect: the Windows-vs-Linux bitwise determinism check has never produced a PASS/FAIL result — it always aborts. (Secondary design flaw: even if that were fixed, names never match across platforms — `quant_infer.exe` vs `quant_infer`, `.lib` vs `.a` — so DIFF_COUNT would stay 0 and the script would report PARTIAL PASS exit 0 without comparing a single byte.)
findings.evidence:
set -euo pipefail
...
find_artifacts() {
  local dir="$1"
  local out="$2"
  # Find all matching files and record relative path + sha256
  while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
    ...
  done < <(find "$dir" -type f \( ...
}
...
find_artifacts "$WIN_DIR" > "$TMPDIR_WIN/artifacts.txt" 2>/dev/null || true

findings.title: GCC Release adds -march=native, so Docker images and dist tarballs are bound to the build CPU
findings.detail: The GCC Release branch adds `-march=native` for every TU in the project. Consequences: (a) the Dockerfile builder stage configures `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` (Dockerfile:18-27), so the binaries baked into the shipped runtime image are compiled for the CI/build host's exact CPU — if that host has AVX-512 (common on runners), auto-vectorized code and any `__AVX512F__`-guarded TU (src/math/math_avx512.cpp:10, added by CMakeLists:67 whenever QUANT_AVX512 is detected, with no runtime CPUID gate on those symbols) can emit 512-bit instructions that SIGILL on the end user's machine; (b) scripts/make_dist.sh:29-31 builds the same Release configuration and publishes it as `linux-x86_64` (line 20) — a label that is a lie under -march=native; (c) it makes the bitwise cross-platform determinism check in scripts/cross_platform_check.sh impossible by construction. There is no build option to turn it off and no runtime dispatch for compiler-generated vector code.
findings.evidence:
if(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE STREQUAL "Release")
    add_compile_options(-O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2)
  elseif(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE STREQUAL "Debug")
    add_compile_options(-O0 -g -DQUANT_DEBUG)
  endif()

findings.title: Release signing silently no-ops when signtool is absent, 'Step 5 verify' verifies nothing, and secrets go out on argv
findings.detail: Line 96 is `if command -v signtool &> /dev/null; then ... fi` with no else branch: on any host without signtool (Linux/macOS release runners, a plain shell), every .exe/.dll is skipped with no warning, yet `AUTHENTICODE_DONE=true` (line 108) and the script ends with 'Release Signing Complete' — directly contradicting its own comment at lines 85-88 ('Unsigned artifacts never ship silently'). SIGN_STRICT=1 (the default) does not help because it only governs signtool's exit code, not signtool's absence. 'Step 5: Verify signatures' (lines 177-182) only tests that the checksum file is non-empty and counts its lines — there is no `gpg --verify` and no `signtool verify`, so a corrupt/absent signature is reported as verified; and when gpg is missing line 172 prints 'GPG signature file prepared' for a file that was never created. Additionally the signing secrets are passed on the command line (`/p "$AUTHENTICODE_PASSWORD"` lines 98/101, `gpg --passphrase "$GPG_PASSPHRASE"` lines 164/167), which is visible in `ps`/process listings and in CI logs, and the default GPG_KEY_ID `0xTRANSFORMERSFUSION2026KEY` (line 48) is not a valid key id, so an unconfigured run dies at step 4 under strict mode.
findings.evidence:
if command -v signtool &> /dev/null; then
                if [[ "$SIGN_STRICT" == "1" ]]; then
                    signtool sign /f "$AUTHENTICODE_CERT" /p "$AUTHENTICODE_PASSWORD" \
                      /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td sha256 /fd sha256 "$file"
                else
                    signtool sign /f "$AUTHENTICODE_CERT" /p "$AUTHENTICODE_PASSWORD" \
                      /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td sha256 /fd sha256 "$file" || \
                      warn "  signtool failed for $(basename "$file") (SIGN_STRICT=0, continuing)"
                fi
            fi

    done

findings.title: No link-time hardening anywhere: no PIE, no RELRO/NOW, no noexecstack, no CFI/spectre mitigations
findings.detail: The whole hardening surface for GCC/Clang is `-fstack-protector-strong` plus `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2` in the Release branch only (line 16/40). A grep across CMakeLists.txt and cmake/ for relro | -pie | fPIE | POSITION_INDEPENDENT | fcf-protection | stack-clash | guard:cf | /sdl returns zero hits, so: no `-pie`/CMAKE_POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE (ASLR does not apply to the executable image), no `-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now` (GOT stays writable — the classic overwrite target), no `-Wl,-z,noexecstack`, no `-fstack-clash-protection`, no `-fcf-protection`/IBT, no `_FORTIFY_SOURCE` for Debug or RelWithDebInfo builds. The MSVC branch (lines 49-68) adds only `/W3 /utf-8` — no `/guard:cf`, `/Qspectre`, `/sdl`. This matters specifically because the same build produces quant_serve / quant_server, a raw-socket HTTP front door (src/server/http_server.cpp) and a dlopen plugin loader (src/server/production_api.cpp): the one part of the project that consumes untrusted network bytes ships with default linker hardening off.
findings.evidence:

  message(STATUS "COMPILER: GCC ${CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_VERSION}")
  add_compile_options(-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -fstack-protector-strong -Wno-unused-parameter)

  if(QUANT_SANITIZE)

    add_link_options(-fsanitize=address,undefined)
  endif()

    add_compile_options(-O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2)

findings.title: QUANT_SANITIZE is a no-op for MSVC, and the sanitizer flags lack -fno-sanitize-recover so UBSan never fails a run
findings.detail: Two defects in the same option (CMakeLists.txt:19 'Enable address sanitizer'). (1) Only the Clang (line 10) and GNU (line 34) branches honour QUANT_SANITIZE; the MSVC branch at lines 49-68 has no such block, so `-DQUANT_SANITIZE=ON` with the project's primary Windows compiler silently does nothing — no diagnostic, no error. (2) The flags are `-fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer` with no `-fno-sanitize-recover=all`, and UBSan's default is to print-and-continue, so a sanitizer build configured through this option reports UB on stdout while ctest still exits 0 — the gate cannot turn red. CI works around this by bypassing the option entirely and hand-rolling flags (`-fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all` in .github/workflows/ci_full.yml:179), and scripts/build_asan.bat does the same (`/fno-sanitize-recover=all`), which is direct evidence the option as shipped is incomplete for anyone using it as documented.
findings.evidence:
if(QUANT_SANITIZE)

findings.title: Warnings-as-errors is off in every build except the local WSL script, and the Clang branch disables the warnings that catch real bugs
findings.detail: `-Werror` appears exactly once in the whole repo (build_linux.sh:20) — not in CMakeLists.txt, not in cmake/*.cmake, not in any .github/workflows file. So the default build, the Docker build (Dockerfile:18-27) and all CI legs compile with warnings allowed and accumulate them silently. Worse, the Clang branch suppresses `-Wno-sign-compare -Wno-float-equal -Wno-cast-qual -Wno-unused-variable -Wno-unused-function` (lines 5-7): sign-compare is precisely the warning class that catches size_t/int length and offset mistakes in this codebase (stride math, packed-byte counts, buffer offsets), cast-qual catches const-discard writes into shared buffers, float-equal catches the accept/reject and zero-guard comparisons. GCC only suppresses `-Wno-unused-parameter`. So the Clang CI legs are structurally blinder than GCC for the same sources, and nothing turns warnings into failures.
findings.evidence:
add_compile_options(-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -fstack-protector-strong
    -Wno-unused-parameter -Wno-unused-variable -Wno-unused-function
    -Wno-missing-field-initializers -Wno-sign-compare -Wno-float-equal
    -Wno-cast-qual -Wno-unknown-argument -Wno-unused-command-line-argument)

findings.title: local_ci.ps1 'quick tests' exclude regex doesn't match the registered test names, and -FullTest failures still exit 0
findings.detail: The quick-test exclude list is `test_protected|test_gpu|test_training|test_native_quant_moe|paged_kv_4m_test`. The registered ctest name is `test_paged_kv_4m` (tests/CMakeLists.txt:193; `paged_kv_4m_test` is only the .cpp filename), so the 256MiB paged-KV test is NOT excluded and runs in the quick set — while `--timeout 120` overrides the tests' own TIMEOUT properties (tests/CMakeLists.txt:24 sets 300/600s), so any test that legitimately needs >120s is killed and reported as failed. The list also omits `test_native_quant`, `test_moe_training`, `test_fuzz_codec` and the rest of the 'training' label set that the Dockerfile excludes, so the 'quick' run is neither quick nor representative. Separately, line 50 prints 'SOME TESTS FAILED' in DarkYellow and falls through — the script then reaches line 65 and exits 0, so a full-suite failure is reported as a successful local CI run.

findings.title: install(TARGETS ...) declares only RUNTIME, so `cmake --install` ships no libraries despite the comment promising them
findings.detail: The P2 block (comment at lines 589-591: 'Tools + public headers + static libs install so a user can `cmake --install build --prefix <dir>` and get a working tree') installs the 11 tool executables with `RUNTIME DESTINATION` only. There is no `ARCHIVE DESTINATION` and no `LIBRARY DESTINATION`, so none of the ~25 static libraries (quant_core/quant_math/quant_format/quant_kernel/quant_model/quant_backend/quant_production/…) are installed; a downstream project that runs `cmake --install` gets headers, quant_config.h and binaries and nothing linkable — i.e. it cannot link against the public headers it just installed. Grep for `install(` across the whole tree returns only this block plus the two header rules (600, 604), confirming no other rule installs the libs. (Also missing from the list: train_64m, gle_report, generate_comparison_visuals.)
findings.evidence:
# P2: install + packaging — `cmake --install` / CPack shipped nothing before
# (zero install() rules). Tools + public headers + static libs install so a
# user can `cmake --install build --prefix <dir>` and get a working tree.
install(TARGETS
  quant_infer quant_train quant_finetune quant_convert quant_info
  quant_bench quant_format_list quant_serve quant_quantize quant_server
  quant_evaluate
  RUNTIME DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_BINDIR})

findings.title: The `coverage` custom target passes `-j` with an empty $ENV{NPROC}, so the target always fails at its ctest step
findings.detail: `COMMAND ${CMAKE_CTEST_COMMAND} --output-on-failure -j $ENV{NPROC}` reads an environment variable named NPROC. NPROC is a command, not an env var, and grep across the entire repo shows this line as its only occurrence — it is never exported by any script or workflow. The expansion is therefore empty, leaving `ctest --output-on-failure -j` with no value (ctest errors out, or receives an empty argument) and the target aborts before lcov --capture, so `cmake --build . --target coverage` (advertised by message(STATUS) at line 470) can never produce a report. The correct form is already used elsewhere in the repo: scripts/coverage.sh:28 uses `$(nproc 2>/dev/null || echo 4)`, and the whole thing could also just be `${CMAKE_CTEST_COMMAND} --parallel`.
findings.evidence:
COMMAND ${CMAKE_CTEST_COMMAND} --output-on-failure -j $ENV{NPROC}
        COMMAND ${LCOV_PATH} --directory ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR} --capture

findings.title: QUANT_BUILD_ADAPTERS defaults OFF and no CI job enables it — the GGUF/Safetensors untrusted-input parsers are never compiled or tested
findings.detail: `option(QUANT_BUILD_ADAPTERS ... OFF)` plus `add_subdirectory(src/adapters EXCLUDE_FROM_ALL)` (line 583) means src/adapters/src/gguf_bridge.cpp and safetensors_bridge.cpp — the loaders that parse attacker-controlled checkpoint files (magic/version/kv-count, hand-rolled JSON header parser, untrusted offset/length slicing) — and src/adapters/tests/test_adapter_bridges.cpp (registered at src/adapters/CMakeLists.txt:105-113) are absent from every default build. grep across .github/workflows/ finds no `-DQUANT_BUILD_ADAPTERS=ON` in any workflow, so these TUs are also outside -Wall analysis, outside ASAN/UBSAN CI and outside ctest — a real test gap on the project's highest-value fuzz surface. The option cannot even be turned on out of the box: src/adapters/CMakeLists.txt:24-34 falls back to `PARENT_LIB_DIR = ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/../build_verify/Release` and creates IMPORTED libraries as `${PARENT_LIB_DIR}/quant_core.lib` — that directory does not exist in the tree and `.lib` is a Windows-only extension, so on Linux/macOS enabling the option yields IMPORTED targets pointing at nothing.
