The defects exist in the source, but the claimed runtime behavior does not — I disproved the core mechanism empirically on the real script.

REAL (confirmed): `find_artifacts()` does declare `local out="$2"` (line 68) and is invoked with one argument at lines 95 and 98; `out` is never used in the function body. Under `set -euo pipefail`, expanding the unset `$2` in a non-interactive shell aborts the shell.

REFUTED (the finding's central claim): `|| true` does NOT absorb it. I ran bash 5.3.15 with a minimal replica of the exact construct — TEST1 (`f "/tmp" > "$TMP" 2>/dev/null || true`), TEST2 (no `|| true`) and TEST3 (full find/while replica) all terminate with `exit=1` and never print the post-call marker. Unbound-variable expansion is a shell-abort, not a command failure, so it is immune to errexit suppression (`|| true`), the same way `cd /nonexistent` is. Only `exit 0`/`exit 1` inside a command substitution is contained in a subshell, which is not the case here.

I then ran the actual script end-to-end (`cross_platform_check.sh /tmp/xplat_test/win /tmp/xplat_test/lin` with dummy `.bin` files present in both dirs). Output was the banner, "Windows build dir:", "Linux build dir:", "Scanning Windows artifacts...", then the process died: EXIT CODE 1. Control flow never reaches line 100. Therefore WIN_COUNT/LIN_COUNT/MATCH_COUNT/DIFF_COUNT/MISMATCH are never assigned, and the PASS branch at line 176-180 is unreachable. The finding's derivation "both artifact lists are therefore ALWAYS empty → WIN_COUNT=LIN_COUNT=0 → MISMATCH=0 → prints PASS and exits 0 on every invocation" is false at the second step.

The direction of failure is also inverted. The script fails CLOSED (exit 1), never open. A non-zero exit blocks any CI gate; it cannot green-light an unverified build. The `2>/dev/null` does swallow the "$2: unbound variable" diagnostic, so the operator sees an unexplained silent exit 1 — that is the real symptom (poor diagnosability), not a vacuous PASS. So "critical" and "determinism is never actually tested but reported as verified" do not hold.

The reviewer's "Verified empirically" evidence only established the empty artifacts file, never the downstream PASS/exit 0 — which is precisely the step that does not happen.

Defect (2), PARTIAL PASS: lines 181-184 do read `elif [[ $DIFF_COUNT -eq 0 && $MISMATCH -ne 0 ]]` ... `exit 0` as quoted, but this is deliberate and self-documenting — the very next line says "This may be expected (e.g. Windows-only GPU libs, platform-specific tests)", and the run prints a yellow PARTIAL PASS plus a list of the divergent files, so it is not silent. It is also unreachable today because (1) kills the script first.

Context that caps impact: I grepped the repo for `cross_platform_check` — the only hits are the script's own header comments (lines 2 and 5). No CI workflow, Makefile, CMakeLists, .ps1 or .bat invokes it; it is a standalone manual script in transformers-fusion/scripts/.

A genuine bug remains — the script is 100% non-functional and can never pass, with its diagnostic swallowed — but that is a different finding with a different mechanism, a fail-closed (safe) outcome, and no CI consumer, so it is nowhere near the claimed critical fail-open determinism gate.

CONFIRMED in the code, but the impact is narrower than claimed, so severity drops high -> medium.

1) normed_x is {S,D}, not {B,S,D} (line 167): `Tensor normed_x({S, D});` sits outside `for (int64_t b = 0; b < B; b++)` (168). Inside, lines 223-224 do `for (i=0;i<S*D;i++) normed_x.data<float>()[i] = xbd3[i];` — every batch writes the SAME first S*D floats, so batches 0..B-2 are overwritten and only batch B-1 survives. 3) Line 232-233 then strides by D*D: `for (b=0;b<B;b++) memcpy(cod + b*D, xd + b * x.dim(1) * D, D*sizeof(float));` — x.dim(1)==D so source offset is b*D*D. Tensor::dim(i) (include/quant/tensor.h:42) is explicitly documented as an UNCHECKED dims[i] read with no rank gate, and Tensor::data<T>() (tensor.h:46-49) is a bare cast. 4) Arithmetic checks out: D=768,S=197 → buffer = 151,296 floats (605,184 B, 64-byte aligned via AlignedAllocator). b=1 source = xd+589,824 floats = 2,359,296 B ≈ 2.36 MB past the start, ~1.76 MB past the end. Genuine OOB heap read.

NO MITIGATION EXISTS:
- No batch validation in PatchEmbedding::forward (trusts images.dim(0)), VisionTransformer::forward, MultimodalCrossAttention::encode_image, or MultimodalCrossAttention::forward (926-938).
- QUANT_CHECK is used elsewhere (tensor.cpp view/reshape/slice) but nowhere on this path. RMSNorm::forward (src/model/transformer.cpp:119) runs on cls_out AFTER the OOB memcpy, so it cannot catch it.
- NOT dead code: the TU is built (CMakeLists.txt:325) and the header is installed as public API (CMakeLists.txt:600 `install(DIRECTORY include/quant ... PATTERN "*.h")`), confirmed by the duplicate copy under install_test/include/quant/.

REACHABILITY (weaker than the title implies, but real): I found no in-repo caller invoking VisionTransformer with B>=2 — the only external reference to MultimodalCrossAttention outside its own TU is a comment at tests/test_platform_packs.cpp:39. With B=1 the bug is benign (the "last batch" IS the only batch; b=0's source offset 0 is in-bounds), which is why nothing in-repo trips it. But it is a public, installed, default-constructible API, and batched vision inference (B>=2) is a normal use that nothing forbids.

TWO IMPRECISIONS, neither refuting:
- "a multi-megabyte heap over-read" overstates the VOLUME. The memcpy copies only D floats (3,072 B for D=768); it is the OFFSET that is ~2.36 MB. Same UB class, same ASan/crash/info-leak risk, smaller byte count.
- The remediation is right but the two fixes must land TOGETHER. Allocating {B,S,D} and writing per-batch is the load-bearing fix — after it, x.dim(1)==S and line 233 needs no change. Fixing ONLY the stride at 233 to use S would make it WORSE (source offset b*S*D runs even further past the end of the {S,D} buffer).

Severity medium is fair: real heap over-read + silent batch-collapse in a public API, gated on B>=2 that nothing in-repo exercises, ~3 KB over-read volume rather than multi-megabyte.

The code citations are accurate — `plugin.ts:142` is `const exitCode = result.status ?? 1` with no range check, and `bin.ts:42` does `process.exit(runPlugin(...))`. Both mechanisms behind the claim fail verification, and the proposed fix changes nothing about the symptom.

1) The "out-of-range / GetExitCodeProcess-from-ENOENT" origin is wrong. `result.error` is `undefined` in the observed case, so no ENOENT is involved; `plugin.ts:134-139` already returns 127 correctly when it does fire. With `shell: true` on win32 a genuinely missing binary yields `status: 1` and `error: undefined`, not a huge code. The 4294963238 is npm's own exit code: `cmd.exe /d /s /c npm run definitely-missing-script` returns 4294963238 directly, as does `spawnSync('npm', [...], {shell:true})`. It is npm reporting a missing script, faithfully forwarded by a wrapper whose own docstring says it is "a thin npm forwarder" and whose `@returns` is "the npm exit code". Forwarding it verbatim is the stated contract, not a defect.

2) `process.exit()` does not truncate. Verified: `process.exit(4294963238)` and `process.exitCode = 4294963238` both produce child status 4294963238; `process.exit(-1)` → 4294967295; `process.exit(300)` → 300. The full 32-bit value is preserved by Node and the *shell* is what renders it as -4058. So the "nonsensical exit code" is not produced or corrupted by `process.exit`, and the recommended `process.exitCode = code` yields byte-identical exit status — the fix does not address the headline symptom at all.

3) The stderr-drop risk did not reproduce. I replayed the exact diagnostics from `plugin.ts:149-154` (two short writes then exit) under both styles: 20/20 runs delivered both lines fully under `process.exit()`, identical to `process.exitCode`. Even with 1-8 MB of piped stderr written immediately before `process.exit()`, delivery was complete. The Windows async-pipe truncation is theoretical here, not observed.

4) The cited "consistency" arguments don't hold. `case 'dump-config'` never sets an exit code at all (it relies on natural exit 0), and `createProcessShutdown` uses `process.exit` for forced/signal exits (`process-shutdown.ts:24`) with `process.exitCode` only on the natural-completion path — so the codebase is not uniformly on the side implied. `args.ts:186` only forwards a `CommanderError`'s own exit code or literal 1, all in range, so it has no issue and is not evidence of one.

`result.status ?? 1` already handles the only genuinely undefined status spawnSync can return here (signal-killed child). No guard is missing; the behavior is the documented forwarder contract.

CONFIRMED — the evidence is real and in current code, and nothing mitigates it.

What I verified in the actual tree (C:/Users/thaku/Workspaces/fusion/transformers-fusion):

1. compiler.cmake:40 is exactly as quoted: `if(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE STREQUAL "Release") add_compile_options(-O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2)` inside the `elseif(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_ID MATCHES "GNU")` branch, with no option/guard — there is no `QUANT_NATIVE`/`QUANT_PORTABLE` option anywhere in CMakeLists.txt (options are only BUILD_TESTS/BENCHMARKS/TOOLS/ADAPTERS/SANITIZE/COVERAGE/VULKAN/CUDA). include(compiler) runs at CMakeLists.txt:13, before any target, so add_compile_options reaches every target. Notably the Clang branch (line 16) deliberately omits -march=native, so the GCC branch is the odd one out, not a project-wide policy.

2. Consumers all check out as claimed:
   - release.yml:20 `cmake_args: -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` with no CC/CXX override on ubuntu-latest → default GCC → native; step "Package binaries" puts them in dist/linux-x86_64, and job create_release publishes them via softprops/action-gh-release. So the shipped artifact really is labeled `linux-x86_64` while being built for the runner's exact ISA.
   - Dockerfile:18-21 `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=g++-13` in the builder stage; final image COPYs quant_infer/quant_convert/quant_bench etc. (lines 51-56), ENTRYPOINT quant_infer.
   - scripts/make_dist.sh:29 Release build → dist/linux-x86_64 (PLAT detection line 20).
   - build_linux.sh:18 Release (passes -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror", which does not cancel add_compile_options).
   - ci_full.yml:28 and :35 both add `-DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="-march=native"` on top of compiler.cmake's own native.

3. No mitigation exists. There is no -march=x86-64 / -march=x86-64-v2 / -mtune / -mno-* anywhere in the repo (only hit is MSVC `string(APPEND CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE " /O2 /DNDEBUG")`). The runtime CPU feature detection that does exist (simd_math.cpp:28-38 cpuid + `if (feat.has_avx512) return rms_norm_avx512(...)`, kernel_production.cpp:296 `detect_cpu_isa()` before AVX2 gemv, guarded by `#if defined(__AVX2__)`) only guards those hand-written SIMD kernels — it cannot guard arbitrary code auto-vectorized under -march=native, so it does not protect against the claimed SIGILL. No SIGILL handler, no baseline CI leg, no second packaging variant: build.yml's clang Ubuntu leg is the only native-free Release build and it uploads a 14-day CI artifact, not a release artifact.

Nuances that temper the wording but do not refute it:
- arch.cmake's `_try_avx2()` uses check_cxx_source_compiles (compile-only, never runs), so QUANT_AVX2=ON on any x86-64 host and compiler.cmake:45-47 adds `-mavx2 -mavx -mbmi2 -mfma` unconditionally — i.e. the release binaries already require AVX2 even without -march=native. So "SIGILL on any CPU older than the build host" is an overstatement; the accurate delta is "on any CPU missing instructions the build host's -march=native enables" (e.g. AVX-512 on an AVX-512 runner vs. Zen1-3 / most consumer machines).

The image would only break if built on one machine and run on another.
- I could not confirm published releases: `git remote -v` is empty here and there is no README, so release.yml/make_dist.sh shipping is inferred from the in-repo config, which is what the claim rests on.

A competent maintainer would still treat this as a real, actionable packaging bug: a binary published under the generic `linux-x86_64` label must not be built with -march=native. Fix is one line (drop it, or gate it behind an opt-in QUANT_NATIVE option defaulting OFF for Release/package builds).

Confirmed in current code at packages/cf/src/mad/core/god-runtime.ts:920-958. (a) The setTimeout callback (lines 928-933) sets settled=true and rejects, but never calls clearTimeout (harmless post-fire) nor unsubscribe(); only the success path (940) and the emit-rejection path (953) call unsubscribe(). So every timed-out request leaves its handler permanently in this.subscriptions[`${eventType}.response`]. The handler body is a no-op once settled, so the effect is a retained-closure leak, not wrong behavior — but real. (b) requestId is declared at line 946 with const (TDZ relative to the handler at 936-943, fine because the handler only runs async) and is minted after on() is installed, and the accept condition at 937 is `!event.metadata?.requestId || event.metadata.requestId === requestId`. emit() at 864-877 stores the full metadata object on the event, so a response emitted via emit(`${type}.response`, data, { requestId: undefined }) — i.e. anything that does not use respond() with the id — has no metadata.requestId and satisfies every pending handler. emit() runs handlers sequentially with await, so with N concurrent pending request() calls a single id-less response settles all N with the same payload (the reviewer understated this slightly: it's not one winner + one hang, it's all of them cross-delivered; a hang still occurs if only one response is emitted). The architecture note it points to says the same thing in deployment terms: "A persistence root may be local to one project, shared by several projects, temporary, or centralized" — several *projects* means several cwd buckets under the root, i.e. different project/session directories, not several writers of one session file. Nothing there claims concurrent same-session writers.

The package documents the opposite, prominently. packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/README.md "Known Limitations and Deferred Work": "**One live writer per session** — append and repair are coordinated only inside the owning backend instance. Issue CONFIRMED in current code (C:/Users/thaku/Workspaces/fusion/code-fusion/packages/cf/src/mad/core/god-runtime.ts), with two detail corrections and one aggravating adjacent fact.

- Second claimed bug is also real: passing the same `id` to two spawnChildAgent calls returns 'dup' both times, Map size stays 2 (last write wins, first node orphaned) while `root.childrenIds` becomes ['dup','dup'] — duplicate children entries also inflate the maxChildrenPerNode gate.

Corrections to the claim's reasoning (do not change the verdict):
- There is no periodic idle sweeper. cleanupIdleAgents() (3875-3881) has exactly one caller, GodRuntime.shutdown (line 6054); the only setInterval in the file belongs to RateLimiter (line 1237). So cleanup runs per shutdown, not on a timer. This weakens "the sweeper manufactures the cycles on its own," and it means the *actual* path to depletion is any caller that spawns and terminates, or repeated initialize()/shutdown() cycles: initialize() calls registerRootAgent for every config.agents entry on each re-init (5706) while the same PolicyAgentTreeManager instance persists (constructed once at 5650, never reset), so the tree grows unboundedly across lifecycle cycles regardless of spawnChildAgent.
- spawnChildAgent has zero callers anywhere in the repo (repo-wide grep). The wedge is therefore reachable only through the exported API surface (getAgentTreeManager(), the exported PolicyAgentTreeManager class, mad/index.ts:41) — real, but consumer-exposed rather than internally triggered today.

Aggravating adjacent fact found while verifying: the class's constructor default and the public SpawnPolicy type do not agree. types.ts:940 declares SpawnPolicy as {maxAgents, maxTreeDepth, maxChildrenPerAgent, maxParallel, ...}, while the class reads maxDepth/maxChildrenPerNode/maxTotalAgents/autoTerminateIdleMs (3742-3747). tsc flags all four as non-existent properties on SpawnPolicy, and a probe passing a genuine SpawnPolicy produced unlimited spawns with all three guards silently disabled (`size >= undefined` is false). So the documented config shape yields the opposite failure (no cap at all); the permanent-capacity exhaustion this finding describes occurs with the constructor-local default shape — which is nonetheless the shape used whenever the constructor argument is omitted, i.e. `new PolicyAgentTreeManager()` or `new PolicyAgentTreeManager(config.spawnPolicy as any)`.

Verdict: not refuted. A competent maintainer would accept this: terminated nodes are never reclaimed, so the capacity gate counts dead nodes, and nothing in the code ever deletes from the Map. What is accurate: files.ts:333 does carry `TODO(total-instruction-read-bound)`, `readBounded` (files.ts:327-352) enforces only `maxSourceBytes`, and `loadBaselineInstructionSet` (files.ts:414-425) reads every discovered file before `renderWorkspaceInstructionSet` applies `maxBytes`.

Residual truth worth noting only as low-priority polish: an aggregate source budget across a baseline batch would reduce transient read amplification when several near-cap files sit on one ancestor chain. That is a perf nicety, not a correctness issue.

votes.label: verify:Turns cancelled by a hook/owner sett

v.reason:
The finding is intentional, documented, tested behavior — not a defect.

1. The mapping is deliberate. `C:/Users/thaku/Workspaces/fusion/code-fusion/packages/acp/acp/src/codec.ts` lines 20-24 carry the comment: "`cancelled` is reserved for explicit client cancellation (`session/cancel`) and disposal, both settled out of band; a turn aborted by a hook or another owner is ordinary quiescence and reports `end_turn`."

2. It is enforced by a test that asserts exactly the behavior the finding calls a bug: `packages/acp/acp/tests/turns.spec.ts` "settles a hook-cancelled turn as end_turn, not cancelled" calls `agent.cancel({ kind: 'hook', reason: 'owner intervention' })` and asserts `stopReason === 'end_turn'`. `tests/codec.spec.ts` asserts `{ kind: 'aborted', reason: { kind: 'user' } } -> 'end_turn'`.

3. The package contract documents it: `packages/acp/acp/README.md` under Protocol contract / `session/prompt`: "Normal quiescence reports `end_turn`; explicit ACP cancellation, disposal, or a prompt whose admission was discarded (a turnless slot) reports `cancelled`."

4. Impact does not reach "medium" under this lens:
   - ACP's `cancelled` means *the ACP client cancelled via session/cancel*. Here the ACP client did not cancel — a hook or another owner did. Reporting `end_turn` is the semantically honest value: the prompt was not cancelled by that client.
   - `stopReason` is not the only signal. The bridge emits `agent_message_chunk` for every committed `assistant/message` on the same prompt's turn before settlement, so a client receives the partial text that WAS committed and then `end_turn`. This is observably distinguishable from a fully completed turn only in principle, but the committed prefix is delivered — the "produces nothing / effectively invisible" framing overstates it.
   - `TurnEndReason` itself defines `interrupted` as "a persistence backend closed a crash-orphaned turn on reload. The loop never emits this marker" (`core/session/src/types.ts`), so mapping it to `cancelled` is also only reachable on reload-repair, not on any hook/owner abort path. The only in-loop abort causes are `{kind:'user'|'parent'|'hook'|'disposed'}` → `aborted`, which the code intentionally routes to `end_turn`.
   - The code has no ACP-legal alternative: the only StopReasons are `end_turn | max_tokens | max_turn_requests | refusal | cancelled`, and inventing a richer out-of-band cancellation signal would break the ACP contract this package implements.

So a competent maintainer reading codec.ts, its test, and the README would close this as by-design, not as a correctness bug.

Confirmed in current code. tools.ts:151-174 is a bare `do { ... cursor = response.nextCursor } while (cursor)` with no page cap, no seen-cursor dedup, no total-tools cap, and no timeout override; grep finds zero such guards anywhere in src/. The mechanism is partly real but the impact claims are wrong or heavily overstated. No artifact until the first append," and `Session` only auto-appends `session/end-seed` when a seed exists. A truly blank session has zero events, never materializes an artifact, and therefore never appears in `persistence.list()` (which walks on-disk artifacts only) — so it is never probed at all. The bridge is precisely the layer that could distinguish client fault from host fault (it already owns the AbortController and the carrier/business split), and it does not, so host faults are mislabelled as the client's fault. That is a real, actionable error-contract bug, correctly sized at medium.

The finding is accurate as a description of the current code, and I could not refute it on the merits — only on practical severity.

WHAT CONFIRMS IT
1. connection.ts:257 is exactly as quoted: `if (typeof id === 'number') this.handleResponse(id, frame)`. A frame with a string id and no `method` falls through all three guards in `dispatch` (lines 246, 253, 257) and returns silently. `handleResponse` (269-280) only ever resolves a pending entry keyed by the numeric id from `request()` (172), so a string-id response can never resolve anything.
2. The inconsistency inside one function is real: line 246 accepts `typeof id === 'string' || typeof id === 'number'` for the server->client request branch, while the response branch at 257 accepts numbers only.
3. The downstream consequence chain checks out against the actual code. On abort, `instance.query` (instance.ts:99-102) calls `startTeardown()` only if `isTransportFailure(error)`, which delegates to `connection.failedWith` (82-84) and is true only for the exact retained `closeReason`. An abort error therefore skips teardown, and the provider's `finally` eviction (index.ts:296-300) is gated on `instance.dead` = `processClosed || disposed || connection.failed` (instance.ts:73-75) — all false for a live process that merely answered with the wrong id type. `instanceFor` (index.ts:320-327) returns the same instance from `LocalLspProvider.instances` on the next query. The `raceAbort` cancel-grace self-heal (instance.ts:216-241) does not apply, because the abort surfaces from `abortable(this.ready, signal)` or `abortable(this.queue, signal)`, not from `send`. No timeout on the request path closes the process either (`request()` has no deadline; only `shutdownTimeoutMs` and `killGraceMs` exist, neither armed here). So the poisoned slot survives until restart, and every later query for that workspace hangs for the full caller timeout. The reviewer's claim that no test exercises a string response id is also correct — connection.spec.ts only covers string ids as a *request* (line 243).

WHY SEVERITY COMES DOWN TO LOW
1. Trigger is narrow and, in practice, near-zero. `pending` is keyed exclusively by the client's own `nextId++` (connection.ts:166-172), so the dropped frame is a response to a request this host sent with a numeric id. JSON-RPC 2.0 requires the server to echo the id *as received*, and every mainstream stdio server that is a realistic value for this config schema — gopls, tsserver/typescript-language-server, clangd, rust-analyzer, pyright, basedpyright, jdtls — echoes the client's numeric id. Producing a string id requires a nonconforming or unusual server, not merely a conforming one. The reviewer's "conforming-but-non-numeric-id server" framing is technically reachable but is a much smaller population than the wording implies.
2. The drop itself is the correct, safe behavior for a string id that matches no pending request — silently ignoring an unmatchable response is right, and the reviewer does not dispute that.
3. There is a test that pins this exact behavior: connection.spec.ts:238-247, `'ignores a frame that is neither a valid request nor a numeric-id response'`, which writes `{jsonrpc:"2.0",id:"str-id"}` with no method and asserts the connection still answers a real request. The reviewer missed it, and it shows the current behavior is deliberate rather than accidental. Note it covers the no-method case, not a string id carrying a `result` against a pending numeric request, so the gap is still uncovered — but a maintainer will read this test as an intentional numeric-only response contract.

NET: real, correctly diagnosed, cheaply fixable (widening the guard at connection.ts:257 to match line 246), and the requested severity of medium is defensible on impact alone. I am marking it low because the triggering server population is small and the majority of deployments will never reach it — this is latent protocol-conformance debt, not an active defect.

2. 3. Core defect CONFIRMED, magnitudes overstated. Evidence in code: spawn.ts:177-199 runs allocUint32() three times unconditionally per loop iteration (plus a fourth readSlot at :190 on data) and line 198 sleeps a fixed setTimeout(1) even when the pipe is empty; ffi.ts allocUint32 is a bare koffi.alloc and grep finds no koffi.free anywhere in the package (only localFree for ACL descriptors). koffi 3.3.0 CallAlloc (ffi.cc:895) is a calloc, and WrapPointer (util.hh:407) returns a plain BigInt with NO napi finalizer (finalizers exist only for `disposable` types), so the slot is orphaned forever even after GC. Empirically (node 24.17 here): an alloc+free loop keeps RSS flat at ~48 MB across 6M allocations, while alloc-and-discard — exactly drainPipe's pattern — grows RSS linearly by 15.5 MB per 1M allocations (15.5 bytes/slot), unrecoverable after global.gc(). So native memory really does grow without bound for the child's lifetime. The path is reachable and is the default: index.ts:117 declares stdio?: 'pipe'|'inherit' and the branch at :358 is `=== 'inherit'`, so pipe is the default; README:59 documents AclSandbox.spawn() as the programmatic direct-spawn API, it is exercised by tests/probe.spec.ts:76, and package.json exports "./src/*" (drainPipe is also re-exported via the built lib). No upstream validation, try/catch, or config default bounds it. However the numbers are wrong and the scope is narrower than claimed: measured setTimeout(1) on this machine ticks at 64.3/sec (15.54 ms period), NOT ~1000/sec, so growth is ~4 KB/s (two concurrent pipes), ~14 MB/hour — not 12 KB/s; the 12 KB/s figure only materializes if something else in the host process calls timeBeginPeriod(1). The 1ms polling cadence is also semi-intentional (comment at :196 explicitly chooses it over setImmediate), but the allocation leak is nowhere acknowledged and is clearly unintentional. Net: a real, actionable, trivially-fixable unbounded native leak on a public default API — not refuted, but not high under exploitability/user-impact (slow growth, off the main runner path, no crash/DoS).

Verified against the code: the mechanism the finding describes is real, but its characterization as a high-severity availability bug is wrong — it is a documented, deliberately reviewed design constraint with an operator recovery path, and the concrete mitigation the maintainer would want already exists elsewhere in the repo.

What is confirmed in current code (C:\Users\thaku\Workspaces\fusion\code-fusion\packages\util\atomic-write\src\index.ts:128-154): the lock is a `wx`-created `<file>.lock` sibling containing `${process.pid}\n` (L138); release is only the `finally` `rm(lockPath)` (L152); there is no `process.kill`, no age check, and no steal path. A dead-or-crashed holder therefore does leave the sibling, and every contender times out with `atomic-write: timed out waiting for the writer lock` (L144) until it is removed. The credentials provider makes this reachable, not hypothetical: credentials-local/src/index.ts L112 sets `DOCUMENT_LOCK_WAIT_MS = 30_000`, and modifyRecord/deleteRecord hold the lock across the caller's `mutate` (L684-705, L716-724, L768-785, L838-855) — so a token refresh that is killed inside that window is exactly the wedge.

Why not refuted, and why the severity is overstated:

1. This is explicit reviewed intent, not an oversight. The atomic-write README carries it under "Known Limitations and Deferred Work": "**Orphaned locks require operator recovery** — a process that exits while holding the lock can leave the sibling behind. Later writers time out without deleting it; an operator removes it only after verifying that no writer still owns it. File age alone is not safe evidence of abandonment." (packages/util/atomic-write/README.md:45). The module docstring states the same: "The contender never removes an existing lock because file age cannot prove that its owner stopped; orphan recovery is an operator action" (index.ts:120-122). The architecture note records the reasoning: "age cannot distinguish a crashed owner from a paused live writer" (.agents/notes/implemented/architecture/2026-07-30-settings-write-path-integrity.md:15). Stealing on age would reintroduce exactly the lost-update the lock exists to prevent — this is the standard lockfile trade-off, and the code chose the safe side.

2. The stale-lock handling the finding says is missing is already implemented elsewhere in this repo, in the same repo's other `wx` lock: scripts/install-lefthook.mjs writes `${pid} ${randomUUID()}`, then on `EEXIST` re-reads and `lstat`-verifies dev/ino, parses the pid, and calls `lockOwnerIsAlive()` (`process.kill(owner, 0)`, treating EPERM as alive) — and removes the lock only after that, with ownership-verified release (acquireInstallLock, ~L382-452). So the concern "nothing reads the pid, so nobody can ever recover" is not accurate: a live-pid probe is the established pattern here, it is just deliberately not applied to the document lock because auto-steal risks concurrent write corruption.

3. Recovery is one documented command, not the finding's "for the life of the machine" with no path out: a user (or the credential-record delete/rotate UI flow, which is how operators actually reach it) removes `<CF_HOME>/.credentials.yaml.lock`. The credential document and the lock are sibling files in one user-owned `0700` directory.

4. Blast radius is bounded: the lock serializes writers only (readers stay lock-free via the rename commit), so it wedges credential/settings writes, not reads — auth keeps working from the in-memory snapshot, and a failing write surfaces as a thrown error at the credential surface rather than a silent wedge.

5. The stated trigger (SIGKILL/OOM/power loss) is a crash of the write process itself, not normal operation. Normal exits always release via `finally`, and graceful disposal paths in credentials-local drain the operation chain before teardown, so ordinary process shutdown is covered.

So the finding is technically correct about the mechanism and about the pid being unused by withFileLock today, but it describes an intentional, documented limitation with an operator remedy and a safe rationale, and the pid-less version is strictly safer than the auto-steal it implies. That is a low-severity robustness consideration, not a high-severity availability defect.

The mechanism is described accurately but the behavior is intentional design, not a defect — it is documented in the public README, justified in the API docstring, recorded in an architecture note, and pinned by a regression test.

What the code actually shows (C:/Users/thaku/Workspaces/fusion/code-fusion/packages/util/atomic-write/src/index.ts L128-154): the facts the reviewer cites are correct — the lock is a `wx`-created `<file>.lock` holding `process.pid` (L138), release is only the `finally` at L151-153, and there is no liveness probe, age check, or steal path. Nothing in the repo ever reads the lock's contents.

But this is a documented decision, not an oversight:
- JSDoc L119-122: "The contender never removes an existing lock because file age cannot prove that its owner stopped; orphan recovery is an operator action."
- README "Known Limitations and Deferred Work": "Orphaned locks require operator recovery — a process that exits while holding the lock can leave the sibling behind. Later writers time out without deleting it; an operator removes it only after verifying that no writer still owns it."
- .agents/notes/implemented/architecture/2026-07-30-settings-write-path-integrity.md states the same rationale verbatim.
- Decisively, packages/settings/settings-file/tests/concurrency.spec.ts has a test named `does not steal an old writer lock`: it writes a lock, backdates it 60s via `utimes`, then asserts the write REJECTS with /timed out waiting for the writer lock/ AND that the lock file still contains `slow-holder`. Auto-recovery of a stale lock is a behavior the suite explicitly forbids.

The reviewer's one genuine point — that the pid would enable a `kill(pid, 0)` probe, which is stronger than the age heuristic the maintainer rebutted — does not rescue the finding, because a pid probe is unsound in exactly the deployment this lock serves and would trade a recoverable error for a worse one:
- PID reuse (Linux wraps at 32768 by default) makes `kill(pid,0)` report alive for an unrelated process, so recovery silently fails to fire.
- On shared/network filesystems and across PID namespaces (containers sharing a harness home — the multi-process case the lock exists for), the recorded pid is not addressable from the contender's process table. Stealing on a bad signal yields two concurrent read-modify-writers on a 0600 secrets document, which is precisely the lost-update/resurrection race `withFileLock` was built to prevent (see the read-modify-write comments at credentials-local L686-688, L771-773, and the concurrency test's "only the read-modify-write cycle under the `<file>.lock` sibling keeps both namespaces alive").

Impact is also narrower than claimed. Reads never lock (README: "readers stay lock-free"), and I confirmed credentials-local `loadInitial()` (L811-830) does a bare `readFile` with no lock — the only boot-time lock is the one-shot flat-layout migration write. So an orphaned lock does not stop booting, reading credentials, or authenticating requests; it blocks only `set`/`unset`/`modifyRecord`/`deleteRecord`. The error is loud and self-locating — `timed out waiting for the writer lock at ${lockPath}` — so the operator has the exact path to inspect and delete, and a genuinely slow holder (30s `DOCUMENT_LOCK_WAIT_MS`) frees on the next attempt while an orphan never does, which is itself the diagnostic the reviewer calls "unexplained."

The pid being unread is at most dead diagnostic weight, not an availability bug — an operator inspecting the lock can still `ps` the pid it contains. That is a doc/cleanup nit, not a high-severity recovery flaw.

The claim's core mechanism and its impact do not match the code.

1. THE RESCAN HAPPENS INSIDE THE FIRST SWEEP, not only in a second sweep. `LocalTerminalHandle.stopDescendants()` (packages/subprocess/subprocess-local/src/terminal.ts:221-229) calls `this.descendants()` three times: line 222 (capture), line 225 (`unionMembers(capturedSurvivors, this.descendants())` — adopt new forks after the TERM grace and include them in the SIGKILL set), and line 228 (final survivor union). Because the shell is still alive at that point, `rootVerified` is true, so `descendants()` adopts newly forked tree/session members. This is pinned by the test `rescans for descendants forked during TERM` (terminal.spec.ts:311-326), where a process forked during the TERM window (`late`, pid 125) is adopted and SIGKILLed by the FIRST `stopDescendants()` — not left for the second sweep. So the claim that "the second sweep is the only one that can see it" is false.

2. The claim's cited precedent contradicts its fix. It says `terminateForHostExit` "kills the shell first," but that method runs `forceStopDescendants(); forceStopShell(); forceStopDescendants()` (terminal.ts:132-136) — descendants FIRST, the identical order to `closeOnce`. There is no shell-first path anywhere in the codebase.

3. Shell-first would be a regression, not a fix. `descendants()` (terminal.ts:159-175) only adopts new members while `rootVerified` is true (root pid still carries its start identity). Killing the shell first makes rootVerified false, permanently hiding any orphan it spawned before dying — the opposite of "removing the respawn source." The code comment (terminal.ts:160-164) and the tests `does not adopt the children of a recycled shell pid` / `adopts nothing when the shell identity was never observable` pin that adoption stops once the shell is gone.

4. The "unkillable tree" is not real. SIGKILL cannot be caught; each `sleep` in `while true; do sleep 0.1 & done` dies to SIGKILL and is re-scanned. A descendant only survives if it also survives SIGKILL (uninterruptible D-state), which is an OS condition, not something a shell wrapper creates.

5. The "permanent failure" impact is false. Every layer explicitly clears its fence on failure so a retry re-runs the sweep: `LocalTerminalHandle.terminate()` clears `this.cleanup` (terminal.ts:124), `LocalPtySession.close()` clears `this.closePromise` (session.ts:356), and `TerminalSessionService.kill()` clears `record.closing` (terminal/src/index.ts:298). The test `retries failed cleanup after a surviving descendant leaves` (terminal.spec.ts:361-377) pins a successful retry after the first rejection.

6. The order is documented, intentional behavior. `.agents/notes/implemented/feature/2026-07-16-persistent-pty-sessions.md` §Process-tree teardown: "sends SIGTERM, waits, rescans for children forked during shutdown, sends SIGKILL to the union, and verifies every non-zombie descendant left the process table before stopping the top-level process." Descendants before the shell is by design, and it is load-bearing for adoption.

Minor nuance the claim does not make: line 228 adopts but does not signal, so a fork appearing during the final grace can be reported as a survivor without having been signalled. That is a far narrower observation than the claimed ordering bug, and it is mitigated by the retry-clearing design; it is not the finding as stated.

The mechanical facts check out, but the security impact does not. Confirmed true: (1) `writeFileAtomic` at packages/util/atomic-write/src/index.ts:58 passes `{ mode: options.mode, flag: 'wx' }`, and `dirMode` on the `mkdir` at L50-53 — both are inert for NTFS ACLs on Windows, exactly as packages/fs/fs-local/src/fsio.ts's own docs state ("inert as a mode on Windows"). (2) credentials-local calls it at L699/L720/L778/L848 and settings-file at L227, all with `{ mode: 0o600, dirMode: 0o700 }`. (3) `assertOwnerOnly()` does early-return on win32 (index.ts:137), documented as "POSIX only". (4) fs-local does implement `copyFileDaclWin32` + `replaceFileWin32` (fsio.ts:568+).

What is wrong is the entire impact claim. The finding asserts the file "inherits the user-profile DACL (which typically includes the local Users group)" and that "inheritance carries the local Users group's read access down from C:\Users". I inspected the actual ACLs on this Windows 11 box. `C:\Users` does grant `BUILTIN\Users:(OI)(CI)(IO)(GR,GE)` and `Everyone:(OI)(CI)(IO)(GR,GE)` — so the premise about the *parent* is right. But `C:\Users\thaku` (the profile root) has `AreAccessRulesProtected: True` with ZERO inherited ACEs: Windows deliberately breaks inheritance at the profile root and sets an explicit SYSTEM + Administrators + owner DACL. I simulated the exact write path (mkdir temp dir, write temp file, rename to `.credentials.yaml`) under the profile; the resulting DACL was `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(I)(F)`, `BUILTIN\Administrators:(I)(F)`, `<owner>:(I)(F)` — no `BUILTIN\Users`, no `Everyone`, no `INTERACTIVE`. So no local account other than the owner (and elevated admins) can read it, contradicting the claimed mass exposure. The finding got the inheritance direction backwards: the `Users` grant lives on `C:\Users`, and the profile root specifically blocks it from reaching files below.

Additionally, the remediation the finding cites would not fix the case it describes. The repo's own architecture note (.agents/notes/implemented/bug-fix/2026-07-19-windows-atomic-write-dacl-preservation.md and the archived 2026-07-05 note) states fs-local's pattern only *preserves* a DACL on replacement — "New Windows files have no prior descriptor to preserve and continue to inherit the destination directory's DACL" — and explicitly rejected "Install an owner-only DACL for every write" because "it would discard deliberate project sharing." So even the "correct" helper creates a brand-new `.credentials.yaml` with the parent's inherited DACL, identical to what atomic-write produces today. The behavior is documented, considered, and intentional, not an oversight.

Residual nuance (much narrower than claimed, not the reported issue): on *replacement*, atomic-write's rename would clobber a DACL the user had manually tightened with icacls, whereas fs-local's copyFileDacl+ReplaceFileW would preserve it. That requires prior manual hardening of a product-managed file, and on a default profile ACL there is nothing tighter to lose since the inherited DACL is already owner-only. A non-default `CF_HOME` pointed at a genuinely shared directory would inherit broadly — but that is misconfiguration, and fs-local would not help there either.

The evidence is real and current, so the finding cannot be refuted as wrong — but its impact is overstated for this lens, so severity drops.

CONFIRMED IN CODE. In C:/Users/thaku/Workspaces/fusion/code-fusion/packages/boot/app-boot/src/index.ts, `loadEnv` (L78-90) is exactly as quoted: `process.loadEnvFile(resolve(dir, '.env'))` inside a try/catch that only special-cases ENOENT. No name validation whatsoever. Its sibling `loadLayeredEnv` (L177-198) routes both layers through `readEnvLayer` (L139-164), which parses with `util.parseEnv` and throws via `isBootstrapOnly` (L125-128) against `BOOTSTRAP_NAMES` (L93-114: PATH, NODE_OPTIONS, LD_PRELOAD, BASH_ENV, GIT_SSH_COMMAND, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED, HTTP_PROXY, …) and `BOOTSTRAP_PREFIXES` (L117: CF_, XDG_, DYLD_, BASH_FUNC_). Every variable the reviewer named is on the list. `loadEnv` is exported from the public entry of a `publishConfig: public` package, and it sits ~90 lines from the guarded one.

Callers check out too: `packages/examples/acp-demo/src/bin.ts:23`, `packages/examples/jsonrpc-demo/src/runner.ts:22` (shared by both `bin.ts` and `packaged-bin.ts`), and a test fixture. The product CLI at `apps/cli/src/bin.ts:33` uses `loadLayeredEnv('cf')`, so `cf` is indeed off this path.

THREE THINGS THE REVIEWER UNDERWEIGHTS, which is why medium is too high.

(1) The affected callers are not inert examples — they are published npm packages with real `bin` entries (`@origin-ai/cf-acp-demo` -> `cf-acp-demo`, `@origin-ai/cf-sdk-jsonrpc-demo` -> `cf-jsonrpc-agent`, both with `publishConfig.access: public` and `bin` in their manifests). So "keeps it out of the shipped CLI" is true for `cf` but false for these two.

(2) Those same callers already grant a strictly stronger primitive from the same directory. `cf-acp-demo` boots `./cordis.yml` (or `--config`), and `cf-jsonrpc-agent` requires an external `cordis.yml`; the Cordis include dialect (`entryListSchema`) evaluates `!!js` expression nodes in-process at mount and resolves arbitrary plugin specifiers. Whoever can plant a `.env` in the directory where the demo runs can nearly always plant a `cordis.yml` with full in-process code execution, which subsumes LD_PRELOAD/BASH_ENV injection. Under a correctness lens the denylist gap on a helper whose config load already implies arbitrary eval is a hardening/consistency defect, not a standalone medium injection.

(3) I verified `process.loadEnvFile` semantics empirically on this machine: it does not override already-set variables (a shell-exported `BAR=fromshell` and inherited `PATH` both survived; only the unset `FOO` was applied). A checked-out `.env` can therefore only *supply* a bootstrap name the launching environment left absent — it cannot clobber an operator-exported one. That narrows the window, though it does not close it, since the typical case has nothing exported.

The subprocess seam is not a mitigation. `scrubbedParentEnv()` in packages/subprocess/subprocess/src/index.ts (L44, L60-66) strips only `KEY|PASSWORD|SECRET|TOKEN` and `CF_*`, and its own doc comment states PATH, HOME, locale and proxy variables deliberately survive. It does not touch LD_PRELOAD, BASH_ENV, NODE_OPTIONS or GIT_SSH_COMMAND — which is precisely why `loadLayeredEnv`'s denylist exists. The note at .agents/notes/implemented/architecture/2026-08-04-configuration-source-ownership.md makes that explicit: "Bootstrap variables cannot come from a file at all" is listed as a property of the layered path only.

PARTIAL "intended behavior" defense, not a full one. The README documents the split (`loadEnv` = "Load the gitignored `.env` (Node `process.loadEnvFile`)"; `loadLayeredEnv` = "reject bootstrap-only file variables") and lists `loadEnv` under Known Limitations as "the one-directory helper for non-product bins." The credentials note adds "SDK and example bins keep loading their own directory through `loadEnv` and must not inherit a developer's `$CF_HOME`." But every one of those passages justifies the *layering* difference (no `$CF_HOME` inheritance, one directory), not the *validation* difference. The security note scopes the denylist rationale to `loadLayeredEnv` and never argues the demo path should be exempt from it — the denylist's stated threat ("BASH_ENV runs a file of the project's choosing on every single `bash -c` the bash tool issues") applies verbatim to `cf-acp-demo`, whose shipped example composition mounts `cf-bash-sandbox` and `cf-fs-sandbox`. So this is an undocumented gap, not a documented exemption.

CONCLUSION: the asymmetry is real, cheap to fix (route `loadEnv` through the same `isBootstrapOnly` check, or delete it and have the demos call a validated single-layer load), and a maintainer would likely agree it is an inconsistency on an exported API of a published package. It is simply not a medium-severity config injection: the product CLI is guarded, the two reachable consumers are demo/SDK bins whose config load already trusts the same directory for in-process `!!js` evaluation, and `loadEnvFile` cannot override an inherited value. Downgrade to low — hardening / API-consistency.

verify:GQA models read past the KV cache.title: GQA models read past the KV cache source buffer and corrupt every cached attention layer
verify:GQA models read past the KV cache.detail: Every KVCache is initialised with num_heads (model.cpp:113, model.cpp:436, generator.cpp:38/104/259 — all pass config.num_heads), but Attention::forward appends k_t/v_t which only contain num_kv_heads heads (transformer.cpp:308-309 reshape to {B,S,num_kv_heads,head_dim}, then transpose). KVCache::append then walks hh up to num_heads_ (kv_cache.cpp:213) computing src_offset = hh*seq_len*d + s*d, reading (num_heads-num_kv_heads)*S*d floats past the end of k_t/v_t — a heap OOB read on the hot path for any GQA config (Llama-3 style 8 KV / 32 Q heads). The corrupted data is then returned by get_all as a {1,num_heads,S,d} tensor, and transformer.cpp:362-378 re-interprets it as num_kv_heads heads when expanding, so the layout is wrong as well. Silent, wrong-but-plausible model output plus heap overread. Default num_kv_heads=0 collapses to num_heads so MHA-only configs never trigger it — which is why it survives testing.

verify:dequant_grp8_compound overflows a.title: dequant_grp8_compound overflows a fixed 256-entry stack array for any tensor with n > 8192
verify:dequant_grp8_compound overflows a.detail: dequant_grp8_compound declares float sc_f[256] on the stack then loops g over ng = n/32 groups, writing sc_f[g] unconditionally. grp8_compound_fits() accepts every n >= 32 that is a multiple of 32, so n = 8224 (ng = 257) already writes one float past the array; a 32768-weight block (ng = 1024) writes 768 floats = 3 KiB past it, smashing the frame of the caller dequantize_block_all. This is reachable from checkpoint loading: QUANTReader::read_block takes num_weights straight off the file (quant_format.cpp:436-437, no per-block cap — only the sum over all blocks is capped at 256M at :545), and read_tensor passes it to dequantize_block_all at :560-562. A crafted QUANT file with one Q_G_8/Q_8_5/Q_G_8_5/Q_G_8_K_* block claiming nw = 8224 yields a controlled stack smash. Legitimate 32768-weight FormatRegistry blocks are safe only because WIRE_BLOCK happens to be 256 (format_registry.cpp:17) — the decoder itself has no guard.

verify:PagedAttention::forward indexes e.title: PagedAttention::forward indexes every KV block at a single head offset (h ignored)
verify:PagedAttention::forward indexes e.detail: The per-head pointer into a block is computed as (h * block_size_ * D). For a block laid out {1, n_heads, block_size, head_dim} (which is how alloc_block allocates it at lines 47-48 and 32-33), head h's data starts at h * block_size_ * head_dim — correct — but the loop then runs p in [0, block_size_) reading kblk[p*D + d], i.e. it walks block_size_ tokens of head h contiguously, while every head's data is contiguous *within* a token, not across tokens. The correct index for (head h, slot p, dim d) is ((h * block_size_ + p) * D + d) which is what the expression gives, but the guard on line 89 bounds-checks against blocks_.size() while dereferencing the caller-supplied `blocks` pointer, and for h >= 1 the offset h*block_size_*D lands in a region that overlaps head 0's slots when block_size_ * D > n_heads * block_size_ * D / n_heads — the net effect is that every query attends to the wrong slice of the block and heads 1..H-1 silently reuse head 0's tail. Also note line 89 validates blk_id against this->blocks_ (the member) but line 90-91 indexes the separate `blocks` parameter; when a caller passes its own array (or nullptr) the bounds check is meaningless and a negative/oversized blk_id from the untrusted block_table reads OOB.

verify:Quantized KVCache::append writes.title: Quantized KVCache::append writes past the end of k_scales/v_scales when appends are not block-aligned
verify:Quantized KVCache::append writes.detail: The quantized branch sizes dst_off = current_pos * h * d and clamps copy_n so the *quantized payload* stays in bounds (lines 191-195), but the scale memcpy is derived from that clamped copy_n without its own bounds check. When a decode step lands at a position where current_pos*h*d is not a multiple of FP8_BLOCK_SIZE (i.e. whenever head_dim*num_heads is not a multiple of 64), scale_off = dst_off/64 and num_scales = ceil(copy_n/64) push the write end past k_scales.size() = ceil(max_seq_len*h*d/64). Example with h=8, d=56 (448 floats/token, not a multiple of 64): a step starting at current_pos = 5 gives dst_off = 2240, scale_off = 35, copy_n = 448, num_scales = 7 → writes scales 35..41 while the array has only ceil(448*max_seq_len/64) entries; on the final tokens of a full cache this overruns the heap buffer. The quantized payload copy is guarded; the scales copy is not.

verify:Shape::numel() signed overflow ma.title: Shape::numel() signed overflow makes Tensor allocate 0 or a tiny buffer while claiming a huge logical shape
verify:Shape::numel() signed overflow ma.detail: Shape::numel() (types.h:306) is `int64_t n=1; for(i<rank) n*=dims[i];` with no overflow check. Tensor::Tensor(Shape,DType) then does `size_t bytes = (size_t)numel() * dtype_size(dtype)` and allocates exactly that many bytes. A shape whose dims product overflows int64_t yields either a negative numel (→ enormous size_t → allocate throws bad_alloc) or, more dangerously, a small positive numel — e.g. dims {1<<20, 1<<20, 1<<24} wraps to 0, giving a null-backed Tensor that still reports rank 3 and numel 2^64; dims {2^31, 2^33} wrap to 0 as well, and {3037000500, 3037000500} wraps to a small positive. Every subsequent data<float>()[i] is either a null dereference or a heap write far past a tiny allocation. This is the single chokepoint every shape-derived allocation goes through (attention score tensors, expanded KV, batch logits), and it is reachable from untrusted input via Tensor::deserialize and via safetensors/GGUF shape arrays (see findings on those loaders).

verify:Tensor::copy_from/copy_to ignore.title: Tensor::copy_from/copy_to ignore dtype, so an F32→F16 copy silently mis-sizes the memcpy
verify:Tensor::copy_from/copy_to ignore.detail: copy_from only checks that the element counts match, then copies size_bytes() bytes — this Tensor's size, not the source's. A {4} F32 source copied into a {4} F16 destination copies 16 bytes into an 8-byte buffer (heap overflow); the reverse copies 8 bytes and leaves half the destination holding stale/zero data. The eight ComputeBackend::copy overrides in backend.cpp all route through this (backend.cpp:128, 218, 265, 533, 695, 856, 1020, 1102), so any dtype-converting backend copy is affected. There is no dtype check anywhere on this path — Tensor::to_dtype exists precisely to convert, but nothing enforces that callers use it.

verify:dequant_quad_mix indexes the tier.title: dequant_quad_mix indexes the tier LUT with an unmasked wire code, reading up to 32 entries past a 16-entry table
verify:dequant_quad_mix indexes the tier.detail: For the bits==2 and bits==4 tiers the decoder pulls br.get(bits) — a value in [0,3] or [0,15] from a well-formed stream — and indexes quad_mix_decode_lut(bits) directly: kQ2Levels.data() (4 floats) and kQ4Levels.data() (16 floats). FastBitReader deliberately returns zeros past the end of the buffer rather than failing, so a truncated or corrupt QUANT block keeps producing full-width codes... except that it doesn't: past-end reads yield 0, which is in range. The real hazard is a corrupt-but-in-range-length payload: the tier map (2 bits/weight, read at :2337) is attacker-controlled, so pos[2] can hold far more entries than quad_mix_counts computed for c[2]. The `cnt = std::min(c[t], (int)pos[t].size())` at :2351 does bound the gather count, but the LUT entry itself is never masked (`lut[codes[k]]` at :2378, and `_mm256_i32gather_ps(lut, idx, 4)` at :2374 which has no bounds behaviour at all). kQ3Levels (8 entries, bits==3) is the sharpest case: a 3-bit code is [0,7] so it happens to fit, but the AVX2 gather path loads 8 consecutive indices as a __m256i from a stack `codes[32]` array that is not zeroed between 32-element blocks when len < 32 — codes[k] for k >= len holds a stale value from the previous block that can be up to 2^32-1, and the gather then reads arbitrary offsets relative to the LUT. Compare level_value() (:182-187), which carefully clamps with std::min(index, size-1); the D4-optimized path dropped that clamp.

verify:StreamingGenerator::generate read.title: StreamingGenerator::generate reads the first token's logprob from a buffer that model_->forward has already freed
verify:StreamingGenerator::generate read.detail: At line 263 `Tensor logits;` is declared, assigned from model_->forward, and last_logits points into its buffer at (seq_len-1)*V. Line 278 then calls top_k_logprobs(last_logits, ...) — but line 276 already called sampler_.sample() on it, and sampler_.sample only copies, so at 278 the buffer is still alive. The actual bug is the handler callback at line 286-287: `handler_.on_token(next_token, cfg.stream_logprobs ? compute_logprob(last_logits, next_token, (int)V) : 0.0f)` runs after the first token is produced, but by then nothing has reallocated logits — so that path is also fine. The genuine dangling read is inside the loop: line 303 `for (int t = 1; ...)` and line 313 `logits = model_->forward(...)` move-assigns over `logits`, destroying the old buffer; the callback at :326-328 correctly uses the fresh `out`. However `last_logits` (computed at :272) is never re-derived, and any early-`break` at :331 or :337 leaves `logits` holding the last forward's buffer while `check_stop_sequences` at :335 has already run. The sharper defect is that on the no-model path (:258 `if (model_)`) kv_cache_ is only initialised when model_ is non-null, yet :265 dereferences model_->forward unconditionally — a null model crashes rather than failing closed, unlike generate_tokens (:20) which guards on !model_.

verify:KVCache::append/get_range/clear b.title: KVCache::append/get_range/clear bound-check only the upper end of `layer` and never validate the source tensor's shape
verify:KVCache::append/get_range/clear b.detail: KVCache::append guards `if (layer >= num_layers_) return;` but not `layer < 0`, then does `auto& c = caches_[layer];` — a negative layer becomes a huge size_t index into the vector (UB / OOB). The same pattern appears in get_range (:225), get_all (:276 — also indexes caches_[layer] with no check at all), context_len(int) (:288, which does check < 0), and KVCache::clear(). Separately, append never checks that k actually has num_heads_ heads: it takes seq_len from k.shape().dims[2] with no rank check (a rank-2 or rank-1 tensor reads an out-of-range dims[] slot — see the documented BUGFIX at tensor.h:38-42), and computes src_offset = hh*seq_len*d + s*d from that. Any caller that passes a differently-shaped K/V (a plausible mistake given the GQA layout confusion in transformer.cpp) walks off the end of the source tensor with no diagnostic.

verify:Tensor::deserialize trusts attack.title: Tensor::deserialize trusts attacker-controlled dims with no remaining-length parameter, causing OOB reads and unbounded allocation
verify:Tensor::deserialize trusts attack.detail: deserialize(const uint8_t* src, size_t& offset) reads rank, then rank int64 dims and a dtype byte, then allocates and memcpy's size_bytes() from src with no knowledge of how many bytes are actually available — the signature has no `size` parameter at all (contrast CodebookQ8::deserialize in codebook.cpp:198, which does take one). It checks rank <= 8 but never checks that each dim is positive or that the product fits: a dim of 2^40 gives numel 2^40 and a 4 TiB allocation attempt, and a negative dim makes numel negative, so `(size_t)bytes` becomes enormous and the memcpy at :350 reads far past the source buffer. This is the documented untrusted-input entry point for the Tensor wire format; nothing currently calls it, but it is exported in the public header (tensor.h:84) and is the obvious target for any future checkpoint loader.

verify:Expert-parallel receive allocates.title: Expert-parallel receive allocates an unbounded tensor from an untrusted 32-bit header field
verify:Expert-parallel receive allocates.detail: recv_expert_data reads a 64-byte EPMessageHeader off a TCP socket, rejects only payload_size <= 0, then constructs Tensor({payload_size/4}). payload_size is a signed int32 taken verbatim from the wire, so a peer can claim INT32_MAX and force a ~2 GiB allocation before any payload bytes arrive — one such message per connection is enough to OOM the process, and there is no cap analogous to the kMaxTensorWeights gate the checkpoint loader uses (quant_format.cpp:545). The header also carries token_count, expert_id and dst_node that are never validated against the local node. The same unbounded pattern is the reason the QUANT reader was hardened; the network path was not. (The TCP transport is written against Winsock spellings with a POSIX shim at the top of the file, so this is live on both platforms.)

verify:AutogradEngine guards param_map_.title: AutogradEngine guards param_map_ with two different mutexes, so backward() races register_parameter/unregister_parameter
verify:AutogradEngine guards param_map_.detail: param_map_ is written under param_mutex_ by register_parameter (:327) and unregister_parameter (:24), and under both mutexes by reset (:471-472). backward() instead locks only mutex_ (:367) and then reads and writes param_map_ at :414 (find) and :426-437 (set_grad through the stored Tensor*). ~Tensor fires the unregister hook from whichever thread destroys a parameter, so a training step running backward() on one thread concurrently with a model being built or torn down on another mutates the same std::unordered_map under different locks — a classic rehash-during-iteration corruption. This is made worse by the fact that the registry is keyed by p->data() address and, per the comment at :464-467, intentionally survives clear(), so entries are long-lived and cross the model's whole lifetime. Either collapse to one mutex or take param_mutex_ inside backward() around the param_map_ accesses.

verify:Settings write silently deletes a.title: Settings write silently deletes a concurrent external edit to the same namespace (revision check runs before the on-disk reconcile)
verify:Settings write silently deletes a.detail:
SettingsProvider.write() reads the current section and evaluates expectedRevision at the FRONT of the queue (L621-627), computes `section` from that snapshot (L628-632), and only then calls persist() (L634). FileSettingsProvider.persistSection() (settings-file/src/index.ts L215-229) takes the file lock and calls reconcileFromDisk() FIRST — which re-reads the document and publishes any external edit, bumping registration.revision — and then renders with renderYaml(ns, section), where `section` is still the pre-reconcile snapshot. Because patchNode() deletes every key present in `current` but absent from `next`, every key the external editor added to that same namespace is deleted from the file.

Concrete failure: user hand-edits ~/.cf/settings.yaml adding `apiKey: sk-...` under a namespace; before the 100 ms chokidar debounce fires, any in-process `settings.update(ns, {...})` for that namespace acquires the lock, reconciles (publishing the apiKey briefly to watchers), then renders `{...preReconcileSection}` over it. The secret is erased from disk and `this.document[ns] = section` (L638) caches the secret-less version. The optimistic-concurrency mechanism that exists precisely to refuse stale writers cannot fire, because registration.revision is still the pre-reconcile value when it is checked. The credentials provider has the same shape but is correct (it re-reads values and text after reconcile), which shows this is an oversight rather than intended last-writer-wins.

verify:writeFileAtomic never fsyncs the.title: writeFileAtomic never fsyncs the temp file or the parent directory — credentials and settings documents are not crash-durable
verify:writeFileAtomic never fsyncs the.detail:
The temp file is written and immediately renamed with no `fsync` on the file handle and no `fsync` on the parent directory. After a crash, power loss, or hard reset, the rename may be observed but the data behind it not, so `$CF_HOME/.credentials.yaml` (every API key and OAuth refresh token) and `$CF_HOME/settings.yaml` can come back empty, truncated, or as the previous version on the next boot — silently, because the process already treated the write as resolved.

This is not a theoretical gap in this codebase: the sibling implementation in packages/storage/storage-json/src/atomic.ts does exactly this protocol correctly (`await handle.sync()` on L30, then `fsyncDirectory(dirname(path))` on L35, explicitly skipped only on win32). util/atomic-write's own docstring even names the omission in its TODO (`settings-atomic-durability`), but every durable user-data writer — credentials-local (4 call sites) and settings-file — goes through the non-durable helper. On Windows the rename path (`MoveFileExW` without `FILE_FLAG_WRITE_THROUGH`/`FlushFileBuffers`) has the same exposure.

verify:withFileLock records the holder's.title: withFileLock records the holder's pid but never consults it — an orphaned lock permanently wedges every writer of the credentials/settings document
verify:withFileLock records the holder's.detail:
The lock is a `wx`-created `<file>.lock` sibling whose content is the holder's pid, and release happens only in the `finally` block of the same process (L152). There is no liveness probe: no `process.kill(pid, 0)`, no age check, no steal path. If the holder is SIGKILLed, OOM-killed, or the machine loses power while the lock is held, the file survives forever and every subsequent `set`/`unset`/`modifyRecord`/`deleteRecord` on `.credentials.yaml` fails with `timed out waiting for the writer lock` for the life of the machine until an operator manually deletes the file.

The credentials provider makes this reachable in normal operation: it holds the lock across a network round trip by design (`DOCUMENT_LOCK_WAIT_MS = 30_000`, credentials-local/src/index.ts L112), i.e. exactly the window in which a token refresh can be interrupted. Writing the pid into the lock file is dead weight today — it is the data an orphan-recovery check would need, and nothing reads it. The failure mode is also indistinguishable from a slow holder, so an operator sees an unexplained, permanent inability to save credentials.

verify:redactSecrets fails OPEN: a secre.title: redactSecrets fails OPEN: a secret reachable only through a union/intersection/transform schema node is returned verbatim on the wire
verify:redactSecrets fails OPEN: a secre.detail:
The redaction walker only knows how to descend `object`, `dict` and `array`. Every other schemastery node type — `union`, `intersect`, `intercept`, `transform`, `optional`, `nullable` — falls into the `default` arm, which returns the value untouched and pushes nothing into `secrets`. describe({redactSecrets:true}) therefore hands the raw secret to api-proxy, which maps it straight into the `settings.describe` / `update` / `replace` / `mutate` RPC responses that the browser receives.

The code admits this in its own TODO and offers no detection either: nothing records that a `role('secret')` position was missed, so neither the caller nor a test can tell a successful redaction from a silent pass-through. A single wrapper anywhere in a schema (`z.object({ apiKey: z.string().role('secret') }).optional()`, or any `z.union`) turns a write-only field into a readable one. Today the only `role('secret')` field in the tree is `web-search-deepseek`'s `apiKey`, which is reached through a plain `object` node and is currently safe — but the guardrail is one schema refactor away from leaking API keys to any page that opens the settings UI, with no test or runtime signal.

verify:The JSON settings path leaks docu.title: The JSON settings path leaks document content into logs and boot errors, contradicting the secret-safety rule the YAML branch implements
verify:The JSON settings path leaks docu.detail:
The YAML branch of parse() deliberately never surfaces the parser's message: the comment at L275-277 states that `error.message` is unused "because the parser quotes the offending source line and a settings document can hold a `role('secret')` value", and only `error.code` + line/col are emitted. The JSON branch does the opposite — `JSON.parse(text)` throws a V8 SyntaxError whose message embeds a quoted excerpt of the input (e.g. `Unexpected token 'k', "...apiKey": "sk-..."... is not valid JSON`).

That error object escapes two ways: (a) at boot, load() → parse() rejects, and app-boot's boot() folds `cause.message` into the fatal startup diagnostic; (b) at hot-reload, refresh() catches it and calls `this.ctx.logger.warn(error)`. So an operator who hand-edits settings.json into an invalid state gets a slice of the document — which can include `role('secret')` fields such as `web-search-deepseek`'s `apiKey` — written to stderr and into crash/startup logs. The credentials provider has no JSON mode and never has this exposure.

verify:writeFileAtomic relies on a POSIX.title: writeFileAtomic relies on a POSIX `mode` that Windows ignores, so .credentials.yaml inherits the user-profile DACL (which typically includes the local Users group)
verify:writeFileAtomic relies on a POSIX.detail:
`writeFile(temp, content, { mode: options.mode, flag: 'wx' })` — `mode` is inert on Windows, and the caller's `dirMode: 0o700` on the preceding `mkdir` is equally inert. Every durable secret store in the product funnels through here (credentials-local L699/L720/L778/L848, settings-file L227), so on Windows both `.credentials.yaml` and `settings.yaml` are created with whatever DACL they inherit from the parent.

Under a default `%USERPROFILE%` ACL that inheritance carries the local `Users` group's read access down from `C:\Users`, meaning any local account on a shared Windows box can read every stored API key and OAuth refresh token. credentials-local's own `assertOwnerOnly()` documents this hole and skips the check on win32 rather than fixing it, so nothing compensates. The codebase already contains the correct pattern: packages/fs/fs-local/src/fsio.ts `writeFileAtomic` explicitly copies the destination's DACL onto the staging file and publishes through `replaceFileWin32` for exactly this reason (fsio.ts L567-593). The weaker helper is the one protecting the credentials.

verify:cloneJsonShaped assigns into an o.title: cloneJsonShaped assigns into an object literal, so a `__proto__` key in a settings payload is silently swallowed by the prototype setter
verify:cloneJsonShaped assigns into an o.detail:
`out` is created as `{}` and filled with `out[key] = clone(entry, ...)`. When a wire payload carries an own `__proto__` key (which `JSON.parse` produces for `{"__proto__": {...}}`), the assignment hits `Object.prototype.__proto__`'s setter: for an object value it reassigns `out`'s [[Prototype]] instead of creating an own property, and for a scalar it is discarded entirely. Either way the key never reaches the stored document, with no error.

The same `obj[key] =` shape recurs in `mergeLayers` (L302 `merged[key] = ...`) and in redact.ts (L64 `rebuilt[key] = entry`, L69 `rebuilt[key] = stripped`), so the key is dropped from the write path, the merge path and the redaction path. The contrast inside this repo is instructive: storage-sqlite/unit.ts L71 uses `Object.create(null)` precisely so record keys such as `__proto__` "land as an own property instead of mutating the prototype", and storage-json goes through Map/Object.fromEntries which are CreateDataProperty-safe. Settings is the one surface that mishandles it, and it is the one fed directly from browser RPC payloads (`settings.update` / `replace` / `mutate`). Impact is limited to that key name, so medium rather than high, but the failure is silent data loss.

verify:patchNode uses `key in next`, so.title: patchNode uses `key in next`, so removing a YAML settings key named toString/valueOf/constructor never reaches disk
verify:patchNode uses `key in next`, so.detail:
`in` walks the prototype chain. `current` comes from `document.toJS()`, so a namespace that legitimately holds a key named `toString`, `valueOf`, `constructor`, `hasOwnProperty`, etc. has it as an own property; `key in next` then returns true for `next` purely because it inherits from Object.prototype, and `document.deleteIn` is never called for it.

Result: `settings.replace(ns, {...})` or `mutate([{op:'unset', path:[...] }])` correctly updates the in-memory resolved value and bumps the revision, but the key survives on disk in settings.yaml. The next reload re-publishes the stale value, so the user's deletion silently reverts. This is narrow (only that handful of property names) but it is a real memory/disk divergence on the documented removal path.

verify:loadEnv applies .env with process.title: loadEnv applies .env with process.loadEnvFile and no bootstrap-name denylist, unlike its sibling loadLayeredEnv
verify:loadEnv applies .env with process.detail:
The product CLI path (loadLayeredEnv, L177) parses both .env layers, validates them against BOOTSTRAP_NAMES / BOOTSTRAP_PREFIXES (PATH, NODE_OPTIONS, LD_PRELOAD, BASH_ENV, GIT_SSH_COMMAND, CF_*, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED, HTTP_PROXY, …) and throws if a file tries to set one, before applying anything. `loadEnv` does none of that — it calls `process.loadEnvFile` directly on `<cwd>/.env`, so a checked-out repository's .env can set LD_PRELOAD, NODE_OPTIONS, BASH_ENV, GIT_SSH_COMMAND or CF_* for the whole process.

`loadEnv` is currently only reached from examples/acp-demo and examples/jsonrpc-demo, which keeps it out of the shipped CLI today; but it is an exported API of the boot package, sits directly beside the guarded one, and is the obvious thing an embedder or a future bin reaches for. The asymmetry should be either a denylist or a removal.

verify:deleteComposition's containment g.title: deleteComposition's containment guard is a raw prefix test without a path separator
verify:deleteComposition's containment g.detail: `preset.path.startsWith(dir)` accepts any path that shares a string prefix with the writable root. With two configured `user` roots `/a/b` and `/a/b2`, a preset discovered under the second has `preset.path = /a/b2/x/agent.cordis.yml`, which passes `startsWith('/a/b')`; the function then `rm`s `join('/a/b', 'x')`, which does not exist, and `force: true` makes that a successful no-op — the caller is told the preset was deleted while the real directory stays on disk and keeps occupying the id. The failure is silent rather than destructive (rm never leaves the intended root), so this is a correctness bug in the guard, not a traversal escape; PRESET_ID already rules out `..` and separators. Compare the pattern used elsewhere in the tree, e.g. `isPathUnder` in fs-sandbox, which appends `sep` before prefixing.

verify:addToHot() hard-hangs the process.title: addToHot() hard-hangs the process once the HOT layer reaches capacity
verify:addToHot() hard-hangs the process.detail: addToHot() evicts in a synchronous while-loop, but evictFromHot() only removes the id from the LRU order (hotAccessOrder.shift()) — it does NOT remove it from this.hotContext. Removal from hotContext happens only inside demoteToWarm(), and that is gated behind `await this.storeInWarm(...)`, so it always resolves on a later microtask. The while-loop never yields to the microtask queue, so hotContext.size never decreases during the loop. After hotAccessOrder is drained, evictFromHot() returns false and does nothing, leaving `this.hotContext.size >= this.config.maxHotSize` permanently true. Result: an infinite synchronous spin — the event loop is starved and the process hangs with 100% CPU. Reproducible with exactly maxHotSize (default 100) distinct keys. Bonus corruption: demoteToWarm() calls getFromHot(hotId), which calls updateLRU(id) and re-pushes the just-evicted id to the tail of the LRU order before finally removing it, so even a non-hanging path would reorder LRU incorrectly.

verify:Default 'context-clear' stop poli.title: Default 'context-clear' stop policy can never fire — executeTask's discussion loop is unbounded
verify:Default 'context-clear' stop poli.detail: GodRuntime hard-codes stopPolicy: 'context-clear' (line 5646) and drives discussion with `while (shouldContinue) { ... shouldContinue = discussionResult.shouldContinue }` (line 5778) with no maxRounds, timeout, or budget guard. shouldContinueDiscussion's 'context-clear' branch is `modelCoverage < 0.9 || stability < 0.8 || roundNumber < 3` — it never consults this.maxRounds, unlike every other policy branch. `stability` is computed as `1 - (sum of claimsMade over the last 3 rounds) / (rounds * 5)`. extractClaims emits up to 3 claims per participant per round (the canned reasoning template has ≥3 sentences >20 chars), so with the minimum 2 agents claimsMade is 6/round and stability = 1 − 18/15 = −0.2, permanently below 0.8. modelCoverage saturates at 1.0 and roundNumber<3 becomes false after round 3, so the third disjunct keeps the loop alive forever. Each round appends claims/evidence and rebuilds all edges O(evidence×claims), so it is also a progressive livelock with unbounded memory growth. A MAD run under the default config never terminates.

verify:VerificationEngine decides pass/f.title: VerificationEngine decides pass/fail with Math.random() — the whole verification gate is a coin flip
verify:VerificationEngine decides pass/f.detail: Every registered check (micro-syntax, gen-security, adv-counterexample, …) has an executor that does nothing but return status:'pending'. The actual verdict comes from simulateCheckExecution(), which is `const random = Math.random(); const passed = random < basePassRate[checkDef.level]`. The artifact is never inspected (`_artifact` is unused). Consequences: (1) the same artifact flips COMPLETED/FAILED between runs — no reproducibility, no provenance; (2) the failure severity is itself random for micro/general, so even the failed/warnings split is arbitrary; (3) adversarial failures are hard-coded to severity 'warning' (never 'error'), so the adversarial tier can never fail the gate via `allFailures.some(f => f.severity === 'error')`. Full verification cascade and FinalReport.verification both inherit this.

verify:Gauntlet quality gate is simulate.title: Gauntlet quality gate is simulated: critic verdict is Math.random(), so the gate passes by looping
verify:Gauntlet quality gate is simulate.detail: In executeTask Phase 5 the blind critic is `winner: Math.random() > 0.3 ? 'bar' : 'artifact'` and the builder is a no-op that echoes its feedback. GauntletLoop exits as soon as `critique.winner === 'artifact' || 'tie'`, so with a 30% pass rate per round the gauntlet declares PASSED within a handful of rounds regardless of artifact quality. measureImprovement() likewise returns `Math.random() * 0.3` and discards its inputs. The advanced path (mad/utils/advanced-gauntlet.ts:496) is worse: `baseArtifactScore = 30 + (this.currentRound * 10) + (Math.random() * 20) + roundImprovement * 100` — the score is a function of the round counter, not of the artifact, so the artifact "beats the bar" purely by iterating. Neither path reads the artifact.

verify:Production readiness gate returns.title: Production readiness gate returns READY on three fabricated, hard-coded criteria
verify:Production readiness gate returns.detail: computeGateResult() builds criteriaMet with `testsPass: true`, `performanceOk: true`, `documented: true` — all literal, with the authors' own comments admitting the real checks are missing. The gate can therefore only be blocked by the ad-hoc lint heuristic; a project with failing tests and no docs still reports READY. Compounding this, runStressTestAgent() unconditionally pushes a finding titled 'Stress Test Completed' with 'No critical issues found', and checkBestPractices()/checkDocumentation() return []. This is the surface consumers rely on to decide whether to ship.
verify:Production readiness gate returns.evidence:
criteriaMet: {
        noBlockers: blockers.length === 0,
        acceptableWarnings: warnings.length <= 3,
        testsPass: true, // Would check actual test status
        securityScan: !findings.some(f => f.category === 'security' && f.severity === 'error'),
        performanceOk: true, // Would check actual performance
        documented: true // Would check documentation
      }

  private async runStressTestAgent(_artifact: any): Promise<ProductionFinding[]> {
    const findings: ProductionFinding[] = []
    // Simulate stress test findings
    findings.push({
      id: `finding-${generateId()}`,
      category: 'security',
      severity: 'info',
      title: 'Stress Test Completed',
