      description: 'Basic stress testing performed. No critical issues found.',

verify:LLMProviderManager.stream() conve.title: LLMProviderManager.stream() converts a failed stream into a successful empty completion
verify:LLMProviderManager.stream() conve.detail: stream() wraps the per-provider generator in try/catch and, on any error (HTTP 4xx/5xx, abort, network), yields a final chunk with `delta: ''` and `isFinal: true` carrying the error only in `metadata.error`, then swallows the exception. Every consumer that keys off isFinal/delta (the only fields most stream loops look at) sees a clean, successful, empty completion — no throw, no retry, no circuit-breaker trip. Combined with the `complete()` retry loop directly above (which retries all errors including non-retryable 401/400), auth failures are silently swallowed on the streaming path and blindly retried on the non-streaming path.

verify:StateManager rejects legal MAD pi.title: StateManager rejects legal MAD pipeline configs; AdvancedMADEngine's finally block masks the original error
verify:StateManager rejects legal MAD pi.detail: transitionTo() THROWS on any transition not in the allow-list, and executeTask awaits it at every phase. 'PLANNING' only permits ['DISCUSSING','VERIFYING','READY','ERROR'] and 'DEBUGGING' the same. So `createGODRuntime({ verification: { enabled: false }, gauntlet: { enabled: true } })` in PLAN/DEBUG mode reaches Phase 5 from PLANNING and throws `Invalid state transition: PLANNING -> GAUNTLET`; the same happens for productionSweep without verification. Separately, AdvancedMADEngine.execute() wraps everything in `catch { return {... status:'FAILED'} } finally { await this.godRuntime.shutdown() }` — shutdown() calls transitionTo('SHUTTING_DOWN') which is not reachable from IDLE, so if initialize() failed the finally throws and the promise REJECTS instead of returning the FAILED result the catch was written to provide, replacing the original cause. Finally, shutdown() sets initialized=false but leaves activeAgents populated, so the next execute() re-registers the same root ids and activeAgents grows by N every session, inflating the discussion participant list and the `agentUtilization` division at line 5922 (which is also NaN when activeAgents is empty).

verify:BYOK: cost is priced off the wron.title: BYOK: cost is priced off the wrong map key, the budget is never enforced, and unknown-provider fallback recurses forever
verify:BYOK: cost is priced off the wron.detail: Three defects in the credential/budget manager. (1) estimateCost does `baseRates[provider?.name.toLowerCase() ?? 'openai']` — but baseRates is keyed by provider *id* ('openai','anthropic',…) while ProviderConfig.name is the display name ('OpenAI','Google AI','Muse'). 'openai'→'openai' happens to match, but every other provider (anthropic, google, deepseek, opencode, muse, and all custom providers) falls through to the `|| 0.00003` default, so dailySpent/monthlySpent and every per-key totalCost are wrong — Anthropic is billed at the OpenAI rate. (2) Nothing anywhere calls getBudgetStatus() or blocks on it: dailySpent/monthlySpent are tracked and alerted on, but no request path refuses to run past the ceiling, so the budget is advisory only. (3) tryFallback() iterates fallbackChain and calls getKey(fallbackProvider); getKey() on a provider with zero keys calls tryFallback(fallbackProvider) again. With the default fallbackChain ['openai','anthropic','google'] and no keys registered, each entry re-enters the chain with a different failedProvider — exponential re-entry over a 3-element array (and unbounded if a custom chain contains a cycle), producing an exponential blow-up of console traffic and stack depth. Additionally, when no healthy key matches the requested model, getKey silently falls back to *unhealthy* keys carrying a different model, so a caller can be handed a key that cannot serve the requested model.

verify:EventBus.request leaks a permanen.title: EventBus.request leaks a permanent listener on every timeout and cross-delivers responses between concurrent callers
verify:EventBus.request leaks a permanen.detail: Two independent bugs in the request/response correlation. (a) The timeout branch only sets settled and rejects — it never calls unsubscribe(), so every timed-out request leaves a permanent handler registered on `${eventType}.response` forever; the handler closure (and its captured data) is never collected and keeps firing no-op checks on every subsequent response. (b) requestId is minted AFTER the subscription is installed, and the handler accepts a response whenever `!event.metadata?.requestId || event.metadata.requestId === requestId`. So a response emitted without a requestId — which is exactly what a non-cooperating responder produces — satisfies whichever pending request's handler runs first. Two concurrent request() calls for the same eventType can therefore resolve with each other's payloads, and the loser hangs until its own timeout (which then leaks per (a)).

verify:IntelligentCache.set() double-sub.title: IntelligentCache.set() double-subtracts an entry's size when eviction selects the key being replaced
verify:IntelligentCache.set() double-sub.detail: set() unconditionally subtracts the old entry's estimated size up front (`this.currentSize -= estimateSize(existingEntry.value)`) but leaves the stale entry in the Map. The eviction loop then runs `while (this.currentSize + size > this.maxBytes && this.cache.size > 0) evictLRU()`, and evictLRU's LRU score (`timestamp + accesses*1000`) can legitimately select that same still-present key. delete() then subtracts the old size a second time. Net effect after the write: currentSize = original − 2×old + new. Once the cache is under memory pressure this drifts monotonically negative, so the cache believes it has unbounded headroom and stops evicting — a slow unbounded-memory leak on exactly the path the maxMemoryMB cap exists to protect. maxEntries (default 10000) is declared in CacheConfig and never enforced anywhere, so entry count is also unbounded.

verify:PolicyAgentTreeManager.terminateA.title: PolicyAgentTreeManager.terminateAgent never removes nodes from the tree, permanently exhausting maxTotalAgents
verify:PolicyAgentTreeManager.terminateA.detail: terminateAgent() recursively marks descendants 'active'→'terminated' and clears childrenIds, but never deletes anything from this.agentTree. spawnChildAgent() gates on `this.agentTree.size >= this.spawnPolicy.maxTotalAgents`, and cleanupIdleAgents() (called from GodRuntime.shutdown, with the default 5-minute idle timeout) terminates agents all the time. Every terminated agent therefore continues to occupy a slot forever. After maxTotalAgents (default 20) spawn/terminate cycles — which the idle sweeper manufactures on its own — every subsequent spawnChildAgent throws 'Max total agents (20) exceeded' and the tree is permanently wedged. getActiveAgents() correctly filters by status, so getTreeStatistics() and spawn capacity disagree. A second, related bug: spawnChildAgent uses `childConfig.id || generateId()`; a duplicate configured id silently overwrites the previous node in the Map while the parent's childrenIds retains the id twice, corrupting the tree.

verify:Published Scheduler never tracks.title: Published Scheduler never tracks cost, so costUsd budgets are entirely unenforced
verify:Published Scheduler never tracks.detail: In the published @origin-ai/cf-god-runtime package, costUsed is declared (line 296), read in isExhausted() (line 326) and snapshot() (line 333), and never written by anything. reserveResources(agentCount, tokens) checks and increments only concurrency and tokens — it never consults budgets.costUsd. So a BudgetPolicy of { costUsd: 0.01 } is accepted (the constructor's 'at least one ceiling' check passes) and then never trips. Since GodRuntime.checkProgress() is defined as `!this.scheduler.isExhausted()`, the progress gate that is supposed to stop a run when budget is exhausted can never fire on cost. releaseResources(_agentId) also ignores its argument and blindly decrements, so an unmatched release silently inflates free capacity. Adjacent in the same package: Router.eligibilityReason() explicitly ignores requiredTools/permissions/capability/contextWindow (line 206-218 — only available/healthy are checked) and DiscussionBus.mustContinue() is hardcoded `return true` (discussion-bus/src/index.ts:216) with no timeout or budget guard, so the bus's documented 'timeout + budget guard' does not exist.

verify:`--host 0.0.0.0` is rejected only.title: `--host 0.0.0.0` is rejected only as a CLI string literal; the webserver still accepts an all-interfaces bind and then auto-trusts every LAN IPv4
verify:`--host 0.0.0.0` is rejected only.detail: The safety rail is a single string comparison inside the commander action of `cf --profile web`. The `WebServer` service still declares `0.0.0.0` as a legal config value (`packages/host/webserver/src/index.ts:61,75`), so any other composition path — a `cordis.yml`/`cordis.patch.yml` overlay, an embedder constructing the service directly, or a future caller that sets `host` from somewhere other than this one flag — binds all interfaces with no refusal. When the bind host *is* `0.0.0.0`, `resolveLanTrust` then enumerates every non-internal IPv4 on the machine and appends them all to the `/api` browser-trust fence's `trustedHosts`. Those are port-less entries, so they match the Host on **any** port. Net effect of reaching an all-interfaces bind by any route other than the CLI literal: the full RPC surface (`session.prompt`, `host.openPath`, `credentials.set`, …) is reachable from every device on the LAN with no authentication — the exact outcome the error message says it prevents. The check belongs in the webserver's schema (or `resolveLanTrust`), not in one argv parse.

verify:No security headers on any static.title: No security headers on any static response, and no CSP in the web app document
verify:No security headers on any static.detail: `content-type` is the only header ever set on the SPA surface. There is no `Content-Security-Policy`, no `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, no `Referrer-Policy`, and no `frame-ancestors`/`X-Frame-Options` anywhere in the serving path (grep over the whole repo for these names returns nothing), and `apps/web/index.html` carries no CSP `<meta>`. The document renders LLM-authored markdown and sits in the same origin as an RPC surface that can run shell commands as the host user, so there is zero output-side containment if a renderer bug ever slips through — the markdown renderer itself looks sound (protocol allowlist, raw HTML kept as literal text, shiki escaping), making this defense-in-depth rather than an open hole. The fix is real but not free: `renderIndexInjections` splices inline `<script>` rows into the head and body, so a CSP must allow `'unsafe-inline'` for scripts until those rows are nonced or externalized; `script-src 'self'` alone would work for everything else since the loader uses `import()`, not `eval`. `nosniff` is free and should ship regardless.
verify:No security headers on any static.evidence:
// frontend-static/src/index.ts:95 — the complete set of response headers
res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': type })
res.end(body)

// apps/web/index.html — no CSP, no referrer-policy, no frame-ancestors
<meta charset="utf-8" />
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.webmanifest" />
<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/favicon.svg" />
<title>CF Local Build</title>

verify:Sourcemaps with full `sourcesCont.title: Sourcemaps with full `sourcesContent` are emitted into the dist that the host serves
verify:Sourcemaps with full `sourcesCont.detail: `sourcemap: true` writes `.js.map` files beside every chunk in `apps/web/dist`, and `frontend-static` deliberately MIME-maps `.map` to `application/json`, so they are served over the same `/` origin as the app. `package.json`'s `files: ["dist", "!dist/**/*.map"]` and `.npmignore`'s `*.map` only strip the maps from the **npm tarball** — they do nothing for the served directory, and `apps/cli`'s `cf web` serves `apps/web/dist` directly. Verified on the built tree: `dist/assets/index-BKSebiLg.js.map` (1.0 MB) carries `sourcesContent` for `packages/client/web/lib/index.js`, `packages/client/ui-primitives/lib/index.js`, `packages/client/ui-slots/lib/index.js` and `apps/web/src/main.ts`. The host-side request fence keeps this off the network for anonymous callers, but any script executing at the loopback origin (an XSS, a malicious plugin bundle from the client-module system, which is loaded as same-origin script) gets the full original sources with no extra request. Gate the maps behind a build profile the way `CF_BUILD_CLIENT_PROFILE` already gates the official environment.

verify:Static responses carry no Cache-C.title: Static responses carry no Cache-Control, ETag or Last-Modified, so content-hashed assets are never cache-validated
verify:Static responses carry no Cache-C.detail: The same `writeHead(200, { 'content-type': type })` sets no freshness or validator headers. Vite emits content-hashed filenames (`vendor-CGZwCgY8.js`, 745 KB; `index-BKSebiLg.js`, 390 KB) precisely so they can be marked immutable, but nothing marks them, and there is no ETag/Last-Modified path back to a cheap 304. Meanwhile `index.html` — the one mutable document that names which hashed assets exist — gets no `no-cache`, so a client that does cache it heuristically can reference assets a rebuild has already rotated away, producing a blank shell until a hard reload. Splitting on the `/` root and the configured index from ordinary assets fixes both sides in one place.

verify:The `script`/`style`/`html` injec.title: The `script`/`style`/`html` injection-row kinds splice caller text verbatim while their type contract only documents the invariant
verify:The `script`/`style`/`html` injec.detail: `renderRow` escapes `<` to `<` for the `global` kind specifically so a row-controlled string cannot break out of its script element — the correct treatment, applied to exactly one of the four kinds. `script`, `style` and `html` interpolate `row.text` / `row.html` directly into `<script>`, `<style>` and the document, while their JSDoc merely states "text must not contain `</script`" with no runtime check. Today's only producers are safe (`bootInjections` builds a static template plus a JSON-stringified constant; `bootThemeInjection` interpolates a schema-validated enum), so this is not currently exploitable — but this is the one injection boundary in the whole web app, the contract is unenforced, and any future plugin that pushes a row containing model- or user-derived text gets a document breakout with no failure at the boundary. One `assert` in `renderRow` closes it permanently.

verify:WebSocket downlinks register no h.title: WebSocket downlinks register no heartbeat, so a silently dropped client leaves its event-stream subscription open indefinitely
verify:WebSocket downlinks register no h.detail: `upgrade()` wires exactly three one-shot listeners — `close`, `error`, and a `message` guard that rejects client traffic with 1008. There is no ping/pong interval and no idle deadline anywhere on the class, and `this.server.clients` is only drained by an explicit `terminate()` inside `close()`, which runs at plugin disposal. A client whose TCP path breaks without a FIN (laptop sleep, Wi-Fi roam, a suspended VM) leaves the socket in `this.server.clients` and, more importantly, leaves the `api.events.mux()` / `api.events.host()` async iterator that `pump` is iterating subscribed on the host. On a long-lived local daemon that is an unbounded accumulation of live stream subscriptions and their buffers. `ws` exposes `ping()`/`pong` on the server side; a 30s interval that terminates a socket with no pong in the window is the standard fix and needs no protocol change.

verify:`clientBuildEnvironment` inlines.title: `clientBuildEnvironment` inlines every `CF_CLIENT_*` env var into the browser bundle with no allowlist
verify:`clientBuildEnvironment` inlines.detail: `clientBuildEnvironmentDefines`, consumed by `apps/web/vite.config.ts`, turns every environment variable whose name starts with `CF_CLIENT_` into a literal `define` substitution in the shipped JavaScript. The only thing standing between an environment variable and the public bundle is the name prefix — `CF_CLIENT_API_KEY`, `CF_CLIENT_TOKEN` or `CF_CLIENT_SECRET` would all be inlined verbatim by a plain `npm run build:web` or `npm run cf web`. The exact-key-set assertion (`assertClientBuildEnvironment`) exists but is only exercised by the `official` CI profile; a developer-machine or ad-hoc build runs the unfiltered path with no check at all. Replace the prefix filter with an explicit allowlist (`CF_CLIENT_TITLE`, `CF_CLIENT_COMMIT_HASH`, `CF_CLIENT_BUILD_PROFILE` — the three the official profile actually names) and fail the build on any other `CF_CLIENT_*` variable rather than silently publishing it.

verify:The browser-trust fence has no en.title: The browser-trust fence has no end-to-end coverage over a live HTTP server
verify:The browser-trust fence has no en.detail: `isTrustedApiRequest` is the DNS-rebinding and cross-site defense for the entire `/api` surface, and its only coverage is `packages/client/connection/tests/api-request-trust.host.spec.ts` — 108 lines of assertions against the pure predicate with hand-built header objects. The next layer up, `node-half.host.spec.ts:22-29`, stubs `register`/`registerUpgrade` entirely, so the wiring in `connection/src/index.ts` (the route handler's `isTrustedApiRequest(req, trustedHosts)`, the privileged-method re-check with an empty trust list, the upgrade rejection path) is never observed over real HTTP. And the one web-lane test that *does* boot the real `cf web` server only asserts the happy path — that the ready line is a loopback URL and that `fetch` returns 200. Nothing in the repo ever sends a rebound Host, a cross-site `Origin`, or a `sec-fetch-site: cross-site` marker at the live server and asserts 403. A regression that drops the fence would go green everywhere.

verify:`clientDocumentTitle` silently no.title: `clientDocumentTitle` silently no-ops if the title placeholder ever drifts
verify:`clientDocumentTitle` silently no.detail: The plugin rewrites the document title by string-replacing the literal `<title>CF Local Build</title>`. If that exact substring is absent — someone edits `index.html`'s title, or a Vite/react plugin reorders `transformIndexHtml` ahead of this one and normalizes the element — `String.replace` matches nothing and the build succeeds with the placeholder title in the shipped artifact. Official builds set `CF_CLIENT_TITLE=CodeFusion` and assert that environment through `assertClientBuildEnvironment`, so the environment is checked while the HTML substitution it exists to perform is not. `smoke-real.e2e.ts` only asserts `document.title` *after* the running app has rewritten it, and no test pins the built `dist/index.html`'s title. Throw (or at least warn) when the placeholder is missing.

verify:The HTTP bridge collapses multi-v.title: The HTTP bridge collapses multi-valued response headers when re-emitting them onto the node response
verify:The HTTP bridge collapses multi-v.detail: `Object.fromEntries(response.headers.entries())` produces one value per header name, so any header the upstream `Response` carries more than one of is silently reduced to its last value. Today the `/api` responses only set single-valued headers (`content-type`, `cache-control`, and the 426 upgrade pair), so nothing is broken yet — but `session.export` already returns a Response assembled from the attachment/download path, and `set-cookie`-style multi-value headers cannot survive this bridge if a future route needs them. Node's `res.setHeader(name, string[])` accepts arrays; passing the raw header list through rather than a folded map removes the foot-gun at no cost.

verify:Blocking Stop hook force-continue.title: Blocking Stop hook force-continues the turn forever with no cap and a hardcoded stop_hook_active of false
verify:Blocking Stop hook force-continue.detail: Both bridges map a deny decision at the agent/turn-stopping extension point to agent.steer(), which enqueues into inbox.nextStep. In core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts the step loop only breaks when turnEnds is set and inbox.nextStep is empty, so the steer creates another step, which ends, which re-fires agent/turn-stopping, which runs the Stop hook again. There is no consecutive-continuation counter, no backoff, and no run-level halt; the code's own TODO admits it. Worse, stop_payload always sends stop_hook_active as false, so the standard Claude Code loop-guard idiom (a Stop hook that exits 2 only when stop_hook_active is false) can never detect that it is already inside a forced continuation. A single misconfigured exit-2 Stop hook therefore spins the agent in an unbounded model-call loop until the user cancels, burning tokens and never letting the session end. The Codex twin has the identical defect at hooks-codex/src/index.ts lines 260-270 with its own TODO.

verify:undefine and stop do not cancel o.title: undefine and stop do not cancel or await an in-flight host-half activation, orphaning a live fiber with registered tools
verify:undefine and stop do not cancel o.detail: activate() at line 810 registers its promise in this.starting and then awaits startFresh(), which itself awaits evaluateHostCode and startHostHalf (group.await plus fiber.await) before assigning plugin.run. Neither undefine (line 210) nor stop (line 456) touches this.starting: undefine computes wasRunning from plugin.run which is still undefined mid-start, retract() no-ops, and registry.delete removes the only handle to the plugin. The in-flight startFresh then completes and sets plugin.run on the now-unregistered object, emits cordis/dynamic-package, and leaves a live fiber hanging under the shared cordis-dynamic group with its harness.handle methods and any registered tools still live. Because the plugin is gone from the registry, no later stop, undefine, or inspect can ever find or dispose it, so the removal guarantee advertised in the cordis_undefine tool description is silently violated. stop is worse UX-wise: it returns not-running for a plugin that starts a moment later.

verify:Runs left in starting-host or cli.title: Runs left in starting-host or client-pending are never reconciled, permanently wedging the plugin in transition-in-flight
verify:Runs left in starting-host or cli.detail: reconcileApprovals only surfaces a Host run whose latest attempt is awaiting-approval, starting-host, or client-pending AND whose package row is still resolvable. A run parked in starting-host or client-pending has no page-side plan and no approval answer, so nothing ever calls resolveRequestRun for it; the request stays armed in the Host registry forever. Any subsequent cordis_run for that plugin is then rejected by resolvePlan starting check and by run pendingRequestFor with transition-in-flight, so the plugin can never be started again in that process. The realistic trigger is a browser tab closing mid-activation (after runHostHalf returns starting-host but before the page settles the client half) or a page that throws between the two. There is no timeout, no page-liveness probe, and no host-side reaper for these orphans.

verify:The sandbox ctx and tool facade i.title: The sandbox ctx and tool facade is escapable through any host-realm function, so the guard stated invariants are unenforceable
verify:The sandbox ctx and tool facade i.detail: guardedService at line 685 and the ctx facade at line 753 wrap host objects in host-realm Proxies and forward host functions wrapped in host-realm arrow functions. From inside the VM sandbox, any of those values yields the host realm: calling .constructor.constructor on ctx.on, or on ctx.tools, returns the host Function and gives full process access with no require trap needed. The tool-registry facade docblock claims the purpose is that package code cannot call another tool directly and bypass ToolRuntime.execute (identity protection, pre-policy, monotonic guards, around dispatch, post-policy, final observation) and that get returns nothing invocable; that invariant does not hold against a non-cooperative package. The module header does admit host-realm helper functions remain an escape route, but the practical consequence is that the only real control is the human approval gate in the host runner, and that gate is granted once per plugin and then clientVersionUpdatesApproved silently extends it to every future package version of that plugin (index.ts lines 348-351), so a user who approved a harmless v1 UI card is authorizing arbitrary host-side code in v2 without ever being asked again.

verify:lastTurn copies and scans the ent.title: lastTurn copies and scans the entire session event log on every tool call, before any hook is known to match
verify:lastTurn copies and scans the ent.detail: lastTurn does an array spread of agent.session.events plus findLast over every session event, including every tool-result blob and message body. Both bridges call it eagerly at the top of the tools/pre-execute and tools/post-execute listeners, so it runs once per tool call per bridge regardless of whether any PreToolUse or PostToolUse group is configured or will match. On a long session with tens of thousands of events and hundreds of tool calls this is a measurable per-call tax on the guard path, duplicated across both dialects. The Codex bridge additionally calls turnBase (which calls lastTurn again) while the surrounding closure already has turn in scope. Compounding it, runPoint awaits each matching hook strictly serially inside the nested group and hook loops with a 10-minute default per-hook timeout, so N matching hooks can hold a single tool call for up to N times 10 minutes with no per-point wall-clock budget.

verify:evaluateHostCode misclassifies an.title: evaluateHostCode misclassifies any runtime-thrown sandbox SyntaxError as a parse failure and returns misleading bracket-balance advice
verify:evaluateHostCode misclassifies an.detail: runInContext of an async IIFE returns a promise, so a SyntaxError thrown inside the package's own running code (a direct throw new SyntaxError, a JSON.parse or new Function the package invokes at runtime, or any host-realm intrinsic that rejects with one) rejects the awaited promise and is then caught by the same handler as a compile failure. isSyntaxError is name-based across realms precisely so sandbox-realm compile errors are detected, but it cannot distinguish compile-time from runtime. The result is rethrown as a failed-to-parse error with the TypeScript-removal and bracket-balance hint from parseErrorMessage, which points the model at the wrong fix entirely and hides the real runtime failure. The existing test at tests/sandbox.spec.ts line 211 only asserts the message format for a runtime SyntaxError, not that the classification is wrong.

verify:TeamJournal.state re-validates an.title: TeamJournal.state re-validates and re-folds the entire Lead session log on every read
verify:TeamJournal.state re-validates an.detail: state() calls foldTeam over the whole Lead session log, which walks every event in that log, not just the four team event types, and runs a zod parse on each team-owned event. There is no incremental cache or observedSeq, in contrast to GoalService.sync in packages/goal/goal/src/index.ts lines 437-447 which does exactly this correctly. The cost is paid on every mailbox.send transaction, every markDelivered, every taskBoard get list update and create, every roster.list, and worst of all messagePrecedes in mailbox.ts lines 274-277, which additionally allocates the full message-id array and runs indexOf twice, so the ordering check for a quiet delivery is itself O(events plus messages). A team session that has run for a while therefore degrades quadratically with log length on the hot message path.

verify:orchestrate publishes inFlight on.title: orchestrate publishes inFlight only after its first await, so a re-entrant open starts a second unguarded activation
verify:orchestrate publishes inFlight on.detail: orchestrate sets this.activity, then calls this.drive(plan) which begins executing synchronously up to its first await, and only afterwards assigns this.inFlight. The serialization check at the top, which returns early when inFlight already has an entry for the plugin, therefore cannot see an activation that has already begun. Any re-entrant call for the same plugin arriving before that microtask, such as a second open from a duplicate cordis/request-run event, or reconcileApprovals running off a subscription that fires during the same turn, passes the guard, overwrites the activity entry, and launches a second drive that races the first on runHostHalf, getClientCode and load. The host-side resolvePlan and pendingRequestFor checks are the only remaining backstop, and they do not cover the direct-panel path where requestId is undefined.

verify:A deadline that fires after the t.title: A deadline that fires after the tool has already resolved converts a successful result into a spurious TOOL_TIMEOUT
verify:A deadline that fires after the t.detail: The wrapper arms deadline and, after awaiting next, unconditionally replaces whatever came back with toolTimeoutResult whenever timeoutOf reports the scoped code. There is no check that the result was actually an abort-shaped result. If a tool completes successfully just before the timeout but the timer callback runs before the awaiting continuation is resumed, the model is told the call timed out even though the work completed and its side effects are committed. For a non-idempotent tool such as a write, a shell command, or an API charge, the model natural recovery is to retry, producing a duplicate side effect. The comment above the check already assumes the tool saw the abort and reached quiescence; that assumption is not verified anywhere in the wrapper.

verify:subagentChildren retains strong A.title: subagentChildren retains strong Agent references released only by a subagent/end edge that may never arrive
verify:subagentChildren retains strong A.detail: subagent/start stores the live Agent object in a Map keyed by runId, and only subagent/end removes it. If the end edge is not emitted for a given runId, whether a child torn down through a path that skips the paired event, a start that races the bridge own disposal window, or a runId collision across a reload, the Map holds a strong reference to the Agent and transitively its entire session event log for the process lifetime. That leak scales with the number of subagents started. The comment on lines 121-125 states the requirement explicitly, saying every retained entry relies on that paired end and a producer that can omit it must provide another release edge, but no such edge exists: there is no agent/disposed fallback and no cap on the map. The SubagentStop hook is also skipped entirely in that case, so the audit trail is silently incomplete.

verify:The /permission command and the p.title: The /permission command and the public set API write the approval-policy knob through different writers with different model-visible effects
verify:The /permission command and the p.detail: apply takes the approval writer as a callback so the two entry points can diverge, and they do. The /permission command passes a closure around ctx.approval.setPolicy, which appends the durable approval/policy event and injects a user message telling the model the policy changed. The public set method passes a closure around setApprovalPolicy, which appends the same durable event but injects nothing. A deployment that switches presets through set therefore leaves the model runtime-context snapshot and its switch notice stale relative to the actual permission state, while a user switching through the command sees the notice. apply is also the only place the sandbox knob is written, so the asymmetry is easy to miss and hard to notice in testing.

verify:tools/list pagination loop is unb.title: tools/list pagination loop is unbounded — a buggy MCP server can hang plugin activation and unload forever
verify:tools/list pagination loop is unb.detail:
`syncTools` drains pages with a bare `do { ... cursor = response.nextCursor } while (cursor)`. There is no page cap, no seen-cursor set, and no total-tools cap, and the cursor is trusted verbatim from an external third-party process reached over stdio or HTTP.

Consequences when a server returns a non-empty `nextCursor` that never repeats a terminal page:
1. `connectGeneration` awaits `enqueueSync`, and `apply()` awaits `connection.ready` (`connection.ts:177`) — the plugin's activation never settles, so `failOnStartupError` never fires and the whole Cordis fiber never activates.
2. `enqueueSync` chains onto `syncChain`, so the never-settling sync permanently wedges the supervisor's serialized sync queue.
3. `dispose()` awaits `syncChain` (`connection.ts:346`), so HMR unload / host shutdown also hangs forever — teardown is blocked behind an untrusted peer.

The reconnect supervisor cannot help: the attempt never fails, it just never completes, so `maxAttempts` is never consulted. A page cap (or cursor-history check) would contain this at the trust boundary.

verify:Responses carrying a string JSON-.title: Responses carrying a string JSON-RPC id are silently dropped, permanently poisoning the pooled LSP instance
verify:Responses carrying a string JSON-.detail:
`dispatch()` accepts a server->client *request* for a string id (line 246), but a *response* is gated on `typeof id === 'number'`. JSON-RPC 2.0 allows string request ids and requires the server to echo the id exactly as received; a conforming-but-non-numeric-id server therefore gets every response discarded.

`pending` is never cleared and never rejects, so `LspConnection.request()` hangs. In `LspInstance.runQuery` that surfaces as the caller's abort/tool timeout — and because the rejection is the abort error rather than the connection's retained `closeReason`, `isTransportFailure(error)` is false, so `startTeardown()` never runs and neither does the `finally` eviction at `instance.ts:296` (`instance.dead` stays false: not closed, not disposed, not failed). The dead instance stays in `LocalLspProvider.instances` and every subsequent query for that workspace reuses it and hangs again until restart.

`dispatch` already treats `typeof id === 'string' || typeof id === 'number'` as sufficient for the request branch (correctly — that is how a numeric-id client request is distinguished), so the response branch dropping the string case is an inconsistency inside one function, not a protocol decision. No test in `connection.spec.ts`/`instance.spec.ts` exercises a string response id.

verify:Turns cancelled by a hook/owner s.title: Turns cancelled by a hook/owner settle as `end_turn`; ACP has no out-of-band `cancelled` and only `interrupted` maps to it
verify:Turns cancelled by a hook/owner s.detail:
`settleAfterQuiescence` resolves `end.kind === 'aborted' ? 'end_turn' : ...` (line 206) and `turnEndToStopReason` maps `'interrupted' -> 'cancelled'`, `'aborted' -> 'end_turn'`. The only path that yields ACP `cancelled` is `inflight.cancelRequested` or `endReason === undefined`.

ACP defines `cancelled` as "the agent cancelled the prompt (via session/cancel) or the agent-side session was aborted". A turn aborted by a hook or another owner is precisely agent-side cancellation, so the bridge misreports it as `end_turn`.

Unlike other channels, ACP gives the automation client no other signal: `session/update` emits only committed `agent_message_chunk`, and no `stop_reason` update is sent. So a client that prompts and waits on the response cannot distinguish "the model finished" from "the model was aborted mid-turn and produced nothing" — the observable contract is identical, and there is no partial-output marker either (the aborted stream's blocks go to `interruptedBlocks()` in the agent loop, not to ACP). This makes cancellation effectively invisible to ACP consumers.

verify:JSON-RPC output writes are fire-a.title: JSON-RPC output writes are fire-and-forget with no callback and no 'error' listener — a broken stdio pipe becomes an uncaught EPIPE crash
verify:JSON-RPC output writes are fire-a.detail:
`write()` calls `this.output.write(json)\n` with neither a completion callback nor any error containment, while the adjacent `flush()` (line 166-173) *does* take a callback and reject on error — so the module already knows the stream can fail, it just does not handle it on the real data path.

In production the output is `process.stdout` (`sdk/server/src/index.ts:55`). When that is a pipe (SDK-managed transports, `HarnessClient` spawns the runtime with `stdio: ['pipe','pipe','pipe']`), a reader that goes away produces EPIPE; Node emits `'error'` on the stream, and with no listener the process dies with an uncaught exception rather than a clean exit. `start()` only attaches `input.on('error')` — the output stream is never guarded.

This is not only a shutdown race. `HarnessSdkJsonRpcServer`'s constructor registers `ctx.on('session/event', ...)` / `agent/status` / `session/created` / `subagent/end`, all of which call `this.transport.notify(...)` synchronously. Any of those firing while the parent's read end is gone (parent crashed, pipe torn down mid-teardown) writes to a broken stdout. No `process.stdout.on('error', ...)` is installed anywhere in the repo.

verify:First-pass image offload budgets.title: First-pass image offload budgets against master attachment bytes, so the second pass drops roughly 4x more images than the bound needs
verify:First-pass image offload budgets.detail:
`toPiContextWithImages` runs `offloadRequestImagesWithPolicy` twice. The first pass (line 229-234) supplies `byteLength: ref => Math.min(ref.bytes, requestImagePolicy.maxBytes)`, and `offloadRequestImagesWithPolicy` is called with `representation: 'base64'` (line 230) — so `collectImageLengths` applies `base64Length(bytes) = ceil(bytes/3)*4` to the *master* attachment size (`llm/llm/src/content.ts:72-75`).

`ref.bytes` is the durable master attachment; the request version the provider actually sees has already been pixel/byte-capped by `readImageRequest`. So the first pass measures an over-estimate and over-removes: with the default 20 MiB bound and ~1 MiB request images, a conversation with 15 request images (≈20 MiB base64) but 2 MiB masters budgets 40 MiB and trims the oldest ones anyway. Only after the trimmed set is materialized does the exact second pass (line 236-241) run — on messages that have already had images irreversibly replaced with placeholders.

The DeepSeek adapter got this right: it passes `representation: 'raw'` for the estimate and a `byteLength` against the exact request version (`llm-deepseek/src/adapter.ts:537-544`). pi-ai inlines every image into every request body, so the over-trim shows up as lost conversation images for long image-heavy sessions.

verify:Stale-file retry fires on any HTT.title: Stale-file retry fires on any HTTP status whose body merely mentions a file id — a non-retriable INVALID_REQUEST becomes a duplicate upload plus an immediate re-send
verify:Stale-file retry fires on any HTT.detail:
`staleFile` is computed as `usedFiles.length > 0 && providerRejectedFileId(detail)` with no status gate. `providerRejectedFileId` only pattern-matches the joined `code`/`type`/`message` text (`/\bfile.../` + `/expired|not found|deleted|.../`) — so a 429 or 500 whose message happens to contain "file" and "not found" (a proxy/gateway error mentioning files, a rate-limit detail quoting the request path, etc.) is classified as a stale file id.

The recovery then (a) invalidates the *correct* cached mapping and (b) `continue`s the request loop with `body` unchanged. Nothing between the offload at line 537 and `JSON.stringify(body)` at line 601 re-runs when `representation` is still `'file'`, and the cached id has just been deleted from the local index — so `ensureUploaded` re-uploads the identical image. The POST is then re-issued with the same payload. If it fails again, `fileAttempt === 1` drops out of the branch and throws.

Net effect on one misclassified transient error: one wasted full image upload plus one duplicated POST — a double cost for a failure that was never retryable. `providerRejectedNormalizedImage` (line 646) correctly gates on `response.status === 400`; the stale-file path should carry an equivalent status gate.

verify:SDK `session/prompt` commits call.title: SDK `session/prompt` commits caller-supplied `contentBlocks` verbatim as a durable user message with no content validation
verify:SDK `session/prompt` commits call.detail:
`handleRequest` dispatches `params as unknown as SessionPromptParams` and `prompt()` then does `createUserMessage({ content: params.contentBlocks, source: { kind: 'user' } })`. `createUserMessage`/`createMessage` (`llm/src/message.ts:192-200`) only brand an id and deep-freeze — they do not validate the block vocabulary, roles, or nesting. The blocks go straight into the durable session log and later into every model request.

A `contentBlocks` payload containing a `{ type: 'tool-result', toolCallId: <any id>, content: [...], isError: false }` block is therefore admitted as a *user* message and reaches the model as an authoritative tool result for a call the model never made — the prompt-injection surface this cluster hunts for. `initialize`'s fields are equally unchecked (`this.model = params.model`, `this.cwd = resolve(params.cwd)` — a non-string cwd reaches `path.resolve` and throws a raw TypeError instead of a JSON-RPC invalid-params).

This is a real asymmetry: the ACP bridge validates the same boundary (`acp/src/content.ts:132-148` rejects unsupported block types before building the message) and the SDK protocol types claim `{ sessionId: string; contentBlocks: ContentBlock[] }`, but nothing on the wire enforces it. Some validation mirroring `admitAcpPrompt`'s closed-union switch belongs here.

verify:Loopback classifier accepts non-c.title: Loopback classifier accepts non-canonical IPv6 spellings and IPv4-mapped IPv6, widening the Host fence in a loopback-only deployment
verify:Loopback classifier accepts non-c.detail:
`isLoopbackHostname` special-cases exactly the strings `'localhost'` and `'[::1]'`. WHATWG URL also emits bracketed `'[::ffff:127.0.0.1]'` for a request to `http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/...`, and the IPv4 branch only checks `parts.length === 4 && parts[0] === '127'` with a regex of 1-3 digits per octet — so `'127.000.000.001'`, `'127.0.0.001'`, `'127.0.00.1'` and `'127.00.0.1'` all return true. All of those are legal, distinct `Host` header spellings; every one of them passes the fence.

This matters most where `isTrustedApiRequest` is called with an empty trust list, which is the loopback pinning of the whole privileged plane (`PRIVILEGED_METHODS` in `client/connection/src/index.ts:145-148`, and the `'loopback'` authority in `rpc-host.ts:82`). For a rebound page served over plain HTTP there is no Origin and no Fetch-Metadata on navigations and image reads, so the Host check is the entire defence and it is what a rebinding attacker writes. The IPv6-mapped case is the sharper one: on an IPv6-capable stack `::ffff:127.0.0.1` is a routable form of loopback that a resolver can name.

Compare `assertTrustedAuthority` (`api-request-trust.ts:54-58`), which deliberately refuses anything WHATWG would rewrite precisely because a non-canonical spelling must "fail the load loudly instead of being ignored until requests 403 or quietly changing the grant". The loopback predicate has no such normalization.

verify:bridge() does not contain a rejec.title: bridge() does not contain a rejection from apiHandler.fetch — the shared /api carrier surfaces carrier faults as HTTP 400
verify:bridge() does not contain a rejec.detail:
`bridge` awaits `apiHandler.fetch(request)` with no try/catch, so a rejection escapes to the webserver's per-request catch, which logs and answers `res.writeHead(400)` when headers are not yet sent (and `res.destroy()` when they are). `apiHandler` is the shared fetch handler composed by `createSharedFetchHandler`, whose non-intercepted path is the whole apiProxy (`rpc-host.ts:79` -> `toFetchHandler(apiProxy)`). Any carrier-level throw — a session that no longer resolves, a bad payload shape the two-level parse rejects by throwing, an abort — is therefore reported to the browser as **400 Bad Request**, i.e. the client's own fault, instead of a 500 or a protocol error envelope.

The downstream symptom is already visible on the browser side: `createWebConnectionRpc.call` throws `transport failure for ${channel}/${endpoint}: HTTP 400` (`client/rpc.ts:44-46`), losing the rpcId-correlated envelope entirely. Mid-stream (SSE downlinks share this bridge) the webserver instead destroys the socket with no error frame.

The bridge already owns an `AbortController` and is the module that documents "carrier vs business" separation; a try/catch around the fetch that emits a 500/envelope before the SSE body starts would keep host faults off the client's tab.

verify:closeBlock synthesizes `CallId(''.title: closeBlock synthesizes `CallId('')` instead of a per-block identity when a tool call arrives with no id
verify:closeBlock synthesizes `CallId(''.detail:
A tool-call block opened because the wire carried `tool_calls` deltas but never a `call.id` assembles to `{ id: CallId(''), name: block.name ?? '', ... }`. `CallId('')` is an empty string that survives `createMessage`/`deepFreeze` into the durable log and into the agent loop, where tool results are correlated by call id — two such blocks collide, and every subsequent tool-result message for the second call lands on the first.

`BlockAssembler.assemble` handles exactly this case by synthesizing a stable per-index id (`llm/src/assembler.ts:126`: `id: partial.toolCallId ?? CallId(`call-${index}`)`), and the same file's sibling `name: block.name ?? ''` silently permits an unnamed tool call with no diagnostic. The OpenAI-compatible wire does send `call.id` on the first delta, so this needs a non-conforming gateway/proxy — but the module is explicitly written at a network trust boundary ("Defensive: fields that the MCP spec declares required ... are guarded with fallbacks because this is a network trust boundary" appears across this cluster), and the analogous empty-credential case in the same package is hard-failed via `assertUsableApiKey` rather than passed through.

verify:Handler throw on a shared RPC cha.title: Handler throw on a shared RPC channel answers a bare-text HTTP 500 instead of a server-response envelope
verify:Handler throw on a shared RPC cha.detail:
`rpcFetchHandler` catches a rejection from `handler(...)` and returns `new Response(`handler failure: ${String(error)}`, { status: 500 })` — plain text, not `{ type: 'server-response', rpcId, result }`.

Two concrete consequences: (1) `client/rpc.ts` only builds the `RpcResult` from a parseable envelope, so the caller sees `transport failure for ...: HTTP 500` and loses the rpcId correlation the protocol exists to provide; (2) `String(error)` renders a non-Error throw as `[object Object]`, discarding the message. The typert gateway itself is well-behaved (`rpcFailure` in `api/gateway/src/index.ts:639-657` converts every throw into `{ ok: false, error }`), so this only bites handlers registered by other plugins on `ctx.connection.rpc.handle` — but that is a public registration seam with no contract enforcement, and the module already has `errorResponse(rpcId, error)` two functions below that could carry a synthetic rpcId.

`rpcFetchHandler` also has no request-signal propagation guard: the `request.signal` passed to `handler` is the bridge's abort controller, which is fine, but the 500 path does not distinguish an abort from a real failure.

verify:One unadmittable image in an MCP.title: One unadmittable image in an MCP result collapses every image block to the same generic diagnostic
verify:One unadmittable image in an MCP.detail:
`prepareImageProjection`'s final `catch` (the `attachments.saveImages(decoded)` path) projects *every* image block through `block => ({ type: 'text', text: imageDiagnostic(block, reason) })`, dropping the `index` argument. When the batch fails, every image in the result therefore gets the identical reason string, so the model has no way to tell which of N images was rejected by admission.

The function already threads `index` correctly in the two earlier branches (`validationErrors.get(index)`, and `byIndex.get(index)`), and `imageDiagnostic(block, reason)` renders `block.mimeType` — so with one bad image among several, all N lines read the same mime type and the same reason, actively misinforming about which bytes were refused. Passing `(block, index)` and reporting the per-index reason where `saveImages` provides one (or explicitly naming that the batch is all-or-nothing) would keep the diagnostic honest.

verify:QUANT_AVX2 is never defined for a.title: QUANT_AVX2 is never defined for any TU — the entire AVX2 kernel set is dead code in every build
verify:QUANT_AVX2 is never defined for a.detail: cmake/arch.cmake sets QUANT_AVX2 as a CMake *variable* and configure_file() writes it into build/quant_config.h via `#cmakedefine`, but **no source file anywhere includes that header** (grep for `config.h` includes across include/src/tools/bench/tests returns nothing), and compiler.cmake only adds `-mavx2`/`/arch:AVX2` flags — it never passes `-DQUANT_AVX2`. Every `#if defined(QUANT_AVX2)` in src/math is therefore false, so math_avx2.cpp, math_avx2_vec.cpp and math_avx2_tiled.cpp compile to empty translation units and the scalar math.cpp is the live implementation on every platform, including MSVC x64 where arch.cmake explicitly forces AVX2 "ON". build/quant_config.h confirms it: `/* #undef QUANT_AVX2 */`. Consequences: (a) all AVX2-named benchmarks (bench_kernels.cpp:66/72/192) silently time the scalar path; (b) the project ships no AVX2 math despite 3 source files and a dedicated cmake arch-detection function; (c) every latent bug in those files is invisible until someone "fixes" the config and suddenly enables hundreds of lines of never-executed code. Related inconsistency: math_avx512.cpp guards on `__AVX512F__` (compiler-defined, so it IS live when QUANT_AVX512 is on) while its AVX2 siblings guard on a macro nothing defines.
verify:QUANT_AVX2 is never defined for a.evidence:
cmake/compiler.cmake:23:  if(QUANT_AVX2)
    add_compile_options(-mavx2 -mavx -mbmi2 -mfma)
  endif()   # <-- no -DQUANT_AVX2

build/quant_config.h:7: /* #undef QUANT_AVX2 */

src/math/math_avx2_tiled.cpp:9:  #if defined(QUANT_AVX2)   // always false
src/math/math_avx2_tiled.cpp:568: #else // !QUANT_AVX2 — scalar fallbacks  // always taken

verify:AdamW (and ZeRO's copy) bias corr.title: AdamW (and ZeRO's copy) bias correction is wrong — updates are sqrt(bias_corr2)x too small during warmup
verify:AdamW (and ZeRO's copy) bias corr.detail: The update is written as `lr_adj = lr * sqrt(bc2) / bc1` applied to `m / (sqrt(v/bc2) + eps)`. Expanding: this equals lr*(m/bc1) * bc2 / (sqrt(v) + eps*sqrt(bc2)), whereas the correct AdamW step lr*(m/bc1)/(sqrt(v/bc2)+eps) equals lr*(m/bc1)*sqrt(bc2)/(sqrt(v)+eps*sqrt(bc2)). The ratio of implemented to correct is sqrt(bc2). With the default beta2=0.999 at t=1, bc2=0.001 so every parameter update is ~31.6x too small, converging toward correct only as t grows. AdamW is the default optimizer for Trainer::compile (trainer_core.cpp:201,1261), finetune.cpp:18, agi_extended.cpp:254 and tools/train.cpp — so the entire warmup phase of every training run is numerically wrong in a way that looks like "training is just slow to converge" rather than a crash. The identical formula is duplicated in ZeroOptimizer::step (zero_optimizer_core.cpp:222,244), so the ZeRO path has the same defect.

verify:DistributedContext keeps reduce_b.title: DistributedContext keeps reduce_buffer_ and the barrier per-instance, so multi-rank TP/FSDP/DDP never actually reduce
verify:DistributedContext keeps reduce_b.detail: reduce_buffer_, reduce_mutex_, barrier_mutex_, barrier_count_ and barrier_gen_ are all non-static members of DistributedContext (distributed.h:40-52). The only configuration in which the primitive works is the one tests/test_all.cpp:77-95 exercises: a *single* shared context object driven by N threads, which is why that test passes. Every production wrapper instead constructs its own — TensorParallelManager::ctx_, DistributedDataParallel::ctx_, FullyShardedDataParallel::ctx_ — and, worse, five call sites build a **fresh context per invocation**: tensor_parallelism.cpp:374 (ColumnParallelLinear::forward), :430 (RowParallelLinear::forward), :505 (HeadPartitioner::sync_output), :536/:544 (SequenceParallel::gather/allreduce), and fsdp.cpp:679 (FSDPBlock::sync_gradients). A fresh object's barrier_count_ starts at 0 and its reduce_buffer_ is private, so with world_size>1 the first thread waits forever for world_size-1 arrivals that no one else can ever produce — a hang, not a wrong answer. Even if callers instead gave each rank its own long-lived context, the private reduce_buffer_ means each rank sums its own data into its own buffer and reads it back: a silent no-op. fsdp.cpp:601-606 already documents this exact hazard for gather_and_install and "fixed" it by special-casing world_size<=1, but the identical pattern is left live in sync_gradients and all five tensor_parallelism sites. Net effect: no configuration of this codebase performs a real cross-rank reduction; DDP/TP/FSDP training is either a hang or an unsharded single-process run.

verify:gemm_tiled's AVX2 micro-kernel co.title: gemm_tiled's AVX2 micro-kernel computes only 16 of the tile's N columns — 75% of every output tile is wrong
verify:gemm_tiled's AVX2 micro-kernel co.detail: TILE_N is 64 (include/quant/math_tiled.h:17) and gemm_tiled tiles N in strides of TILE_N, so n_tile is typically 64. It then dispatches to the 6x16 micro-kernel whenever n_tile >= 16 (line 348). But micro_6x16_ab (and its _atb/_abt/_atbt variants at :132/:160/:190) has no inner column loop at all — per k it loads exactly b0 = B[k*ldb+0..7] and b1 = B[k*ldb+8..15] and stores exactly 16 floats back to C. Columns 16..n_tile-1 are never read from B and never written to C, so they keep whatever beta*C left there. I compiled a verbatim copy of micro_6x16_ab with clang++ -mavx2 -mfma and ran it at M=6,K=64,N=64 (the shape bench_gemm_tiled.cpp checks): 288 of 384 output entries are wrong, max_abs_err=7.98 versus a 1e-4 tolerance. bench_gemm_tiled.cpp:26-38 has a parity gate that would catch this, but per finding #1 the AVX2 file is not compiled today, so the gate only ever exercises the correct scalar path and the bench reports PARITY_OK. The moment QUANT_AVX2 is correctly defined this becomes a silent 75%-wrong GEMM in the inference hot path.

verify:vec_fp16_to_fp32 decodes subnorma.title: vec_fp16_to_fp32 decodes subnormals 4x too small, and the AVX2 copy has the same bug in its scalar tail
verify:vec_fp16_to_fp32 decodes subnorma.detail: For an FP16 subnormal (exp==0, mant!=0) the value is mant * 2^-24. The code computes `m = mant/1024.0f` (mant * 2^-10) then multiplies by 1.5258789e-5f (2^-16), giving mant * 2^-26 — a factor of 4 too small. The encoder in the same file is correct: vec_fp32_to_fp16 (line 525-527) shifts by (1-exp) and >>13, which round-trips 2^-24 to code 1, so encode and decode are asymmetric and any weight below ~6.1e-5 is silently shrunk. This is on a live path: src/codec/quant_engines_fp.cpp:415,421,441 call these for the FP16 weight engine, so small-magnitude quantized weights decode at a quarter of their true value. math_avx2_vec.cpp:531 repeats the same formula for the n%8 scalar tail after an F16C main loop, so in an AVX2 build the conversion is correct for the first n-(n%8) elements and 4x wrong for the last up-to-7, i.e. the result depends on n mod 8. Note math_avx2_vec.cpp is currently dead (finding #1), so today the fully-broken scalar version in math.cpp is what runs.

verify:DDPMode::ASYNC self-deadlocks: sy.title: DDPMode::ASYNC self-deadlocks: sync_gradients and its own worker thread both lock the same non-recursive mutex
verify:DDPMode::ASYNC self-deadlocks: sy.detail: sync_gradients() takes async_mutex_ whenever mode_ == ASYNC (line 104-106), and async_sync_loop() takes async_mutex_ (line 353) immediately before calling sync_gradients() (line 354). std::mutex is not recursive, so the worker thread locks it, re-enters sync_gradients, and blocks forever on its own lock. This fires on the first loop iteration — 10ms after construction — and only when world_size > 1, because the `world_size_ <= 1` early-return at line 102 masks it otherwise. So ASYNC mode appears to work in every single-process smoke test and hangs immediately in any real multi-rank run. The constructor at line 18-21 starts the thread unconditionally, and ~DistributedDataParallel (line 25-28) then join()s it, so even a teardown path hangs. The mutex also does nothing useful for correctness: sync_gradients only holds it while calling sync_gradients's own body, providing no exclusion against a concurrent user-called sync_gradients.

verify:ZeroOptimizer::reduce_scatter_gra.title: ZeroOptimizer::reduce_scatter_grads never clears comm_buffer_ between parameters, so every gradient accumulates all previous ones
verify:ZeroOptimizer::reduce_scatter_gra.detail: The loop over parameters accumulates each rank's gradient into the shared static comm_buffer_ at indices [0,n) and reads the sum back, but never zeroes the buffer before the next parameter. comm_buffer_ is a static member that persists across calls, and `resize(n, 0.0f)` only zero-fills *newly grown* elements, so the values from parameter i remain in place when parameter i+1 is processed. Parameter 0 gets a correct all-reduce; parameter 1 gets (its own reduce) + (parameter 0's reduce); parameter k gets the sum of the reduces of parameters 0..k. The pollution also never resets between steps, so the error grows monotonically for the life of the process. The final `p->grad().zero_()` for non-owners (line 209-210) masks nothing — the owning rank applies a gradient that is a mixture of many unrelated parameters. Contrast internal_reduce_scatter (line 294), which does `std::fill(...)` after use, confirming the omission here is an oversight rather than a design choice. Note the comment at :184 says "reduce-scatter" but this is an all-reduce followed by zeroing, not a scatter.

verify:internal_all_gather writes world_.title: internal_all_gather writes world_size x local_bytes into a buffer sized for local_bytes — heap overflow on any multi-rank use
verify:internal_all_gather writes world_.detail: internal_all_gather is documented (zero_optimizer.h:152) as taking a `float* local_data` sized local_bytes, and its only caller, all_gather_params (line 298-317), passes exactly that: `float* local_data = param->data<float>(); int64_t byte_count = n * sizeof(float);` where n is the parameter's own numel. The gather phase then loops r over all world_size ranks and does `memcpy(local_data + r*local_floats, &comm_buffer_[r*local_floats], local_bytes)` — writing local_bytes at offsets 0, local_bytes, 2*local_bytes ... (world_size-1)*local_bytes. Only the r==0 write lands in bounds; the remaining world_size-1 writes run off the end of the Tensor's allocation, corrupting whatever the refcounted Buffer's heap neighbours are. For any parameter and any world_size>1 this is an out-of-bounds write of (world_size-1) * param_bytes. The correct contract needs a destination buffer of local_bytes*world_size, or the gather should copy into a caller-supplied global tensor (as DistributedContext::all_gather at distributed.cpp:103-123 does).

verify:AVX2 gelu/geglu approximate erf w.title: AVX2 gelu/geglu approximate erf with an order-9 Taylor series that diverges for |x| > ~3
verify:AVX2 gelu/geglu approximate erf w.detail: gelu (line 283-299), geglu (line 645-660) and the tiled apply_gelu (math_avx2_tiled.cpp:425-441) compute erf via the truncated Maclaurin series x - x^3/3 + x^5/10 - x^7/42 + x^9/216. This alternating series is only accurate for small argument; the first neglected term is ~x^11/(11!!) which already contributes ~0.02 of error at x=2 and swamps the sum by x=3.5. At v=4.95 (x = v/sqrt(2) = 3.5) the partial sum evaluates to 1+erf ~ 167 instead of ~2, so gelu returns ~413 instead of ~4.95 — a ~83x error on the activation output, not a precision loss but a completely wrong value. GELU pre-activations routinely reach |x| in this range, so any model using GELU would produce garbage in exactly the regime where the activation's tail behaviour matters most. The scalar math.cpp:113 and the non-AVX2 tiled path correctly call std::erf, so this is a divergence between the two implementations that a parity test would catch if the AVX2 file were compiled (see finding #1). No argument reduction (e.g. |x|>2.5 -> clamp to 1.0) is present.

verify:Non-AVX2 gemm_tiled_act / gemm_ti.title: Non-AVX2 gemm_tiled_act / gemm_tiled_bias_act silently drop GELU and SiLU, and both paths overrun C by ldc-M rows
verify:Non-AVX2 gemm_tiled_act / gemm_ti.detail: The scalar fallback branch (the `#else` at line 568, which is the branch that actually compiles today per finding #1) handles only Activation::ReLU. GELU and SiLU fall through with no action and no warning, so a caller requesting SiLU gets a plain linear GEMM result — a silent wrong answer rather than an error. The same two functions in the AVX2 branch are correct on activation choice but share a second bug: apply_activation(C, M * ldc, act) at line 483 and :500 applies the activation across M*ldc contiguous floats. When ldc > N (padded/strided C) that walks into the row padding, and when the caller passes an ldc larger than the allocated row stride it reads and writes past the end of C. The scalar path has the identical `for (int64_t i = 0; i < M * ldc; i++)` at :657/:661. The loop should be per-row over N columns, not a flat M*ldc sweep. The tensor-level wrappers at :554/:562 pass C.numel() (correct) but the raw-pointer API — the one bench_kernels.cpp:385 uses — hits the broken form.

verify:Bucket::numel is never assigned b.title: Bucket::numel is never assigned by build_buckets, silently disabling TOP_K compression and corrupting the FP8 path
verify:Bucket::numel is never assigned b.detail: build_buckets() sets `current.size` (size_t) and `current.buffer` for each bucket but never touches `Bucket::numel` (include/quant/ddp.h:21), which therefore stays at its default 0 for every bucket in every DDP instance. allreduce_bucket keys both compression branches on it: the TOP_K_SPARSE guard `bucket.numel > 0` (line 132) is permanently false, so sparse compression silently degrades to a plain all-reduce with no indication that the requested compression is not in effect; and the FP8_QUANT branch allocates `std::vector<uint8_t> compressed(bucket.numel)` (line 140) — a zero-length vector — then loops `for (i = 0; i < bucket.numel; i++) buf[i] += (float)((int8_t)compressed[i]) * scale;` which does nothing, and finally divides every gradient by world_size (line 150-151) without ever having summed them. The result under FP8_QUANT is each rank's local gradient scaled by 1/world_size and never combined across ranks — a silently wrong training run. The standard all-reduce at :154 also passes `bucket.numel` (=0) as the element count, so even the non-compressed path is a no-op. The fix is to set `current.numel = current_numel` alongside `current.size` at lines 68 and 79, or to use `bucket.size` consistently.

verify:math::max() unconditionally loads.title: math::max() unconditionally loads 8 floats, reading up to 7 floats past the end for any tensor with fewer than 8 elements
verify:math::max() unconditionally loads.detail: max() guards only against an empty tensor (QUANT_CHECK(n > 0)), then does `__m256 mxv = _mm256_loadu_ps(p);` — an unconditional 8-float load at index 0 — and starts the loop counter at i=8. For any tensor with n in [1,7] this reads 8-n floats beyond the end of the Buffer. Small tensors are ubiquitous (scalars, per-head norms, 1-D gates, rank-1 slices), so this is an out-of-bounds read on a very common path, and because AlignedAllocator over-allocates it usually appears as a silent wrong max rather than a crash: the horizontal reduce at :607-611 folds in whatever bytes follow the allocation, so max() can return a value that is not present in the tensor. The scalar math.cpp:324-331 version is correct (starts from p[0] and iterates i=1..n). The correct AVX2 form needs a masked load or a scalar prologue for n<8, mirroring how gemv/dot handle their tails. Currently latent because the file is not compiled (finding #1).

verify:ImageNetClassifier's feature-dim.title: ImageNetClassifier's feature-dim fallback branch is dead-on-arrival: it always throws
verify:ImageNetClassifier's feature-dim.detail: feat_dim is computed as `feat.numel() / B` on the line above, so by construction `feat_dim != 768` is logically equivalent to `feat.numel() != B*768`. The branch then calls `feat.reshape({B, 768})`, and Tensor::reshape (src/core/tensor.cpp:176-179) is `QUANT_CHECK(new_shape.numel() == shape_.numel(), "reshape: size mismatch"); return view(new_shape);`. So whenever the condition is true, the numel check fails and the call aborts. The only way to reach the reshape without throwing is the case where it is provably unnecessary. Any ViT whose patch projection emits a feature width other than the hard-coded 768 — the exact scenario the `(feat_dim != 768)` guard was written to handle — aborts the process instead of degrading. The loop below (:192-198) also hard-codes `768` for the reduction, so even a successful reshape would be wrong for a genuinely different width; the real fix is to reject or adapt to the actual feat_dim rather than to reshape into a fixed constant.

verify:QUANT_AVX2 is never defined as a.title: QUANT_AVX2 is never defined as a preprocessor macro, so the whole AVX2 math library compiles to empty TUs
verify:QUANT_AVX2 is never defined as a.detail: quant_config.h.in:7 uses `#cmakedefine QUANT_AVX2`, and quant_config.h is generated into CMAKE_BINARY_DIR and made visible through the `quant_config` INTERFACE target — but no source file anywhere includes quant_config.h (grep over src/, include/, tools/, engines/, bench/, tests/, inferno/ returns zero includes), and no CMake command ever adds a QUANT_AVX2 compile definition (grep for -DQUANT_AVX2 in the generated build/build.ninja returns 0 hits, while -DQUANT_USE_CUDA/-DQUANT_USE_DIRECTX/-DQUANT_USE_VULKAN do appear). Result: `#if defined(QUANT_AVX2)` is ALWAYS false. src/math/math_avx2.cpp:10 (`#if defined(QUANT_AVX2)`) and math_avx2_vec.cpp:8 compile to empty translation units, math_avx2_tiled.cpp:9 never takes its AVX2 branch and always compiles the `#else // !QUANT_AVX2` scalar fallbacks at line 568, and src/math/math.cpp:8 `#if !defined(QUANT_AVX2)` is always true, so the scalar implementations are what ship — while cmake/compiler.cmake:23 still prints 'ARCH: AVX2 detected' and adds -mavx2 -mavx -mbmi2 -mfma, and CMakeLists:67 still pulls in math_avx512.cpp. Proof of intent: .clangd line 7 and .vscode/c_cpp_properties.json line 32 both pass `-DQUANT_AVX2` to the IDE. The build system silently disables a whole SIMD library on every platform and configuration.

verify:coverage.sh zeroes gcda counters.title: coverage.sh zeroes gcda counters AFTER running the tests, then captures — report is always ~0%
verify:coverage.sh zeroes gcda counters.detail: Step 3 (line 33) runs the whole ctest suite and the .gcda counters are written. Step 4 then calls `lcov --zerocounters` (line 51) which resets every counter in the build tree, and only afterwards `lcov --capture` (line 54) + genhtml. Everything measured by the test run is wiped before capture, so the generated HTML/summary reports 0% for every file (or genhtml gets an empty .info). The `2>/dev/null || true` on the zerocounter call also hides the only signal that lcov is misbehaving. Any coverage number produced by this script has been silently wrong since it was written.

verify:GCC Release adds -march=native, s.title: GCC Release adds -march=native, so Docker images and dist tarballs are bound to the build CPU
verify:GCC Release adds -march=native, s.detail: The GCC Release branch adds `-march=native` for every TU in the project. Consequences: (a) the Dockerfile builder stage configures `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` (Dockerfile:18-27), so the binaries baked into the shipped runtime image are compiled for the CI/build host's exact CPU — if that host has AVX-512 (common on runners), auto-vectorized code and any `__AVX512F__`-guarded TU (src/math/math_avx512.cpp:10, added by CMakeLists:67 whenever QUANT_AVX512 is detected, with no runtime CPUID gate on those symbols) can emit 512-bit instructions that SIGILL on the end user's machine; (b) scripts/make_dist.sh:29-31 builds the same Release configuration and publishes it as `linux-x86_64` (line 20) — a label that is a lie under -march=native; (c) it makes the bitwise cross-platform determinism check in scripts/cross_platform_check.sh impossible by construction. There is no build option to turn it off and no runtime dispatch for compiler-generated vector code.

verify:Warnings-as-errors is off in ever.title: Warnings-as-errors is off in every build except the local WSL script, and the Clang branch disables the warnings that catch real bugs
verify:Warnings-as-errors is off in ever.detail: `-Werror` appears exactly once in the whole repo (build_linux.sh:20) — not in CMakeLists.txt, not in cmake/*.cmake, not in any .github/workflows file. So the default build, the Docker build (Dockerfile:18-27) and all CI legs compile with warnings allowed and accumulate them silently. Worse, the Clang branch suppresses `-Wno-sign-compare -Wno-float-equal -Wno-cast-qual -Wno-unused-variable -Wno-unused-function` (lines 5-7): sign-compare is precisely the warning class that catches size_t/int length and offset mistakes in this codebase (stride math, packed-byte counts, buffer offsets), cast-qual catches const-discard writes into shared buffers, float-equal catches the accept/reject and zero-guard comparisons. GCC only suppresses `-Wno-unused-parameter`. So the Clang CI legs are structurally blinder than GCC for the same sources, and nothing turns warnings into failures.

verify:The `coverage` custom target pass.detail: `COMMAND ${CMAKE_CTEST_COMMAND} --output-on-failure -j $ENV{NPROC}` reads an environment variable named NPROC.
