verify:Windows process inspector leaks n.title: Windows process inspector leaks native koffi memory on every liveness probe
verify:Windows process inspector leaks n.detail: `allocNative` calls `koffi.alloc()`, which allocates process-lifetime native memory that is only released by `koffi.free()`. There is no `koffi.free` call anywhere in this package (repo-wide grep returns zero hits outside koffi's own docs). `snapshotWindowsProcesses` leaks one 568-byte PROCESSENTRY32W per snapshot (line 273), and `windowsProcessState` leaks four 8-byte FILETIMEs per call (lines 296-299) — called once for *every* pid reachable from the tree root in `processTree`, and once per `isAlive`. `isAlive`/`processTree` are invoked from `LocalTerminalHandle.inspectForeground` (every PTY readiness poll, default 50 ms in terminal-bash config) and from `survivors()` (every 25 ms during teardown waits). Empirically verified in this environment: 5M `koffi.alloc('uint32',1)` without free grows RSS by 79 MB; with `koffi.free` the growth is 1.9 MB. On a Windows host with one persistent terminal this is on the order of tens of MB per hour of foreground sends, with no upper bound.

verify:drainPipe leaks 3-4 native koffi.title: drainPipe leaks 3-4 native koffi slots per iteration and busy-polls the event loop at 1 kHz
verify:drainPipe leaks 3-4 native koffi.detail: The drain loop allocates three `allocUint32()` slots (each a `koffi.alloc`, never freed — see `ffi.ts` `allocUint32`) on *every* iteration plus a fourth per data read, and always sleeps exactly 1 ms, even when the pipe is empty. Two compounding defects: (1) native memory grows ~12 KB/s for as long as the child lives, unbounded — a background/long-running command confined through `AclSandbox` with the documented default `stdio: 'pipe'` grows the runner's RSS indefinitely; (2) the loop spins at ~1000 iterations/second for the whole child lifetime, consuming a full core-ish share of event-loop work for an idle process. `spawnSandboxed` (the pipe path) is the class default and is publicly reachable via the package's `./src/*` export. The `stdio: 'inherit'` runner path does not use this function.

verify:Linux PTY readiness polling enume.title: Linux PTY readiness polling enumerates all of /proc (plus per-thread syscall and /proc/<pid>/mem reads) every 50 ms
verify:Linux PTY readiness polling enume.detail: `LocalPtySession.pollReadiness` (terminal-bash/src/session.ts:432) runs every `pollIntervalMs` (default 50) while any foreground send is outstanding — i.e. for the entire duration of every `terminal_send` / persistent-bash command, up to `timeoutMs` (30 s). Each iteration awaits `LocalTerminalHandle.inspectForeground()`, which does: (a) `this.descendants()` → `LinuxProcessInspector.processTree` (full readdir of /proc + a `readFileSync(/proc/<pid>/stat)` for every pid) **and** `processSession` (a second full readdir + stat sweep of every pid); (b) `foregroundPgid`; (c) `isStdinWaiting(pgid)` — a third full /proc readdir, then `/proc/<pid>/task` readdir for every matching pid, then `readFileSync(/proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/syscall)` for every thread, and `open(/proc/<pid>/mem)` + `readSync` for select/poll/epoll cases (`readMemory`, line 147). On a host with N processes and T threads this is O(N + T) syscalls plus `/proc/mem` reads twenty times per second, per active terminal — with several concurrent background bash jobs this dominates CPU and burns significant I/O. There is no caching or dirty-flag between polls and no throttle below 50 ms.

verify:macOS isAlive() re-runs a full `p.title: macOS isAlive() re-runs a full `ps -axo` for every identity on every poll
verify:macOS isAlive() re-runs a full `p.detail: `MacProcessInspector.isAlive` shells out to `/bin/ps -axo pid=,ppid=,lstart=` and reparses the whole process table *per call*. `LocalTerminalHandle.survivors(members)` calls `isAlive` once per tracked member, and `waitForMembers` re-evaluates survivors every 25 ms for up to `graceMs`. With k descendants alive this is k `ps` process spawns every 25 ms (≈400/s for k=10) throughout every teardown wait, plus one `ps` per `descendants()`/`processTree()` call during readiness polling. On macOS this is by far the most expensive operation in the terminal readiness/teardown path and it is pure repeated work: the table does not change between two `survivors()` calls 25 ms apart in the common case. Linux (`/proc` stat read) and Windows (handle wait) both avoid this; only macOS pays it.

verify:The default `stdio: 'pipe'` confi.title: The default `stdio: 'pipe'` confined spawn path never places the child in a kill-on-close job
verify:The default `stdio: 'pipe'` confi.detail: `spawnSandboxedInherited` (used by the runner) creates a `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` job, starts the child suspended, assigns it, then resumes — an orphan backstop. `spawnSandboxed` — which is what `AclSandbox.spawn` uses for its **documented default** `stdio: 'pipe'` (index.ts line 372) — creates no job at all. If the host process dies while a piped confined child is running, the child survives unconfined-by-parent-lifetime and is never terminated by the OS. Additionally, the `PROCESS_INFORMATION.hProcess` is closed only inside `waitForExit`, which is reached only when the caller awaits `wait()`; a caller that spawns and abandons the child (or takes the `stdio:'pipe'` handle and never awaits) leaks the process handle and both pipe read ends. The runner path is unaffected (it always passes `stdio: 'inherit'`), so this is a latent defect in the package's public API rather than the shipped command path — but it is the same class whose docs promise "child dies with the caller".

verify:Sandbox provider caches 'unavaila.title: Sandbox provider caches 'unavailable' permanently, so probes never re-run after the backend becomes usable
verify:Sandbox provider caches 'unavaila.detail: `selectRunner` memoizes the chain verdict with `this.selectedRunner ??= this.chainVerdict()`. `chainVerdict` walks the platform chain once, probing each candidate functionally, and returns the literal `'unavailable'` when none passes. Because `'unavailable'` is not `undefined`, the `??=` never re-evaluates, and the very next line throws `SandboxUnavailableError`. Consequence: a transient failure of the *first* probe (bwrap present but failing under the 5 s `probeTimeoutMs` at startup, Landlock launcher probing unusable because `/tmp` or `/proc` was not ready, `sandbox-exec` unavailable at first call, ACL probe racing an antivirus lock) permanently pins the provider to "no sandbox backend" for the life of the process — every later confined command fails closed with `SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE` even after the runner becomes perfectly usable, with no recovery short of a full server restart. Since the design deliberately makes probes lazy ("cached the bounded result"), caching the *failure* rather than only the *success* is inconsistent with that intent.

verify:Truncated-command spill files are.title: Truncated-command spill files are never deleted after the command settles
verify:Truncated-command spill files are.detail: When a collected stream exceeds its in-memory cap (`maxOutputBytes`, default 64 KB), `OutputCollector.spillAll` creates `cf-subprocess-<pid>-<n>-<rand>-<label>.log` under a per-process `mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'cf-subprocess-'))` directory and appends the complete stream (up to `maxSpillBytes`, default 64 MB per stream). `seal()`/`finalize()` only close the fd — they never unlink — and `unlinkSync` appears solely inside `discardSpill`, which runs only when the stream *exceeds* `maxSpillBytes` or when it fits back in memory. Nothing else in the repo deletes a spill file: grep for `spillPath` shows only producers and renderers (`[output truncated; full output: <path>]`). So every bash/pwsh command whose stdout or stderr passes 64 KB leaves a permanent file holding the full command output on the user's machine, unbounded over a session (hundreds of MB of build logs are routine). These files contain whatever the model's command printed, including tokens echoed by failing CLIs, and sit in a shared OS temp directory indefinitely. There is no retention policy, no TTL, and no cleanup at service dispose.

verify:terminal close() kills descendant.title: terminal close() kills descendants before the shell, letting a survivor respawn an unkillable tree
verify:terminal close() kills descendant.detail: `LocalPtySession.closeOnce` first `await this.terminal.terminate()`, which runs `LocalTerminalHandle.closeOnce` → `stopDescendants()` (SIGTERM the tracked tree, wait grace, SIGKILL, wait) → **then** `stopShell()` (SIGTERM the shell, wait, SIGKILL the shell) → **then** `stopDescendants()` again. Because the interactive shell is still alive during the first descendant sweep, any foreground/background child it is running can simply fork a replacement immediately after being SIGKILLed (a `while true; do sleep 0.1 & done` wrapper, a build system, `npm`, a test runner). That replacement is created after the tracked set was captured, and the shell is only killed later — so the second sweep is the only one that can see it, and by then the shell is dead and cannot respawn again, but the *first* sweep already burned the entire SIGTERM grace window. If any descendant then ignores SIGTERM and the second sweep's `graceMs` expires before it is adopted, `stopDescendants` returns survivors, `closeOnce` throws `terminal cleanup failed; surviving pids: …`, and `TerminalSessionService.kill` leaves `sessions` populated with `record.closing = undefined` — the session can never be closed, and `tool-terminal`'s `terminal_close` / `tool-bash-persistent`'s shell reset both fail permanently for that agent. Killing the shell first (as `terminateForHostExit` does: descendants, shell, descendants) removes the respawn source before the long sweep.

verify:processSession() returns an empty.title: processSession() returns an empty list on macOS and Windows, so session/daemon descendants escape teardown
verify:processSession() returns an empty.detail: `LocalTerminalHandle.descendants()` unions `processTree(rootPid)` with `processSession(rootPid)` to capture members that have left the ppid tree — exactly what a double-fork/`setsid` daemon, a `nohup`'d process, or a `systemd-run`-style detachment produces. `MacProcessInspector.processSession` and `WindowsProcessInspector.processSession` both unconditionally return `[]` (windows-inspector.ts:104-106 does the same), and `MacProcessInspector.processTree` also returns `[]` for a root pid whose entry is missing. Net effect: on macOS and Windows a child that reparents itself to init/launchd escapes `stopDescendants` entirely and survives `terminal cleanup` — reported as `surviving pids` (teardown failure) or silently left running if it also leaves the ppid tree before the first scan. The capability is advertised on the `ProcessInspector` interface and the union is the documented mechanism, but two of the three platform implementations are hard stubs with no compensating fallback (e.g. scanning by process group, or using a Windows Job Object for the whole PTY tree, which the package already builds elsewhere in the ACL runner).

verify:E2B adapter issues 50+ control-pl.title: E2B adapter issues 50+ control-plane requests per second per running command
verify:E2B adapter issues 50+ control-pl.detail: `pollMs` defaults to 20 ms and every tick is one E2B cloud API call (the config doc says so explicitly: "each tick is one control-plane request"). `E2BSubprocessHandle.waitForCommand` (process.ts:511) loops `sandbox.files.read(paths.status)` on that cadence for the *entire* lifetime of every collect-mode or inherit-mode command — which is the default for bash/pwsh, because `hasPipeOutput` is false unless a stream is `pipe`. With default `graceMs`-style command durations of tens of seconds, a single background `npm install` costs ~3000 remote file reads; five concurrent background jobs saturate 250 req/s against E2B's API, inviting rate limiting or sandbox suspension. On top of that, the PTY path adds `inspectForegroundOnce` → `sandbox.commands.run("ps -o tpgid= -p <pid>")` (terminal.ts:353) on every terminal-bash readiness poll (50 ms → 20 req/s per active foreground send). Both loops are unthrottled relative to the actual information gain: the exit-code file changes exactly once.

verify:bwrap grants an ephemeral --tmpfs.title: bwrap grants an ephemeral --tmpfs /tmp while writableRoots() promises the real host /tmp and os.tmpdir()
verify:bwrap grants an ephemeral --tmpfs.detail: `bwrapProfileArgs` for `workspace-write` emits `--tmpfs /tmp`, which mounts a *new, empty, memory-backed* /tmp inside the sandbox. The shared definition of "workspace-write" in `writableRoots()` (sandbox/src/roots.ts:52) returns `[workspaceRoot, '/tmp', tmpdir()]` canonicalized — the real host temp directories — and that helper is what Seatbelt's profile *and* the in-process fs fence (`fs-sandbox/src/index.ts:138`) consume. So on Linux: the write tool (fs-sandbox) happily accepts a write to `/tmp/x` or `$TMPDIR/x` under `workspace-write`, but bash under bwrap writes to a throwaway tmpfs and silently discards the data on exit. The `roots.ts` doc comment explicitly claims the bwrap and Landlock "own their grant spellings" with "parity pinned by test", yet this is not a spelling difference — it is a semantic difference (empty vs. real), and the fs/bash asymmetry is exactly what the module header says it exists to prevent. Practical impact: a model that writes to `/tmp` in bash and reads it back with the read tool sees a file that never existed, or vice-versa.

verify:Sandbox denial is inferred from a.title: Sandbox denial is inferred from a raw stderr substring, so ordinary permission errors are reported as policy denials
verify:Sandbox denial is inferred from a.detail: `matchesSignature` returns true for any non-zero exit whose stderr merely *contains* one of the backend's denial substrings, anywhere on any line. The windows-acl dialect is `['access is denied', 'access to the path', 'permission denied']` (sandbox-local/src/index.ts:205) — which is also the ordinary English of Windows ACL/NTFS errors, `npm`/`git` failures, `type C:\...\SAM`, opening a locked file, `rm` on a read-only file, etc. Under `workspace-write` (and under `read-only` for reads outside the readable set) such a command gets `sandbox.denied: true`, which the tool renders as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` plus the escalation hint, teaching the model that the *harness policy* refused it and that it should immediately retry with a wider `sandbox_permissions` + a user approval prompt. The same applies to `read-only` bash under bwrap where `read-only file system` is unambiguous — but the windows-acl strings are not. This costs an unwarranted human approval round-trip and can normalise escalation for a denial that a wider mode will not fix. A tighter rule (deny only when the failing path is inside a root the policy actually governs, or when the mode is `read-only`) would remove most false positives.

verify:session.list re-walks the whole p.title: session.list re-walks the whole project/session directory tree once per cold blank session
verify:session.list re-walks the whole p.detail: `listVisibleSessionSummaries()` runs `summarizeCold()` for every persisted session that is not attached. A cold session whose projection-cache hint is `blank: true` (the common state for every unused "New Session" click) always reaches `probeColdSessionMetadata`, which calls `persistence.readFrom(meta.id, 0, signal)` (line 534). On the JSONL backend `readFrom` has no seek hook, so it calls `loadStored` → `findLog`, and `findLog` (packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/index.ts:774) re-does `readdir(root)` plus, for EVERY project directory, `rejectLegacyFlatArtifact` (2 `exists()` = open+close each) and 2 more `exists()` calls — each of which on ENOENT additionally `stat`s the parent (`assertLogParentAllowsAbsence`). Then `readStableFile` does stat+readFile+stat and the whole artifact is JSON-parsed, just to check `!events.some(e => e.type === 'turn/start')`. Cost per blank probe is therefore O(1 + P) syscalls + a full log parse, where P = number of project directories, and blank sessions accumulate without bound. `exists()` in the same file already proved `locate(meta)` gives the exact path, so the tree walk is pure redundancy. `session.list` is the primary sidebar RPC, so a user with ~100 blank sessions and ~20 project dirs pays ~8,000+ serialized syscalls plus 100 full log parses per list.

verify:mux/host SSE fan-out has no backp.title: mux/host SSE fan-out has no backpressure: FrameQueue buffers every session event for a stalled client without bound
verify:mux/host SSE fan-out has no backp.detail: `FrameQueue.push()` unconditionally appends to an unbounded array and `iterate()` is the only drain point. `sseResponse` (packages/host/apiproxy/src/fetch/handler.ts:203-213) does `controller.enqueue(...)` for every frame with no `desiredSize` check, and `new ReadableStream({start})` uses the default highWaterMark 0, whose queue is still unbounded. A slow, paused or stalled SSE consumer therefore causes the host to retain every `session/event` frame of every session (full tool results and assistant messages included) in memory for that client. Notably the ZIP export path in the same package implements exactly this control (`ResponseCapacityGate` + `highWaterMark: RESPONSE_HIGH_WATER_MARK_BYTES`, session-export.ts:291/454) — the live event stream, which carries far more data, has none. This is the cluster's "unbounded growth" risk on the main data plane.

verify:Spill artifacts are never deleted.title: Spill artifacts are never deleted anywhere in the spill stack — unbounded disk growth in the OS temp dir
verify:Spill artifacts are never deleted.detail: `saveTextFile` creates `<root>/session-<hash>/<random>-<name>` on every oversized tool result and there is no delete, purge, TTL, quota or LRU anywhere in packages/spill (grep for `rm`/`unlink`/`purge` over the package returns nothing), nor any cross-package cleanup of the spill store. When `root` is not configured, `privateRoot()` returns a `mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(),'cf-spill-'))` directory that is created lazily once per process and is never removed on shutdown either, so every host boot leaks a new world-adjacent temp tree. The spill seam (packages/spill/spill/src/index.ts) documents that it owns no retention policy and points at `@origin-ai/cf-output-retention`, but that package is the head/tail *preview* retainer, not a file GC — so the ownership of deletion is genuinely unassigned. Long-lived sessions that repeatedly spill large tool output will grow the filesystem without limit.

verify:Baseline instruction load reads e.title: Baseline instruction load reads every candidate file in full before the render budget is applied — no aggregate read cap
verify:Baseline instruction load reads e.detail: `loadBaselineInstructionSet` discovers the user-global file plus every candidate in every directory of the root→cwd chain, then `await readBounded(file, config.maxSourceBytes, ...)` for each. `readBounded` enforces only a *per-file* cap (and only bounds streaming when a `size` is available), and the configured `maxBytes` render budget is applied afterwards in `renderWorkspaceInstructionSet` — so a directory chain containing N near-cap `AGENTS.md` files reads and materializes N × `maxSourceBytes` UTF-8 bytes into JS strings only to then discard most of them. The code itself flags this at line 333 (`TODO(total-instruction-read-bound): enforce an aggregate source budget across a complete baseline or reconciliation batch`). A repo with large AGENTS.md files at several directory levels makes every session start/resume and every instruction reconciliation pay the full cost.

verify:findProjectRoot treats an fs prov.title: findProjectRoot treats an fs provider failure as "no marker" and keeps walking up, silently adopting an ancestor project's instructions
verify:findProjectRoot treats an fs prov.detail: `existsAsMarker` collapses *every* provider exception into `false`, so a transient `ctx.fs` failure on the real root marker makes `findProjectRoot` continue upward past the intended project boundary and return a higher ancestor (or the filesystem root). `discoverInstructionFiles` / `reconcileInstructionContext` then load that ancestor's `AGENTS.md` into the session's context as if it belonged to this project. The adjacent `statFile`/`probeScopeInstruction` code deliberately distinguishes `present`/`absent`/`unavailable` (a tri-state probe) — `existsAsMarker` is the one place that throws that distinction away. The in-code TODO (line 152-153) states the same hazard: "continuing upward can cross into an ancestor project."

verify:Automatic pressure compaction awa.title: Automatic pressure compaction awaits ctx.llm.resolveModelInfo (an adapter round-trip) on every single agent step
verify:Automatic pressure compaction awa.detail: `_registerAutomaticCompaction` installs an `agent/pre-step` hook that always `await this.compactIfNeeded(agent, 'pressure', signal)`. In `compactIfNeeded`, before the cheap `measurement.totalTokens < spec.thresholdTokens` early-out can be evaluated, the code does `const context = (await this.ctx.llm.resolveModelInfo(target.provider, target.model, signal)).context` (line 293). `Llm.resolveModelInfo` forwards to `registration.adapter.resolveModel(...)` (packages/llm/llm/src/index.ts:654-658), i.e. an async adapter-owned resolution, and the result is not cached at this call site. So every step of every agent — including steps that are nowhere near the pressure threshold — pays an adapter resolution plus the resulting microtask/event-loop hop inside the pre-step waterfall. `resolveModelInfo` should be resolved once per routed target (or its `contextWindow` folded into the policy table at switch time) and the threshold test run first.

verify:JSONL append rollback and torn-ta.title: JSONL append rollback and torn-tail repair truncate to a size captured with no inter-process lock, while the format documents a shared root as a legal deployment
verify:JSONL append rollback and torn-ta.detail: `appendLines` records `{ size: before } = await handle.stat()`, writes, fsyncs, and on any write/sync failure calls `rollbackAppend(path, before)` which does `truncate(path, size)`. `commitRepair`/`repair` likewise `truncate(path, offset)` to an offset computed from an earlier read. Both assume this process is the only writer of that artifact — the per-id `serialize()` chain in PersistenceCoordinator is in-process only. Yet format.ts:171 explicitly says of the root: "A configured root may be local or shared; this grouping does not prescribe its deployment." Under any two processes sharing a root, a rollback in host A (whose `before` snapshot predates a successful append by host B) truncates host B's committed events off the log — silent committed-prefix data loss that no revision check can recover, because the events are gone from disk. Either the shared-root claim should be withdrawn, or appends/repairs need an exclusive lock (or size-independent framing).

verify:Every search request re-materiali.title: Every search request re-materializes every attached session's full document set + sha256 fingerprint, and the index rebuilds persisted_docs rows for each persisted session once per process — all on the request path
verify:Every search request re-materiali.detail: `_reconcile` runs on every `searchSessions`/`searchEvents` call. `_observeStable` then, for each live session, runs `observeSession(session.header, session.events)` which does `structuredClone` of every event, `buildSessionEventSearchDocuments` over the whole log, and a `sha256(JSON.stringify({header, events}))` — O(total session bytes) per attached session per search — none of it cached across requests (only the resulting fingerprint is compared against the temp table, which discards the derived documents). For persisted sessions whose revision is new to the index, `_replacePersistedSession` then deletes and re-inserts every `persisted_docs` FTS row inside one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, blocking the whole search service. On a fresh boot with many stored sessions, the first search pays a full corpus (re)index in a single synchronous SQLite transaction.

verify:Session-log ZIP entry paths are b.title: Session-log ZIP entry paths are built from an unvalidated ImageAttachmentRef parsed out of the stored log
verify:Session-log ZIP entry paths are b.detail: `collectImageRefs` walks the raw JSONL of the exported artifact and does `refs.set(String(ref.attachmentId), ref)` with no shape validation; `mediaEntryPath` then interpolates that raw value into the archive path (`media/${String(ref.attachmentId)}.${MEDIA_TYPE_EXTENSIONS[ref.mediaType]}`) and `deps.attachments.readImage(ref)` is called with it. Session ids get `safeSessionIdSegment()` and spill names get `encodeSegment()`, but attachment ids get neither, and an `attachmentId` outside the four known media types silently yields an entry named `media/<id>.undefined`. Exploitability is low today because the local attachment store hard-validates `^sha256:[a-f0-9]{64}$` before serving bytes, so the export fails closed — but the zip path construction is the one place in this file that trusts log-supplied strings, and a non-local/less-strict backend would produce a traversal-shaped entry (`media/../../x.png`) on extraction.

verify:Windows ACL sandbox and process-i.detail: vitest.config.ts:57-65 (`windowsOnlyCoverageExclusions`) removes `packages/sandbox/sandbox-windows-acl/src/**` (2,530 lines: token.rs-equivalents, Win32 ABI table, spawn ACL, workspace SID) and `packages/subprocess/subprocess-local/src/windows-inspector.ts` (325 lines) from the coverage gate on every non-win32 host, and vitest.config.ts:49-51 removes the whole `subprocess/*` tree. verify:correctness category is explicitl.title: correctness category is explicitly off, so no-debugger and every other core correctness rule is dead
verify:correctness category is explicitl.detail: oxlint documents `correctness` as its default-on category ("Code that is outright wrong or useless (default)"). The repo sets it to `"off"` and never re-enables it, so the entire linter is whatever the ~90 hand-listed `typescript/*` rules happen to cover. Empirically, on a probe file the repo config reports `no-unused-vars` and the configured type-aware rules but silently accepts `debugger`; the same file under `-D correctness` reports `no-debugger`. A committed `debugger` statement ships and stalls the CLI at runtime. Because the value is an explicit `off` rather than an omission, a future oxlint bump can never re-enable it either. Nothing else in the gate matrix would catch it: coverage is statement-based, and `lint:contracts-ready` is the only lint step.

verify:isolatedModules is never enabled.title: isolatedModules is never enabled while every consumer is a per-file transpiler
verify:isolatedModules is never enabled.detail: No tsconfig in the repo sets `isolatedModules: true`, and tsconfig.base.json explicitly sets `verbatimModuleSyntax: false`. Every downstream tool is a single-file transpiler that cannot see across-file type information: tsdown/esbuild (`build:lib:*`), Vite/Vitest, tsx (`npm run cf`), and `ts.transpileModule` in vitest.shared.ts:22. Under that toolchain, `export { SomeType }` for a type-only binding (without `export type`) typechecks and then throws `SyntaxError: The requested module does not provide an export named 'SomeType'` at runtime in the built `lib/` output. The only automated proof that package imports resolve at runtime is `builtBinSmokeGate`, which covers ~11 packages out of the ~200 in the workspace.

verify:Five of the seven required PR job.title: Five of the seven required PR jobs have no timeout-minutes
verify:Five of the seven required PR job.detail: `node-24` (line 39), `node-24-coverage` (84), `node-24-consumers` (137), `node-compat` (215) and `python-sdk` (251) declare no `timeout-minutes`, so each inherits GitHub's 360-minute default. These five are exactly the jobs `all-checks-passed.needs` aggregates, so a single hung Vitest worker or a wedged `tsc -b` holds the branch-protection verdict — and every superseding push cancels the run (concurrency `cancel-in-progress: true`, line 19) — for up to six hours per attempt. `windows-native` already demonstrates the intended posture with an explicit 120.

verify:e2e.yml runs on every non-fork PR.title: e2e.yml runs on every non-fork PR but can never gate the merge
verify:e2e.yml runs on every non-fork PR.detail: The comment above `all-checks-passed` explains that `needs` "cannot reach across workflow files" and therefore omits the master-only jobs in ci-master.yml. It does not mention `.github/workflows/e2e.yml`, which triggers on bare `pull_request` (line 34) and therefore runs on every same-repo PR, consuming the `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY_EXTERNAL` secret and exercising the real agent loop end-to-end. Because that job cannot be listed in `needs`, the only status check that can aggregate it is a branch-protection rule naming `e2e` directly — and if that rule is not configured, real-API regressions merge silently. Same applies to `sandbox.yml`'s confinement proofs (though those are master-only by design). Either the e2e job should be folded into a `uses:`/`needs`-reachable workflow, or the omission should be documented alongside the `windows-native` one so the branch-protection requirement is not accidentally dropped.

verify:122 tracked .js/.cjs/.mjs and .co.detail: `ignorePatterns` bans `**/*.js`, `**/*.mjs` and `**/*.config.ts` outright, so 36 tracked `.mjs`/`.cjs` files and 86 tracked `.config.ts` files never see a lint pass — including `scripts/install-lefthook.mjs` (a ~700-line postinstall script that rewrites `.git/config`, registers merge drivers and takes a filesystem lock), `scripts/apply-patches.mjs`, `scripts/verify-built-package-invariants.mjs`, `.github/issue-management/policy.mjs` (executed in CI with a write-capable GitHub App token), and every `vitest*.config.ts` / `vite.config.ts` / `tsdown.config.ts`. verify:GitLab CI has no test, lint or ty.title: GitLab CI has no test, lint or typecheck stage at all
verify:GitLab CI has no test, lint or ty.detail: The pipeline declares only `stages: [build, publish]` and the `workflow:rules` gate restricts runs to tags matching `python-vX.Y.Z`. There is no lint, typecheck, unit-test or coverage job anywhere in the file — the only `build` jobs assemble Python wheels, and the `publish` job uploads them to GitLab's PyPI registry. Anyone opening a merge request against the GitLab mirror merges with literally zero CI, including the wheel publish path that the same file validates only at tag time. If GitLab is purely a package-registry mirror this is defensible, but nothing in the file says so, and the file is the only CI definition a GitLab-side reviewer sees.

verify:Four whole package trees are carv.title: Four whole package trees are carved out of the 100% coverage gate with no TODO
verify:Four whole package trees are carv.detail: The repo enforces a per-file 100% gate, but `coverage.exclude` carries ~95 hand-written globs. Most carry a `TODO(gui): cover and remove` marker so the debt is visible; four do not, and they exclude entire product packages: `packages/extensions/*/src/**/*.{ts,tsx}` (all four extension packages, 44 source files — cordis-host-runner, cordis-client-runner, tool-cordis, ui-cordis), `packages/client/ui-tool/src/*`, `packages/client/ui-slots/src/*`, `packages/client/ui-layout/src/*`, `packages/client/web/src/*` and `packages/host/webserver/src/*`. These are also the packages whose `src/index.ts` / `src/invariant.ts` are separately excluded nearby, so the package is doubly invisible. A new file added under `packages/extensions/*/src/` is never counted, and nothing in the config signals whether that is deliberate policy or forgotten debt. The block has grown to 131 lines, which is the failure mode the per-file gate exists to prevent.

verify:The duplication gate excludes all.title: The duplication gate excludes all test code and all JS, in the loosest mode
verify:The duplication gate excludes all.detail: `npm run duplication` (`jscpd --config .jscpd.json packages scripts`) is a blocking gate in `ci-primary`, `ci-consumers` and `ci-windows-observational`, but the config sets `mode: "mild"` (looser than jscpd's default `strict`), `minTokens: 60` / `minLines: 6` (so a 5-line or 59-token clone is invisible), `ignore: ["**/tests/**"]` (the largest source of copy-paste in the repo), and `format: ["typescript", "tsx"]` — which drops the 36 `.mjs`/`.cjs` files and every `.js` file from the scan. `packages` and `scripts` are also the only two roots scanned, so `apps/cli/src/plugin.ts` and the `website` tree are never checked. A gate that is configured this far below its own detection threshold is closer to dead than to protective.

verify:Model-generated C++ is compiled a.title: Model-generated C++ is compiled and executed with no real sandbox; the static-analysis guard is dead code on this path
verify:Model-generated C++ is compiled a.detail: The flywheel self-improvement loop writes model-emitted code (`solution`, produced by `generate_new_tokens` at line 2394-2395, or the template fallback) into a .cpp file and compiles+runs it via `std::system()` (compile at 1912, execute at 1940 via run_with_timeout). The 'sandbox' is only a temp directory (`get_sandbox_path()`, line 759-763) with no OS-level isolation (no landlock/seccomp/container). Critically, `Sandbox::static_analysis()` — the guard that flags `system(`/`popen(`/`curl|sh` — is never invoked from `sandbox_compile_and_test` or `sandbox_benchmark`; a repo-wide search shows it is called only from tests (tests/test_agi_safety.cpp:112, tests/test_hotswap_compact.cpp:197, tests/test_guard_probes.cpp:165). The only live guardrail is `check_input(task)` (line 2379), which inspects the TASK string, never the generated SOLUTION that is actually compiled and executed. Any model output (or a task crafted to steer generation) achieving a compiling payload runs arbitrary code as the host user. This is the single most exploitable issue in either project.

verify:SafetyGuardrails blocklist is a c.title: SafetyGuardrails blocklist is a case-sensitive literal substring match, trivially bypassable and applied to the wrong input
verify:SafetyGuardrails blocklist is a c.detail: `check_input`/`check_output` guard by `input.find(p)` over a fixed pattern list (`"system(", "popen(", "execve(", "dlopen("`, etc.). `std::string::find` is case-sensitive and matches the exact substring, so `system (` (space before paren), `System(`, or `execvpe(` all slip past. The list also omits common equivalents (`execvp`, `posix_spawn`, `popen` variants with whitespace, shell redirection into interpreters). Combined with the fact that `check_modification` (line 52) delegates entirely to `check_input(change)` and `check_input` is the only gate before the flywheel compiles and runs model output, this guard provides no meaningful containment. It is the sole safety control standing between generated code and `std::system()`, and it is both bypassable and mis-scoped (task-only, per the adjacent finding).

verify:HTTPClient builds a curl command.title: HTTPClient builds a curl command line by string-concatenating the auth token, host, and path, then runs it through popen() — command injection and SSRF
verify:HTTPClient builds a curl command.detail: `auth_token_`, `host`, and `path` are interpolated raw into a shell command passed to `popen()`/`_popen()`. A token containing `"`, `$()`, backticks, or `;` escapes the quoted `-H "Authorization: Bearer ..."` argument and executes arbitrary commands. The same sink appears three times (range_request ~206, get_content_length ~237, get_binary ~280). Additionally the URL is assembled as `"https://" + host + path` with no validation — no scheme/host allowlist, no block on link-local/metadata addresses — so any caller-controlled host yields SSRF against internal services (e.g. 169.254.169.254). `curl -L` also follows redirects to arbitrary destinations. Tokens and URLs should be passed via exec-argv (no shell) or at minimum escaped.

verify:quant_server binds INADDR_ANY wit.title: quant_server binds INADDR_ANY with no authentication whatsoever and reflects Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
verify:quant_server binds INADDR_ANY wit.detail: `QuantHTTPServer` has no auth mechanism at all: no token, no check_auth, nothing — a repo-wide search for auth/token/Authorization in tools/quant_server.cpp returns zero hits. It binds to `INADDR_ANY` (line 150), so any network-reachable client can drive `/api/generate`, `/api/tokenize`, `/api/detokenize`. Every response also sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (line 219 and in send_sse_headers line 233), so a malicious web page in a victim's browser can invoke the inference endpoint cross-origin. The only bound is a 64KB request cap; `max_tokens` is clamped to 4096 but each request allocates a KVCache and runs up to that many forward passes across `num_workers` threads, so unauthenticated remote callers can trivially saturate CPU. This is a shipped tool binary (`EXPOSE 8080` in the Dockerfile).

verify:HTTPServer binds INADDR_ANY and t.title: HTTPServer binds INADDR_ANY and treats an empty auth token as "no auth required" for /v1/* endpoints
verify:HTTPServer binds INADDR_ANY and t.detail: The OpenAI-compatible server binds to `INADDR_ANY` (line 367). `check_auth` (line 254-275) returns `true` immediately when `token.empty()` — and `auth_token_` defaults to empty and is only set via the opt-in `set_auth_token()`. So out of the box the server is world-reachable and completely unauthenticated on `/v1/completions`, `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/models`. Rate limiting is likewise off by default (`rate_limiter_.set_limits(0, 0)` at line 159; `allow()` returns true when `max_rps_ <= 0`). The default posture for a model server should be loopback-only and fail-closed on missing credentials, not open-to-all with auth silently disabled.

verify:WASMDeploy::compile_to_wasm inter.title: WASMDeploy::compile_to_wasm interpolates source_path into a std::system() command with no escaping
verify:WASMDeploy::compile_to_wasm inter.detail: `source_path` is a caller-supplied `std::string` concatenated into `"emcc -O2 -o output.wasm \"" + source_path + "\" 2>&1"` and executed via `std::system()`. Double-quoting does not neutralize an embedded `"`, `$()`, backtick, or newline, so a path like `x"; touch /tmp/pwned; echo "` executes arbitrary commands. The same weak pattern is used in `MobileDeploy::deploy_android` (line 476, concatenating `ANDROID_HOME` into a logged command) and throughout agi_flywheel (see the Windows cmd.exe finding). Paths reaching this API may originate from user- or model-supplied input, so it is a live command-injection sink rather than a theoretical one.

verify:RateLimiter per-IP bucket map gro.title: RateLimiter per-IP bucket map grows without bound — remote memory-exhaustion DoS
verify:RateLimiter per-IP bucket map gro.detail: `RateLimiter::allow()` does `auto& b = buckets_[ip]` (line 124), inserting a new `Bucket` for every distinct client IP with no eviction, TTL, or size cap. The map lives behind a mutex for the process lifetime. Because the server binds INADDR_ANY and `get_client_ip` derives the key from `getpeername`, an attacker who can source traffic from many addresses (botnet, IPv6 privacy rotation, spoofed-source reflection where applicable) forces unbounded `std::unordered_map` growth until memory is exhausted. The correct fix is an LRU/clock eviction or a bounded hash with a fallback bucket. This is reachable only when a positive rate limit is configured (`max_rps_ > 0`), but that is exactly when an operator believes they are protected.

verify:web-fetch-http has no SSRF/privat.title: web-fetch-http has no SSRF/private-network protection, and it is a model-facing tool
verify:web-fetch-http has no SSRF/privat.detail: `validateFetchUrl` enforces only http/https, no embedded credentials, and a length cap — the docstring states "SSRF / private-network blocking is deferred". The provider is wired into the model-facing `web` tool composition (examples/acp-agent/web.cordis.yml registers `@origin-ai/cf-web-fetch-http` alongside `@origin-ai/cf-tool-web`), so a prompt-injected or malicious model can direct a fetch to `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`, `http://127.0.0.1:<admin-port>/`, or RFC1918 hosts and read the response body back into context. The same-origin redirect check (provider.ts:83) only constrains redirects after the first hop; the initial URL is unconstrained. Since this runs in a local agent with the user's network position, the blast radius includes cloud metadata credentials and localhost-only admin panels.

verify:YAML `!!js` nodes are executed vi.title: YAML `!!js` nodes are executed via new Function + eval at config load — arbitrary code execution from any config file
verify:YAML `!!js` nodes are executed vi.detail: `evaluate` builds `new Function('ctx','expr', 'with(ctx){ return eval(expr) }')`, and `interpolate()` walks parsed YAML applying it to every `__jsExpr` node produced by the `!!js` tag (vendor/include/src/index.ts:10-15 registers the tag on the entry-list schema). Any config file in the boot chain — the profile patch file at `$CF_HOME/profiles/<name>/<PROFILE_PATCH_FILENAME>` (loaded by loadOptionalPatches), entry lists, or a repo's `cordis.yml` — can therefore carry `!!js "process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('...')"` and achieve code execution at plugin activation. This is a deliberate Cordis-style feature, but it turns "untrusted config" into "untrusted code": cloning a repo and running `cf` in it executes that repo's `!!js` expressions with the user's privileges. There is no sandbox, no opt-in flag, and no warning at the load site. At minimum this deserves a trust prompt or an explicit allowlist for `!!js` in non-profile config.

verify:Windows execution paths build cmd.title: Windows execution paths build cmd.exe command lines by raw string concatenation of filesystem paths (injection via TEMP)
verify:Windows execution paths build cmd.detail: On _WIN32, `run_with_timeout` (line 1453), `sandbox_benchmark` (lines 1805, 1825) and `sandbox_compile_and_test` (line 1907) interpolate `binary`/`exe_path`/`src_path`/`stdout_file`/`stderr_file` directly into `cmd.exe /c ""<path>" > "<path>" ..."` and `cl.exe ... /Fe"<path>" "<path>"` strings passed to `std::system()`. These paths are derived from `get_sandbox_path()` (line 759-762), which reads the `TEMP` environment variable. A `TEMP` value containing `"`, `&`, `|`, or `^` breaks out of the quoting and executes arbitrary commands with the process's privileges. Notably the POSIX branch of `run_with_timeout` DOES escape (lines 1488-1493 use `escape_path`), so the Windows branch is an inconsistency as well as a hole. Passing these as exec-argv (CreateProcessW with an argv array) rather than a shell string removes the class entirely.

verify:Bearer token comparison uses non-.title: Bearer token comparison uses non-constant-time operator!=, enabling a timing side channel
verify:Bearer token comparison uses non-.detail: `check_auth` compares the presented `Authorization` header against `"Bearer " + token` with `it->second != want`. `std::string::operator!=` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so an attacker who can measure response latency byte-by-byte can recover the API key over many requests. The server is network-reachable (INADDR_ANY) and rate limiting is off by default, so the sampling cost is low. Use `CRYPTO_memcmp`, `std::secure_compare`, or a manual constant-time loop that always scans the full length and accumulates a difference without early exit.

verify:Patched node-pty honors CF_NODE_P.title: Patched node-pty honors CF_NODE_PTY_SPAWN_HELPER, letting env control which binary is executed as the PTY spawn helper
verify:Patched node-pty honors CF_NODE_P.detail: The local patch makes node-pty's unixTerminal.js read `process.env.CF_NODE_PTY_SPAWN_HELPER` and, if set, `path.resolve()` it and use it as the spawn-helper executable — bypassing both the sibling-of-execPath fallback and the packaged `native.dir + '/spawn-helper'`. Any code able to set environment variables in the host process (another plugin, a config `!!js` expression, a wrapper script) can point this at an arbitrary executable that then runs on every PTY spawn, giving a durable code-execution/persistence hook inside the terminal subsystem. The fallback `process.execPath + '-spawn-helper'` (line 19-20) similarly trusts a file adjacent to the Node binary, which on a shared or world-writable install dir is plantable. If the env override is only needed for one embedded-runtime consumer, scope it to that consumer or require an explicit allowlist rather than unconditional env trust.

verify:win32 shell:true forwards unescap.title: win32 shell:true forwards unescaped argv to cmd.exe, so npm arguments corrupt, expand and redirect
verify:win32 shell:true forwards unescap.detail: On win32 the npm forwarder runs through cmd.exe with `shell: true`, and Node builds the command line by simply joining `['npm', ...args].join(' ')` — no quoting or escaping (Node itself emits DEP0190 for exactly this call: "arguments are not escaped, only concatenated"). Every value that reaches this call is user argv, and `anchorPathSpec` deliberately rewrites path specs into absolute paths that commonly contain spaces. Reproduced on this machine with the exact call shape: (1) `add "C:/Users/thaku/my plugin"` — cmd.exe splits at the space and npm receives `C:/Users/thaku/my`, reporting `npm error path C:\Users\thaku\my\package.json` (ENOENT), which breaks the documented `anchorPathSpec` contract in reference/README.md ("Relative path specs ... are anchored to the invoking directory first, so `add .` from a plugin checkout installs that checkout"); (2) `add "x%CD%y"` — cmd expands the environment variable and npm receives `xC:\cfrevy` (`npm error Unsupported URL Type "xc:"`); (3) `add "x>y"` — cmd applies redirection and npm's stdout is written to a file named `y` in the profile directory instead of the terminal (observed: `C:\cfrev\y` containing npm's output), silently creating/truncating a file. `&` and `|` are command separators on the same string. Fix: quote/escape each argv element (or use `windowsVerbatimArguments` with a proper cmd-quoting helper) whenever `shell` is used.

verify:npm-not-found detection is unreac.title: npm-not-found detection is unreachable on win32 — wrong message and wrong exit code
verify:npm-not-found detection is unreac.detail: `result.error.code === 'ENOENT'` is how spawn reports a missing executable, but that only happens when no shell is used. On win32 the code deliberately sets `shell: true`, so the spawned program is always `cmd.exe` (which exists); a missing `npm` instead surfaces as cmd.exe's normal nonzero status with `result.error === undefined`. Verified with the exact call shape and `PATH` stripped to `C:\Windows\System32`: `error: undefined | status: 1`, stderr `"'npm' is not recognized as an internal or external command"`. Consequence on Windows: the guidance at line 137 (`npm not found on PATH — install npm to manage profile plugins`) never prints, the code never returns the documented 127, and instead the generic line 149 (`npm failed in profile directory <dir>`) is printed — which actively misattributes the failure to the profile's allowScripts policy, the very thing reference/README.md promises as the diagnostic for this path. The branch is only reachable on POSIX, i.e. only where it is least needed.

verify:cf plugin creates $CF_HOME before.title: cf plugin creates $CF_HOME before the one-way legacy ~/.dsh migration can ever run
verify:cf plugin creates $CF_HOME before.detail: `runPlugin` resolves the profile directory and calls `initProfile`, whose `mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true })` creates `$CF_HOME` (`~/.cf/profiles/<name>`). The legacy `~/.dsh` -> `~/.cf` migration is invoked from exactly one place in the whole repo — `profile-boot.ts:103` inside `prepareProfile` — which `cf plugin` never reaches (plugin mode uses `resolveProfileDir` + `initProfile` + `readProfileManifest` directly). `migrateLegacyCfHome` is guarded by `if (exists(home)) return 'fresh'` (packages/util/home-paths/src/index.ts:102), so once `~/.cf` exists the migration is permanently skipped. A legacy user whose first command is `cf plugin --profile web add <pkg>` (the documented way to add plugins / create any non-shipped profile) therefore strands all of their `~/.dsh` data — sessions, settings, credentials — forever: every later `cf --profile ...` sees `~/.cf` and returns `'fresh'` without ever consulting the legacy directory. Fix: call `migrateLegacyCfHome()` in `runPlugin` (or in `resolveProfileDir`'s caller path) before `initProfile`.

verify:cf plugin has no help surface at.title: cf plugin has no help surface at all: `cf plugin --help` exits 1 with a wrong message
verify:cf plugin has no help surface at.detail: The root disables its help option at line 126 (`.helpOption(false)`), and commander propagates `_helpOption` to every subcommand through `copyInheritedSettings`, so `plugin` inherits `null` too. `web` re-states `.helpOption(false)` at line 158 (it wants the booted app's help), but `plugin` never re-enables its own — so the plugin mode has no help anywhere. Verified against the real `parseCfArgs`: `['plugin','--help']` and `['plugin','-h']` both return exit 1 printing `error: required option '--profile <name>' not specified`, and `['plugin','--profile','tui','--help']` forwards `--help` to npm rather than showing `cf plugin`'s usage. This contradicts the root behaviour at line 139 (a bare `cf -h`/`cf --help` does print launcher help) and leaves the only command shape advertised in the root help examples (`cf plugin --profile tui add <package>`) with no discoverable flag list. No test in `tests/` covers `cf plugin --help`. Fix: call `.helpOption(true)` (or an explicit help handler) on the `plugin` subcommand, mirroring the root's hand-written help branch.
verify:cf plugin has no help surface at.evidence:
const plugin = program.command('plugin').description('manage a profile\'s plugins by forwarding the remaining arguments to npm in the profile directory')
  plugin
    .requiredOption('--profile <name>', 'the profile whose plugins to manage (initialized on first use)')
    .allowUnknownOption()
    .argument('[args...]', 'npm arguments, forwarded verbatim (install <pkg>, uninstall <pkg>, why <pkg>, ...)')

verify:rejectParentOptions('plugin') is.title: rejectParentOptions('plugin') is dead code for --profile; confusing message instead
verify:rejectParentOptions('plugin') is.detail: Commander runs `_checkForMissingMandatoryOptions()` before the action handler, and `plugin` declares `requiredOption('--profile <name>')`. So for the exact case `rejectParentOptions` was written to catch — a parent-level `--profile` — commander's mandatory-option check fires first and the guard never runs. Verified: `parseCfArgs(['--profile','x','plugin','add','y'])` prints `error: required option '--profile <name>' not specified`, even though the user did type `--profile x`, while the sibling `cf --profile x web` correctly prints the intended diagnostic `error: web takes none of parent --profile, --patch, --dump-config, or --dump-default-config`. The same happens for `['--profile','web','plugin']`. Users get a message telling them to supply an option they already supplied, and the carefully worded guard at lines 148-154 is unreachable for the first option it names. Fix: make `plugin`'s `--profile` non-mandatory and validate it inside the action (after `rejectParentOptions`), or check parent options in a `preAction` hook.

verify:Launcher's agent-presets overlay.title: Launcher's agent-presets overlay overwrites `roots`, discarding every roots value from other patch layers
verify:Launcher's agent-presets overlay.detail: `composeProfile` builds `rows` from `[bundlePatches, profile.patches, homePatches, overlays]`, then pushes a final overlay that spreads that composed config and assigns `roots:` afterwards — so the spread is pointless for `roots` and the key is unconditionally replaced with a single-element array. Per reference/README.md a patch "replaces the targeted row's complete `config` value rather than deep-merging keys", and `roots` is a real config field (`packages/preset/agent-presets/src/index.ts:88`, `z.array(...)`), so it is settable from a bundle, a profile `cordis.patch.yml`, the home `$CF_HOME/cordis.patch.yml`, or a `--patch` overlay — all of which are composed *below* this launcher overlay. Any such `roots` entry (an extra shared preset directory, or a `{ trust: 'user' }` root a deployment needs for authoring — the shape `tests/web-agent-presets.e2e.ts:493-498` itself uses) is silently dropped on every boot, with no warning, so those presets stop being discovered. The shipped base/web patches currently set only `default: standard`, which is why no test catches it. Fix: append the shipped root to the composed `roots` (deduped) instead of replacing the array.

verify:No error boundary around the disp.title: No error boundary around the dispatch; installFailLoud cannot catch a rejected top-level await
verify:No error boundary around the disp.detail: `bin.ts` awaits `runProfile` / calls `runDumpConfig` / `runPlugin` at module top level with no try/catch, and profile-boot installs `installFailLoud` at line 229 — *after* `composeProfile` (line 214), and only as a `unhandledRejection` listener (app-boot `proc.on('unhandledRejection', handler)`). A rejected top-level `await` in an ES module does NOT emit `unhandledRejection`; verified: `node --input-type=module -e "process.on('unhandledRejection',…); await Promise.reject(new Error('boot-boom'))"` exits 1 printing the raw `Error: boot-boom` stack, with the listener never firing, while registering `uncaughtException` instead *does* fire. So for every failure that reaches the top of `bin.ts` — `cf: invalid profile name`, `cf: failed to read overlay …/nope.yml: ENOENT`, a YAML parse error in `cordis.patch.yml`, `cf: profile bundle … declares no cf.bundle`, and `boot()`'s own `cf: plugin tree failed to load: …` — the user gets Node's default uncaught-exception stack dump, the curated `cf: fatal load failure: …` line and the `release` teardown passed at profile-boot.ts:229-231 never run, and the exit path is only incidentally 1. Exit code is correct, but the error UX is a raw V8 stack for ordinary usage/config mistakes, contradicting README.md's claim that these are "reported" cleanly. The built-bin tests only assert `stderr.toContain(...)`, so a stack dump passes them. Fix: wrap the switch in try/catch, print one `cf: <message>` line to stderr, run the release, set `process.exitCode = 1`.

verify:Un-normalized npm status passed s.title: Un-normalized npm status passed straight to process.exit(), which wraps it and can drop trailing stderr
verify:Un-normalized npm status passed s.detail: `plugin.ts:142` does `const exitCode = result.status ?? 1` with no range validation and `bin.ts:42` feeds it directly to `process.exit()`. Observed on this machine with the real npm forwarder: `spawnSync` returned `status: 4294963238` (an out-of-range/`GetExitCodeProcess`-style value from an ENOENT during the space-split case above); `process.exit()` silently truncates out-of-range codes (verified: `process.exit(-1)` and `process.exit(4294963238)` both do not throw and produce a wrapped shell status), so callers see a nonsensical exit code instead of a stable npm/cf code. Second, `process.exit()` does not wait for pending writes: on Windows `process.stderr` attached to a pipe is asynchronous, and `runPlugin` writes `cf: npm failed in profile directory …` plus the git-hosted `allowScripts` hint (lines 149-154) immediately before returning — those diagnostics are at risk of being discarded when stderr is piped (CI, `2>log`). Both this branch and `args.ts:186` would be safer writing `process.exitCode = code` and letting the event loop drain, which is exactly what `case 'dump-config'` and `createProcessShutdown` already do.

verify:A misspelled launcher flag is rep.title: A misspelled launcher flag is reported as "--profile <name> is required"
verify:A misspelled launcher flag is rep.detail: Because the first unknown token starts the app-argument boundary (`allowUnknownOption()` + `passThroughOptions()`, lines 127-129), a typo'd launcher flag never reaches commander's unknown-option handler (and `showSuggestionForTypo` therefore never runs). The action then reports the generic missing-profile error. Verified against the real parser: `cf --profil web`, `cf --porfile web` and `cf --unknown-global-flag` all exit 1 with `error: --profile <name> is required` — telling a user who *did* type a `--profile`-shaped flag that they omitted it, with no hint of which token was unrecognized. The pass-through contract itself is documented and fine; the defect is that the error never names the leading token(s) it could not interpret, which is the single most likely launcher mistake. Fix: when `options.profile === undefined`, include the leading unrecognized `--*` tokens in the message (or suggest the nearest launcher flag) before falling through to the generic text.

verify:allowScripts hint misses npm's ot.title: allowScripts hint misses npm's other git-host shorthands (gitlab:, bitbucket:, git://)
verify:allowScripts hint misses npm's ot.detail: reference/README.md promises that "Git-hosted plugins that ship sources build during install through their `prepare` script, the first `add` fails with npm's `allowScripts` hint (and a cf pointer at the profile's `package.json`)". The regex only matches `git+`, `github:`, and a `.git` URL/fragment. npm also accepts `gitlab:user/repo` and `bitbucket:user/repo` git-host shorthands and plain `git://host/repo.git` — the last is covered by `\.git(?:#|$)`, but `gitlab:`/`bitbucket:` are not, and neither is the bare `user/repo#ref` GitHub form npm resolves to git. For those specs a user gets only the generic `cf: npm failed in profile directory …` and must know npm's allowScripts policy themselves, which is the exact guidance this branch exists to supply. Fix: broaden the pattern to `/^(?:git\+|gitlab:|bitbucket:|[^:/\s]+\/[^/\s]+(?:#|$))|\.git(?:#|$)/`.

verify:A bundle resolution failure is tr.title: A bundle resolution failure is treated as "not a bundle", silently removing it from cf.profile.bundles
verify:A bundle resolution failure is tr.detail: `exportsPatch` collapses *any* `resolveBundleDir` failure into `false` (comment: "npm reported success yet the package is unresolvable — treat as plain"). That boolean feeds both branches of `reconcilePlugins`: line 67 (`isBundle && !plugins.includes`) to add, and line 82/83 (`dependencySet.has(pkg) && !exportsPatch(pkg)`) to *remove* an existing entry. The comment only justifies the add side. So if resolution transiently fails for a package that is already a bundle and is still listed in `dependencies` — e.g. `cf plugin --profile x install --omit=dev` / `--omit=optional` removing an on-disk bundle, a broken/hoisted layout, or a `package.json` that is temporarily unreadable — the entry is spliced out of `cf.profile.bundles` and written back with `writeProfileManifest`, with no diagnostic (the warning at line 70-74 only fires for dependencies that were *not* already present). The profile then boots without that bundle and the reason is never surfaced. Fix: distinguish "resolved but declares no cf.bundle" (removable) from "could not resolve" (leave alone and warn), by returning a tri-state instead of a boolean.

verify:No coverage for cf plugin --help,.title: No coverage for cf plugin --help, npm-missing, or specs containing spaces
verify:No coverage for cf plugin --help,.detail: The plugin-mode tests stop at happy-path arg routing (`tests/args.spec.ts:48-58`) and two manifest-reconciliation e2e cases (`tests/built-bin.e2e.ts:625` and `:674`), both of which use temp paths with no spaces and a locally present npm. Nothing exercises: (a) `cf plugin --help` / `cf plugin -h` (finding: exits 1 with "required option '--profile <name>' not specified"); (b) the `npm not found on PATH` / exit-127 path (finding: unreachable on win32, so a Windows regression there is invisible); (c) a `--profile x add "./some dir"` spec — the temp checkout fixture at `built-bin.e2e.ts:627` is `cf-plugin-checkout-XXXX`, which has no space, so the win32 space-splitting bug in `anchorPathSpec` passes CI. These are exactly the three CLI paths that are currently broken, so the gap is what let them land. Add these three cases; (c) must use a directory name containing a space.
